lessons.plain: Before you choose how big a remote desktop setup needs to be, you need to know how much network it will use at its busiest moment. Azure Virtual Desktop streams each user's screen to them and sends their keyboard and mouse input back, so a slow or lossy connection feels like a slow computer even when the server is fine. Capacity planning means estimating how much bandwidth, how little delay, and how little packet loss the network must provide. The estimate depends on how many people will be connected at the same time and what kind of work they do. It is a figure you check and adjust, not a fixed number.
lessons.guessPrompt: A branch office has 50 people with remote desktops, but only about 20 of them are ever working at the same moment. Would you size the internet link for 50 people or for 20, and why?
lessons.teach:
Bandwidth is how much data a connection can carry each second, usually measured in megabits per second (Mbps). Latency is the time a packet takes to travel from one end to the other, measured in milliseconds (ms). Packet loss is the share of packets that never arrive. An Azure Virtual Desktop session depends on all three, because screen updates, keyboard and mouse input, and any redirected devices travel over a remote display protocol, which is the set of rules that carries the desktop picture to the user. Capacity planning means estimating how much of each the site must support at its busiest moment.

Why it works: each active session needs a fairly steady stream of data while the user works, and that stream grows with screen change, video, and graphics. Concurrency is the number of sessions active at the same time. It, not the total user count, drives the bandwidth you need. Multiply the per-session figure by peak concurrency, then add headroom for spikes and for other traffic sharing the same link.

Worked example. A branch has 40 named users. Peak concurrency is about 60 percent, so 24 sessions are active at once. Assume an average of 2 Mbps per session for mixed office work. Step one: 24 times 2 gives 48 Mbps. Step two: add 30 percent headroom, so 48 times 1.3 is about 62 Mbps. The branch link must sustain about 62 Mbps in the direction that carries screen data to users at peak. Step three: measure round-trip latency from the branch to the chosen Azure region and confirm it sits well under your target, and confirm packet loss is near zero, because loss hurts responsiveness even when bandwidth is plentiful.

Common mistake: sizing from the named user count, or from an average measured on a quiet day. That underestimates peak concurrency and leaves the link saturated at the start of the shift.

Consequence: when a link saturates, screen updates queue, frames drop, and typing lags, so users report a slow desktop even though the session host is healthy. Latency and loss are diagnosed separately from CPU and memory. The per-session figures in this lesson are for practice arithmetic; use current vendor guidance for real sizing.

questions.prompt: A dental clinic has 25 staff who use Azure Virtual Desktop. Peak concurrency is 80 percent, so 20 sessions are active at the busiest time. Each session needs an average of 3 Mbps. Headroom for spikes and other traffic is 25 percent. Step one: 20 x 3 = 60 Mbps of steady session traffic at peak. Step two is missing. Step three: the clinic link must carry the final figure in the direction that sends screen data to users.
choices: Divide 60 by 1.25 to get 48 Mbps of headroom-free traffic
Add 25 percent of the 25 staff, which is 25 Mbps, to get 85 Mbps
Multiply 60 by 1.25 to get 75 Mbps, which is the required link capacity
Multiply 60 by 0.25 to get 15 Mbps of spare capacity
questions.why: Headroom is added by multiplying the peak session total by 1 plus the headroom fraction, so 60 x 1.25 = 75 Mbps is the required figure.

questions.prompt: A warehouse has plenty of bandwidth on its Azure Virtual Desktop link, yet users say typing feels delayed while file transfers are quiet. Which measurements should you check first to explain this?
choices: The total number of named users on the staff list
The average bandwidth recorded on a quiet holiday
Round-trip latency and packet loss between the site and the chosen Azure region
Peak session host CPU and memory only
questions.why: Latency and packet loss affect responsiveness even when bandwidth is ample, and the teaching text says they are diagnosed separately from CPU and memory.

questions.prompt: A law firm has 120 named users. Peak concurrency is 45 percent, the average per session is 1.5 Mbps, and headroom is 20 percent. Which figure is the correct link requirement at peak?
choices: 65 Mbps
97 Mbps
81 Mbps
180 Mbps
questions.why: 120 x 0.45 = 54 concurrent sessions, 54 x 1.5 = 81 Mbps, and 81 x 1.2 = 97.2, which rounds to about 97 Mbps.

questions.prompt: A planner sizes a branch link from an average taken on a quiet day, when only 12 sessions were active, rather than from the busiest period. What is the most likely result?
choices: The link is oversized, so the session hosts run out of CPU
Users see no change because bandwidth is averaged across the whole day
The link is undersized for the busiest period, so screen updates queue and typing lags at the start of the shift
Session hosts need more memory because the link is sitting idle
questions.why: An average from a quiet period underestimates peak concurrency, so the link saturates when the busy shift starts and the desktop feels slow even though the hosts are healthy.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide whether a branch office's internet link is large enough for its Azure Virtual Desktop users. Name one limit or tradeoff in your method.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with peak concurrency, not the headcount, because only the sessions active at the same time load the link. I would estimate a per-session bandwidth based on the workload, multiply by the peak number of sessions, and add headroom for spikes and other traffic on the same connection. Then I would measure round-trip latency to the chosen region and packet loss, since those decide whether the sessions feel responsive. The main limit is that my per-session figure is an estimate, so the result is only as good as the workload assumption. A heavier user, such as one with video calls, can break the plan. I would therefore check real usage over a representative week and treat the number as something to revise.
rubricPoints: Size from peak concurrent sessions, not total named users
Multiply a per-session bandwidth estimate by concurrency and add headroom
Check round-trip latency and packet loss, not only bandwidth
State that per-session estimates depend on workload and need validation

suggested.rationale: A sizing scenario that requires choosing between headcount and concurrency adds the most, and no listed mission or planned engine covers network capacity sizing directly.

lessons.plain: Azure Virtual Desktop lets people use a Windows desktop that runs on a computer in a data center. The computers doing the work are called session hosts. Designing their network means deciding how they reach the company's directory for sign-in and how the service reaches them, without leaving them open to the whole internet. Think of a worker in a locked office who calls out to a service desk when needed, rather than leaving the front door open for anyone to walk in. Getting this right is what makes the desktops both reachable and safe.
lessons.guessPrompt: A session host has no public IP address, and its network security group blocks all inbound traffic from the internet. Can users still connect to it, and what must the host still be able to reach?
lessons.teach:
A session host is a virtual machine that users sign in to and run their desktop or apps on. A virtual network (VNet) is a private network in Azure that holds your VMs. A subnet is a range of addresses inside that VNet. A network security group (NSG) is a set of allow and deny rules applied to traffic entering or leaving a subnet or VM. The Azure Virtual Desktop control plane is the group of Microsoft-run services that brokers user connections. Active Directory is the directory that authenticates users and hosts, and DNS is the name lookup service that turns names like corp.local into addresses.

Why it works: Azure Virtual Desktop uses reverse connect. The session host opens outbound HTTPS connections (TCP 443) to the service, and the user's client connects through that service. Nothing needs to reach the host from the internet, so inbound RDP on TCP 3389 is not required. The network design therefore rests on three things: outbound reach to the required service endpoints, DNS that resolves the domain controllers, and a private path from the VNet to those domain controllers for domain join and sign-in.

Worked example: Session hosts sit in subnet snet-avd in VNet vnet-hub. Step 1: an outbound rule allows TCP 443 to the WindowsVirtualDesktop service tag, so the hosts can reach the broker. Step 2: the VNet's DNS servers are set to the domain controllers, so the hosts resolve corp.local and join the domain. Step 3: no rule allows inbound 3389 from the internet. Result: users connect through the service while the hosts stay private.

Common mistake: adding a broad deny-all outbound rule to the subnet and then wondering why the hosts show as unavailable in the host pool. Consequence: the VMs are running, but the host pool cannot reach them, and users cannot connect.

The rule to hold: a session host needs outbound paths to the service and to the domain, and it needs no open public inbound RDP.

questions.prompt: Lakeside Credit places its session hosts in subnet snet-desk inside VNet vnet-lakeside, and the hosts must join the domain corp.lakeside. Step 1: an outbound NSG rule allows TCP 443 to the WindowsVirtualDesktop service tag, so the hosts can reach the broker. Step 2: this step is missing. Step 3: no inbound rule allows TCP 3389 from the internet. Which choice completes step 2 so the hosts can resolve and join the domain?
choices: Give each session host a public IP address so it can reach the domain controllers.
Open inbound TCP 3389 from the internet so administrators can reach each host directly for domain join.
Add a deny-all outbound rule so traffic to the domain stays private.
Point the VNet's DNS servers at the domain controllers so the domain name resolves.
questions.why: Domain join depends on DNS resolving the domain name to the domain controllers, which is set by pointing the VNet's DNS servers at them, while the other choices either open inbound RDP or block the outbound paths the design needs.

questions.prompt: A team says their session hosts need an inbound rule from the internet on TCP 3389 so users can connect. Under the reverse connect design, what is actually true?
choices: Users connect directly to each host on 3389, so the inbound rule is required.
Inbound rules are only needed when the hosts sit in a different VNet from the domain controllers.
The host must accept inbound traffic on 443 from the service, so the rule should target 443 instead.
The host opens outbound HTTPS on TCP 443 to the service, so no internet inbound RDP rule is needed.
questions.why: With reverse connect the host initiates outbound TCP 443 connections to the service and users connect through the service, so inbound RDP from the internet is not required.

questions.prompt: At Northwind Labs, the security team added a deny-all outbound rule to subnet snet-pool in vnet-nw-east, and the hosts now show as unavailable in the host pool. Which single change most directly restores the hosts' connection to the broker?
choices: Allow outbound UDP 53 to any destination only.
Allow outbound TCP 3389 to the domain controllers.
Allow outbound TCP 443 to the WindowsVirtualDesktop service tag.
Allow inbound TCP 443 from the WindowsVirtualDesktop service tag.
questions.why: The hosts must reach the broker by making outbound TCP 443 connections to the WindowsVirtualDesktop service tag, and the deny-all rule blocks that path, so allowing it restores availability.

questions.prompt: Bramble Freight's hosts can reach the broker, but they cannot join the domain corp.bramble. Their VNet DNS setting still uses the default resolver rather than the domain controllers. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The VNet DNS setting does not point at the domain controllers, so the domain name fails to resolve.
The session host has no public IP, which blocks domain join.
The outbound 443 rule is missing, so the broker cannot be reached.
The subnet NSG allows too many inbound ports.
questions.why: Domain join needs DNS to resolve the domain name to the domain controllers, and since the broker is already reachable the broken piece is the DNS setting rather than the outbound 443 path.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why an Azure Virtual Desktop session host usually needs no inbound RDP rule from the internet, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on outbound-only connectivity.
lessons.modelAnswer: The usual pattern is reverse connect. The session host opens outbound HTTPS connections to the Azure Virtual Desktop service, and the user connects through that service, so nobody needs to reach the host directly from the internet. That means I do not open inbound RDP on 3389, which removes a common attack target. The host still needs outbound paths to the service, to Entra ID sign-in, and to the domain controllers through correct DNS. The tradeoff is that the design depends on outbound rules being right. If a broad deny-all outbound rule or a firewall blocks a required endpoint, the host shows as unavailable even though the VM is healthy. So troubleshooting starts with outbound reachability and DNS, not with inbound ports.
rubricPoints: Reverse connect: the session host opens outbound connections to the service, so inbound RDP from the internet is not needed.
Outbound HTTPS to the AVD service and sign-in endpoints must be allowed, for example via the WindowsVirtualDesktop service tag.
DNS must resolve the domain controllers so the host can domain join and authenticate users.
Tradeoff: correct outbound rules become critical, and a blocked endpoint makes a healthy VM look unavailable.

suggested.rationale: Tracing the path from a session host through its NSG, DNS, and outbound routes to the service is the hands-on skill this objective needs, and no current mission covers Azure networking.

lessons.plain: Remote desktop traffic is the constant stream of screen updates, keystrokes and mouse movements between a person and a computer somewhere else. By default that stream is relayed through a service in the cloud, which adds an extra hop and some delay. RDP Shortpath lets the two ends talk more directly when the network allows it. RDP Multipath lets that direct link use several network routes at once, so one failing route does not freeze the screen. Quality of service, or QoS, is a set of rules that tell network equipment which traffic to handle first when a link is busy. Together these decide how responsive a remote session feels, and planning them means checking the network before promising a good experience.
lessons.guessPrompt: A worker in a branch office connects to a remote desktop hosted in a cloud region. Typing feels laggy, yet large file downloads from the same place run fine. Name one thing on the network path that could explain the lag, and say what you would check first.
lessons.teach: RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol) carries the session between a client and a session host, the virtual machine that runs the user's desktop. By default, the session goes through a cloud gateway that relays traffic, so the host never needs an open inbound port. RDP Shortpath is a feature that adds a direct path between client and host, usually over UDP (a fast protocol that does not wait for confirmation of each packet). Managed Shortpath uses private connectivity such as a VPN or a dedicated link. Public Shortpath works across the internet. To find a direct route, each side learns its public address through STUN (a lookup service that reports your address as the outside world sees it). If a direct route cannot be built, a TURN relay (a server that forwards traffic between two hosts that cannot reach each other) can be used instead. RDP Multipath opens several UDP routes at the same time and spreads traffic across them, so loss on one route does not stall the session. QoS marks packets with a DSCP value (a small code in the packet header) so routers can prioritise interactive traffic. Worked example: the client in a branch office starts on the gateway path. It learns its public address, tries a direct UDP route, and succeeds because outbound UDP is allowed. Latency falls and the session moves to the direct path. Common mistake: enabling Shortpath but blocking outbound UDP in a firewall. The session still connects, silently stays on the gateway path, and users keep reporting lag. Marking packets with QoS also does nothing if the routers in the path ignore those marks. Shortpath and Multipath reduce the number of hops and the impact of loss, and QoS only helps where the network honours the markings.

questions.prompt: A dental practice has twelve staff who use Azure Virtual Desktop clients from the front desk. The admin turns on RDP Shortpath (a feature that adds a direct path between client and session host) for the host pool. Staff still report lag, and the connection logs show every session still on the gateway path. The practice firewall allows DNS but blocks all outbound UDP (a fast protocol that does not wait for each packet to be confirmed) to the internet. Step 1: Shortpath is enabled in the host pool settings. Step 2: The client cannot build a direct route, so the session stays on the gateway. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: Once the direct route forms, the session moves to it and lag drops.
choices: The admin opens inbound UDP on each session host's public address so the gateway can reach the host directly.
The admin turns on RDP Multipath, which removes the need for any direct route because it uses only the gateway.
The admin adds a DSCP mark (a small code in the packet header) to every packet at the firewall so the route is prioritised.
The admin allows outbound UDP from the practice's clients to the internet, so the client can learn its public address and build the direct UDP route.
questions.why: The direct route needs outbound UDP from the client, so allowing that traffic is the step that lets the route form and the session move off the gateway.

questions.prompt: A logistics company's sessions run over a link that drops packets in bursts. Which feature is designed so that loss on one UDP route does not stall the whole session?
choices: STUN lookups that report the client's public address
DSCP marking applied at each router along the path
RDP Multipath, which opens several UDP routes at once and spreads traffic across them
A TURN relay that forwards all traffic through a single server
questions.why: Multipath opens several UDP routes simultaneously and spreads traffic across them, so loss on one route does not stop the session.

questions.prompt: A county council marks its virtual desktop packets with DSCP values, but users on the wide area network still see lag during busy hours. Which explanation best fits what the teaching text says about QoS?
choices: STUN has failed to report the client's public address to the cloud.
The marks are being applied to UDP packets only, which is not allowed.
DSCP marks only work when the session host runs its own gateway.
QoS helps only where the network honours the markings, so routers that ignore them leave the lag unchanged.
questions.why: The teaching text states that marking packets does nothing if the routers in the path ignore those marks, so QoS only helps on networks that honour the markings.

questions.prompt: Two session hosts in a research lab sit behind separate networks that cannot reach each other at all, and no direct route can be built between the client and the host. Which fallback does the teaching text describe for this case?
choices: A TURN relay, which is a server that forwards traffic between two hosts that cannot reach each other
Opening a permanent inbound port on the session host
Managed Shortpath over a dedicated link
Turning on Public Shortpath, which works across the internet
questions.why: The teaching text says a TURN relay can be used when a direct route cannot be built, because it forwards traffic between hosts that cannot reach each other.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how RDP Shortpath differs from the default gateway path, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on Shortpath. Speak as if they have never configured a remote desktop service before.
lessons.modelAnswer: By default a remote session is relayed through a cloud gateway, so every keystroke and screen update takes an extra hop. Shortpath builds a direct UDP route between the client and the session host when it can, usually after both sides discover their public addresses. The main limit is that it depends on the network allowing that direct UDP traffic. If a firewall blocks it, the session still works but quietly stays on the relayed path, so users see the old lag and nothing looks broken. Teams should check which transport a session actually uses before assuming Shortpath is helping. Multipath adds resilience on top, and QoS marking only helps if the network equipment honours it.
rubricPoints: Explains the default gateway relay and the extra hop it adds
Describes Shortpath as a direct UDP route found through address discovery
Names a real limit, such as firewalls blocking UDP or fallback to the relayed path
Notes that QoS markings only help where the network honours them

suggested.rationale: Tracing which path a packet takes, and where a blocked route falls back, is the skill this objective needs and the planned path tracer would train it.

lessons.plain: Azure Private Link is a way to reach a cloud service through a private address inside your own network instead of over the public internet. Think of it as a door to the service that opens only from inside your building, with a private phone number that only your staff can dial. For Azure Virtual Desktop, this means session hosts and the people connecting can reach the AVD service without their traffic crossing the open internet, and you can switch off the public door entirely if you choose. Planning it means deciding which private doors to create, and making sure every name points to the right door.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company wants its virtual desktop sessions to work even if the public internet path to the service is blocked. Before reading anything, what do you think has to change about how the session hosts find and reach the service, and what could go wrong if only one of those changes is made?
lessons.teach:
A private endpoint is a network interface with a private IP address inside your own virtual network. It represents one specific resource in a service, so traffic sent to that address stays on your private network. Azure Private Link is the feature that connects a private endpoint to the service it stands for. A private DNS zone is a name directory: it answers a service's name with an address, and you can link it to a network so that only callers inside that network receive the private answer. For Azure Virtual Desktop, you plan separate private endpoints for the host pool (where session hosts register and accept connections) and for the workspace (where users discover their desktops), and each needs matching DNS records.

Why it works: the private IP is only useful if callers look up the name and get that IP. The DNS link does the steering.

Worked example. A session host sits in subnet 10.1.0.0/24. Step 1: the host pool gets a private endpoint with address 10.1.2.5 in a separate endpoint subnet. Step 2: a private DNS zone is linked to the session host's virtual network and holds a record mapping the host pool's service name to 10.1.2.5. Step 3: the session host asks DNS for that name and receives 10.1.2.5. Step 4: it connects over the private path. If public network access is then disabled, any attempt to reach the public address is refused.

Common mistake: creating the private endpoint but not linking the DNS zone. The name then resolves to the public address, so traffic either fails once public access is disabled or quietly leaves the private network.

Consequence: users see sessions that will not launch, or session hosts show as unavailable, right after public access is turned off. A working private endpoint alone is not enough; the name must resolve to it from every network that needs it.

questions.prompt: Northwind Dental publishes its Azure Virtual Desktop workspace through a private endpoint. The team follows these steps. Step 1: the workspace private endpoint is created in endpoint subnet 172.20.8.0/24 with address 172.20.8.11. Step 2: a private DNS zone is created and linked to the hub virtual network where the branch clients resolve names. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: a branch client looks up the workspace name and receives 172.20.8.11, so it connects privately. Which action completes Step 3?
choices: Create a second private endpoint for the host pool in the same endpoint subnet
Add a DNS record in the private zone that maps the workspace's service name to 172.20.8.11
Move the branch clients into the endpoint subnet 172.20.8.0/24
Enable public network access on the workspace so the name keeps its public answer
questions.why: The name must resolve to the private endpoint's address, and that mapping is a record inside the linked private DNS zone, so adding that record is the missing step.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is a private DNS zone in the context of Azure Virtual Desktop private endpoints?
choices: A subnet that holds the private endpoint network interfaces for the host pool
A rule in the session host image that blocks public internet traffic
A name directory that answers a service's name with an address and can be linked so only chosen networks get the private answer
A managed queue that stores user sign-in requests until a session host is free
questions.why: The teaching text defines a private DNS zone as a name directory that returns addresses, with links controlling which networks receive the private answer.

questions.prompt: A host pool has a private endpoint at 192.168.30.7 and its private DNS zone is linked to the hub network 192.168.10.0/24. A new spoke network 10.50.0.0/16 hosts session hosts that cannot reach the host pool once public access is off. What is the most direct fix?
choices: Link the existing private DNS zone to the spoke virtual network so its lookups return 192.168.30.7
Increase the address space of the spoke to a /8 range
Copy the address 192.168.30.7 into a hosts file on each session host
Re-enable public network access on the host pool for the spoke only
questions.why: Callers in the spoke only receive the private answer if that network is linked to the zone, so linking the existing zone steers their lookups to the endpoint.

questions.prompt: A team turns off public network access for their Azure Virtual Desktop workspace. The private endpoint shows as approved and healthy, yet users in a branch office see sessions that will not launch. The branch network is not linked to the private DNS zone. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The private endpoint has the wrong network interface type
The branch's name lookup still returns the public address, which public access now refuses
The endpoint subnet is too small to hold a second address
The workspace needs a larger number of session hosts before it can accept users
questions.why: Without the zone link the branch resolves the name to the public address, and with public access disabled that path is refused, even though the private endpoint itself is working.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would plan Azure Private Link for an Azure Virtual Desktop host pool. Name one limit or tradeoff of disabling public network access.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by listing every network that needs to reach the service, including the subnet for session hosts and any network where users connect from. For the host pool and the workspace I would create separate private endpoints in a dedicated endpoint subnet, then link a matching private DNS zone to each network so the service name resolves to the private address. I would test name resolution from a session host before changing anything else. One tradeoff is that once public network access is disabled, anyone or anything outside the private paths is locked out, including administrators working from home who have no private route. So I would plan a private connection path for those users first, and keep a tested rollback before switching public access off.
rubricPoints: A private endpoint gives the service a private IP inside your virtual network
Separate endpoints or DNS records are needed for the host pool and the workspace
A linked private DNS zone must make the service name resolve to the private address
Disabling public access has tradeoffs, such as locking out users without a private route

suggested.rationale: Tracing whether a service name resolves to a private address and whether the path stays inside the network is the core skill this objective needs, and the planned virtual network path tracer would practise it.

lessons.plain: Monitoring and troubleshooting network connectivity means keeping watch on whether the path between a user's device and their remote desktop is working, and finding exactly where it breaks when it isn't. Think of a parcel service: you track each stage, and when a parcel is stuck you find the depot where it stopped instead of guessing. In a remote desktop setup, users may see frozen screens, slow typing, or failed sign-ins, and the cause could be the user's own network, the cloud service that relays connections, a firewall rule, or the virtual machine itself. The skill is to measure first, then narrow the problem down one segment at a time.
lessons.guessPrompt: A user says they can start their remote desktop, but the screen freezes every few seconds, while a colleague on the same office network has no problem. Without any tools, name the three places you would check first and say why each one is a likely suspect.
lessons.teach: A session host is the virtual machine that users actually work on. The Azure Virtual Desktop service sits between the user's client and the session host, brokering connections. Reverse connect means the session host opens an outbound, encrypted connection to that service, so you do not need inbound ports open to the internet. A network security group (NSG) is a list of allow and deny rules that filters traffic on a subnet or network card. Flow logs record which traffic was allowed or refused and by which rule. Network Watcher is Azure's set of diagnostic tools. Its connection troubleshoot test sends a probe from a source to a destination and reports whether it arrives and, if not, where it stopped. Round-trip time (the delay for a message to go out and return) and packet loss (messages that never arrive) explain a freezing screen better than a simple up or down check. Azure Monitor collects these metrics, and the Azure Virtual Desktop Insights view summarises host health and per-session latency. Worked example: after a rule change on Monday, session hosts show as unavailable, but sign-in still works. A connection test from a session host to the service on port 443 reports refused. The flow log shows an NSG rule denying outbound traffic to the service tag. Traffic to the service is now blocked, so the fix is to allow that outbound path. Common mistake: opening inbound port 3389 to the internet to fix connectivity. That is rarely needed, it exposes the virtual machine, and it does not address the real block. Consequence: if outbound paths are blocked, session hosts drop out of the pool and users cannot start sessions. Measure each segment before changing rules.

questions.prompt: Lakeside Clinic runs a host pool named pool-clinic-east with three session hosts. Staff say their screens freeze for a few seconds at a time, but they can still sign in and see their desktop. Step 1: the host health view shows all three hosts as available, so the hosts are not down. Step 2: a connection test from one session host to the service on port 443 succeeds, so that path is open. Step 3: the team measures round-trip time from a healthy session host, which averages 45 ms, with packet loss at 0.1 percent. Step 4: the next action, which you must choose, is to compare the same measurements for the affected staff sessions against the healthy host, before any rule is changed. Which action completes the diagnosis?
choices: Add an inbound rule that allows port 3389 from any address so the team can reach the hosts directly.
Restart all three session hosts so the freezing clears on its own without further measurement.
Compare round-trip time and packet loss for the affected sessions against the healthy host to find which sessions are slow.
Delete the network security group on the subnet to see whether the freezing stops.
questions.why: Measuring round-trip time and packet loss for the affected sessions against a healthy baseline isolates which segment is slow without changing any rule first.

questions.prompt: In Azure Virtual Desktop, what does reverse connect mean?
choices: The session host copies its disk contents to the service each night so sessions can resume after a failure.
The session host opens an outbound, encrypted connection to the service, so no inbound internet ports need to be open.
The user's client sends a probe to every session host each minute to confirm it is still reachable.
The service opens an inbound connection into each session host, so the hosts must accept traffic from the internet.
questions.why: Reverse connect is the pattern where the session host initiates an outbound encrypted connection, which removes the need for inbound ports open to the internet.

questions.prompt: A company called Orchid Legal finds that its session hosts are marked available, yet a connection test from a host to the service fails. The test report shows the traffic stopping at the network security group on subnet snet-hosts-02. What is the best next step?
choices: Turn off Network Watcher so that its probes stop adding load to the subnet.
Resize the session hosts to a larger virtual machine size, since a bigger machine will get the traffic through.
Open inbound port 3389 to the internet on the hosts so administrators can troubleshoot from outside.
Check the flow log for the rule that refused the traffic, then allow the outbound path that rule blocks after confirming its scope.
questions.why: The flow log names the denying rule, and correcting that outbound block addresses the real cause rather than exposing the hosts or changing unrelated settings.

questions.prompt: Which measurement best explains why a session screen freezes while the session host still shows as available?
choices: Host CPU and memory percentage alone, because high usage is the only cause of a frozen screen on a running host.
Round-trip time and packet loss on the network path, because delayed or dropped messages can freeze a screen even when the host is up.
Free disk space on the operating system drive, because a full disk is the only thing that stops a display from updating.
Number of users signed in to the pool, because a crowded pool always produces a frozen screen regardless of network timing.
questions.why: Round-trip time and packet loss show whether messages are delayed or lost on the path, which an up or down check cannot reveal.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would tell whether a user's slow remote session is caused by something inside the session host's subnet or by a problem on the path to the service. Name one limit of the tools you would use.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with the session-level picture in Azure Virtual Desktop Insights, which shows round-trip time and whether a session is degraded for everyone or just one user. If latency is high for the whole pool, I suspect the path or the service region. If only one user is affected, I look at their client network first. Next I run a connection troubleshoot test from the session host to the service endpoint, and check the NSG flow logs for any denied outbound traffic. If the test passes and flows are allowed, the problem is more likely inside the virtual machine. The main limit is that these tools only see traffic that passes through Azure. They cannot see the user's home router or the internet provider's routing, so I would need the client-side connection diagnostics to cover that part.
rubricPoints: Separates a pool-wide problem from a single-user problem using session-level latency data
Uses a connection test and NSG flow logs to check the outbound path from the session host
Names a limit, such as the tools not seeing the user's own network or internet routing
Explains that opening inbound ports is not the first fix for connectivity faults

suggested.rationale: Tracing a path hop by hop and finding the first failing segment is the core skill, and the planned virtual network path tracer would let the learner practise exactly that.

lessons.plain: When many people share a computer environment, each person's settings, documents and app data must live somewhere every server can reach. In Azure Virtual Desktop, a user's saved profile is usually kept on a shared network drive in the cloud, so whichever session host they land on loads the same profile. Planning this storage means deciding what kind of storage holds those profiles, how large it must be, how fast it must respond when hundreds of people sign in at once, where it sits geographically, and how safe the copies are. Get these wrong and people wait minutes to sign in or lose their settings. The skill is matching the storage choice to the number of users, their sign-in pattern, and the distance to the servers they use.
lessons.guessPrompt: Imagine 500 people sign in to their virtual desktops between 8:55 and 9:05 every weekday, and each profile is a few gigabytes. What would you check first about where those profiles are stored, and why?
lessons.teach:
A user profile is the collection of settings, desktop data and app data that makes a person's environment their own. Session hosts in Azure Virtual Desktop are often pooled and can be replaced, so a profile cannot live only on the host. Instead it is stored on a file share that every session host can reach over SMB, the standard network file-sharing protocol. Profile containers, usually virtual disk files holding each user's profile, are mounted at sign-in by a component called FSLogix.

Planning storage means answering four questions. Capacity: how many gigabytes will all profiles need, including growth? Performance: how many input and output operations per second (IOPS) and how much latency will the sign-in rush demand, since many users load profiles in the same few minutes? Location: the storage should sit in the same Azure region as the session hosts, because every extra network hop adds delay to every file read. Resilience: how many copies are kept, and where, if the storage fails?

Worked example. A company has 400 users with an average profile container of 6 GB. Capacity is 400 times 6, which is 2,400 GB. Add 25 percent headroom to reach 3,000 GB. Next, 300 users sign in between 08:45 and 09:00, roughly 20 logons a minute. The storage must serve that burst, not just the average day. The plan therefore picks a premium tier in the same region as the hosts, confirms its performance at the chosen size during the burst, and only then accepts the design.

Common mistake: sizing only for total gigabytes and choosing a cheap standard tier because the capacity number looks fine. Storage that passes a capacity check can still be too slow for the morning sign-in peak.

Consequence: slow shared storage makes every sign-in wait for the profile to mount, and users see a spinning screen or a timeout. Planning covers the share's size, speed, region and copy count before any host is built.

questions.prompt: A design firm has 150 users, and the average profile container for each user is 8 GB. Step 1: 150 times 8 gives 1,200 GB. Step 2: add 20 percent headroom, which brings the target to 1,440 GB. Step 3: 120 users sign in between 07:50 and 08:05, so the storage must handle that burst, not only the daily average. Step 4 is missing. Which step completes the plan before the design is accepted?
choices: Choose the cheapest standard tier, because a 1,440 GB total already meets the capacity target.
Place the share in a different region from the session hosts so that one regional outage cannot take down every profile.
Double the 1,440 GB figure to 2,880 GB, since headroom should be at least 100 percent of the total.
Confirm the chosen tier's IOPS and latency at 1,440 GB during the 120-user burst, and only then accept the design.
questions.why: The plan is accepted only after the chosen storage is shown to perform at its size during the sign-in burst, because capacity alone does not prove it is fast enough.

questions.prompt: A small clinic's helpdesk reports that a user's desktop settings disappeared after a pooled session host was rebuilt. Which storage principle explains the problem and the fix?
choices: Profiles should be kept only on each host's local disk, because local disks are fastest.
Profiles are stored inside the host image, so a rebuild from the image restores them.
Profiles belong in the user's email mailbox, which is copied to every host at sign-in.
Profiles must sit on a shared file share that every host can reach over SMB, because pooled hosts can be replaced.
questions.why: Because pooled hosts can be replaced, the profile must live on a shared file share reachable by all hosts over SMB rather than on any one host.

questions.prompt: A logistics company has 90 users, with an average profile container of 10 GB, and wants 30 percent headroom. Which total capacity should the plan target?
choices: 900 GB
questions.why: Multiplying 90 users by 10 GB gives 900 GB, and adding 30 percent of that (270 GB) gives 1,170 GB.

questions.prompt: A retail chain uses a standard tier with plenty of gigabytes in the same region as its session hosts. At 08:30, 200 users sign in and many time out waiting for profiles to mount, even though the total capacity is sufficient. What is the most likely cause and the correct planning response?
choices: The capacity is too small, so the chain should add more gigabytes to the share.
The region is wrong, so the chain should move the share to another continent.
Users are signing in at the same time, so the chain should stagger sign-in into shifts and leave the storage unchanged.
The tier was chosen for capacity alone and cannot meet the burst IOPS and latency, so the plan should check performance at peak and choose a tier that meets it.
questions.why: Capacity can pass while performance fails at the sign-in peak, so the fix is to verify IOPS and latency during the burst and select a tier that meets them.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says we just need enough terabytes for all user profiles and the cheapest storage tier will do. In your own words, explain what else you would check when planning storage for AVD user data, and name one tradeoff of the option you would pick.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would say capacity is only the first check. Multiply users by average profile size and add headroom for growth, but then test the morning sign-in burst, because every session host reads its profile at logon and many reads at once demand speed, not just space. So I would put the profile share in the same region as the session hosts to keep latency low, and choose a tier whose performance at the planned size covers the burst. The tradeoff is cost: higher-performance tiers charge more per gigabyte, and buying extra size just to gain speed can waste money, so I would size against a tested need rather than a guess. I would also decide the copy count and regional resilience, because a failed share blocks every sign-in. The cheapest tier is only right if the burst test passes.
rubricPoints: Capacity estimate comes from users times average profile size, plus growth headroom
Performance must cover the sign-in burst, not just average daily use
Keep storage in the same region as the session hosts to limit latency
Name a tradeoff: higher performance costs more, so size against a tested need
Resilience matters because a storage outage blocks all sign-ins

suggested.rationale: An exam-style sizing scenario with a sign-in burst and a cost tradeoff is best reasoned through rather than read, and no listed mission covers Azure storage.

lessons.plain: FSLogix is a tool that makes a Windows user's profile and settings follow them across remote desktop sessions. Each user's profile lives in a container file, and that file has to sit somewhere every session host can reach quickly. Setting up storage for FSLogix means choosing where those container files live, using a file share that speaks the SMB protocol, and making sure the right people and computers can open only their own files. If the storage is slow or the permissions are wrong, users wait at sign-in or get a blank desktop.
lessons.guessPrompt: If four hundred people share one pool of virtual desktops and each person needs their own saved settings, what two things would you need to get right about the storage before anyone signs in at nine in the morning?
lessons.teach:
FSLogix profile containers are virtual disk files, usually VHD or VHDX, that each hold one user's profile. When the user signs in, the session host attaches that disk over the network, so the storage must be a file share that speaks SMB, the Windows file-sharing protocol. In Azure, the usual home is an Azure Files share. A premium file share is backed by solid-state storage and has lower latency, and its throughput grows with the size you provision, so a small share is slow even when it is nearly empty.

Two permission layers apply, and both must pass. The first is a share-level role, a role-based access control assignment on the storage account that lets a user or group reach the share at all. Users typically receive a data-access role such as Storage File Data SMB Share Contributor. The second is NTFS permissions, the file-level access list inside the share. The common pattern is that the top folder lets users create their own subfolder, and each subfolder is then owned by that user alone. Administrators who must change those file-level lists need a higher, elevated role.

Worked example: four hundred users sign in between 08:55 and 09:05. Each container is about 3 GB, and the share is premium and sized so its throughput covers the logon burst. First, the session host authenticates to the share with Kerberos, the network sign-in protocol that proves identity to Azure Files. Second, the share role lets the user open the share. Third, NTFS lets the user open only their own folder. Fourth, the container mounts and the desktop loads.

Common mistake: sizing the share for capacity and ignoring throughput, so the nine o'clock logon burst stalls. The consequence is that users wait several minutes at sign-in, and when FSLogix cannot open a container, users may land in a temporary profile whose changes are lost at sign-off. A correctly sized premium share with both permission layers set is what keeps profiles intact and logons fast.

questions.prompt: A law firm, Calder and Finch, has 80 staff whose FSLogix profile containers sit on a premium Azure Files share. The share is sized so its throughput covers the morning logon burst. An administrator, Priya, holds only the data-access share role (Storage File Data SMB Share Contributor). She tries to add a helpdesk user to the NTFS list on a staff member's subfolder and is refused. Her steps so far: 1. Her session authenticates to the share with Kerberos. 2. The share-level role lets her open the share. 3. [MISSING STEP] 4. She edits the subfolder's NTFS list and the change succeeds. What belongs in step 3?
choices: She is given a larger premium share so that throughput covers the change.
The share is converted to standard storage so NTFS edits are cached.
Her account is moved into the on-premises domain so Kerberos can verify her.
She is given the elevated role that allows changing file-level permissions.
questions.why: Changing file-level NTFS lists requires a higher elevated role, because the data-access share role only lets her reach the share and not alter its file permissions.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is a FSLogix profile container?
choices: A group policy that decides which apps appear in the start menu.
A local copy of the user's desktop saved on the session host's C drive.
A shared app package that installs software for all users at sign-in.
A virtual disk file holding one user's profile, attached over SMB at sign-in.
questions.why: A profile container is a VHD or VHDX file that holds one user's profile and is attached over the network when the user signs in.

questions.prompt: A premium file share is provisioned at a small size and is almost empty. Three hundred users sign in together at 08:50 and logons stall. What is the most likely cause?
choices: Kerberos is turned off, so every sign-in retries the connection.
The containers are too large and must be split into one file per app.
Free space is high, so Azure holds back spare capacity from the users.
Throughput follows the provisioned size, so the small share cannot deliver burst bandwidth.
questions.why: On a premium share, throughput grows with the provisioned size, so a small share is slow during a burst even when it is nearly empty.

questions.prompt: A dental group has 35 staff on a premium share. Maria's account holds the share-level data-access role and she can open the share, but she cannot open her own subfolder. What is the most likely fix?
choices: Check and correct the NTFS entry on her own subfolder, since the share role does not grant folder-level access.
Increase the share's quota so the folder becomes visible to her account.
Turn off Kerberos on the session host so it falls back to local folders.
Add a higher RBAC role on the storage account so it overrides the folder list.
questions.why: The share role opens the share, but folder access is controlled by the NTFS list, so the entry on her own subfolder must be checked and corrected.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a user with a correct account can still be refused access to an FSLogix profile share, and name one limit or tradeoff of the storage tier you would pick for a large pool.
lessons.modelAnswer: A user can be refused even with a correct account because access to an Azure Files share is checked in two layers. The share-level role on the storage account decides whether the user can reach the share at all, and the NTFS permissions inside the share decide which folders they can open. If the user has the role but their own folder is missing the right NTFS entry, or the reverse, the container will not mount. Kerberos authentication also has to succeed from the session host, so a machine that is not set up for it fails before permissions are even checked. For a large pool, the main tradeoff of premium storage is cost: you pay for provisioned capacity to get throughput, so you must size the share for the sign-in burst, not for the average day, and revisit that size as the pool grows.
rubricPoints: Access is checked in two layers: a share-level role and NTFS permissions on the folder.
Kerberos authentication from the session host must succeed before any permission check matters.
Premium file share throughput scales with provisioned size, so the size must match the logon burst.
Premium storage costs more, so sizing is a tradeoff against cost that must be revisited as the pool grows.

suggested.rationale: An exam-style scenario asking which permission layer or tier fits a logon problem adds the most, since no listed mission covers Azure file share storage.

lessons.plain: A storage account is a managed Azure container for data. In Azure Virtual Desktop it often holds the user profile files that follow each person from one remote desktop to another. Think of it as a shared network drive you do not have to run yourself. Setting it up for this job means choosing the file-share type and speed tier, deciding how each session host proves who it is when it connects, and deciding who may open which folder. Get any of these wrong and users see slow sign-ins, blank desktops, or access-denied errors that look like the desktop itself is broken.
lessons.guessPrompt: If two hundred people sign in to remote desktops each morning and each needs their own settings files loaded within seconds, what would you check first about where those files live: the disk size, the speed of the storage, or who is allowed to read each person's folder?
lessons.teach:
A storage account is the Azure container that holds file shares, blobs and other data. For Azure Virtual Desktop the common use is an Azure file share, which is a folder that other machines reach over SMB (Server Message Block, the Windows file-sharing protocol). FSLogix is a tool that saves a user profile as one disk-image file so it loads quickly at sign-in. Its files are stored on the share. The performance tier decides the speed: standard shares run on hard disks, while premium shares run on solid-state disks and suit many simultaneous sign-ins.

Why it works: each session host connects to the share over SMB and must prove its identity. Identity-based authentication means the share trusts the same directory that signs users in, either Microsoft Entra Domain Services or on-premises Active Directory Domain Services synced to Entra. Access then has two layers. Azure role-based access control (RBAC, a role assigned at the share level) grants a broad right such as Storage File Data SMB Share Contributor. Inside the share, NTFS permissions (the file-system access lists) control individual folders, so each user gets control only over their own profile folder.

Worked example: a pool of 200 users with a premium share in the same region as the hosts. Step 1: create a premium FileStorage account. Step 2: create one file share on it. Step 3: enable identity-based authentication against the domain. Step 4: grant the user group the share-level role. Step 5: set NTFS so each user owns their folder and the admin group keeps access. Step 6: point the FSLogix profile path at the share.

Common mistake: granting the share-level role to everyone and skipping NTFS, or leaving the share open on a public endpoint. Consequence: a session host without the right permission cannot attach the profile, so users get a temporary profile and lose their settings at each sign-out.

Treat the storage account as part of the session host design. A share the hosts cannot reach or cannot authenticate to is a failed sign-in, however good the desktops are.

questions.prompt: A dental clinic group with 35 staff uses light, daytime sign-ins on a standard-tier file share in its own Azure region. The team is building the setup in this order. Step 1: create a Standard-tier storage account in the same region as the session hosts. Step 2: create one file share on that account. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: grant the staff group the share-level role Storage File Data SMB Share Contributor. Step 5: set NTFS permissions so each staff member controls only their own profile folder and the admin group keeps access. Step 6: point the FSLogix profile path at the share. Which step belongs in the blank at Step 3?
choices: Change the performance tier to premium because the share will serve staff at the same time
Enable identity-based authentication so the share trusts the same directory that signs staff in
Assign the Owner role on the storage account to each staff member's personal login
Open the share to a public endpoint so every session host can reach it without signing in
questions.why: Identity-based authentication lets each session host prove its identity against the directory that signs users in, which must happen before the share-level role and NTFS layers can apply.

questions.prompt: A team wants a file share for FSLogix profiles that will serve about 400 users who all sign in during the same ten minutes each morning. Which performance tier fits this load, and why?
choices: Standard, because hard disks are cheaper and sign-in speed does not matter for profiles
Standard, because the tier only changes how much data the share can hold
Premium, because solid-state disks suit many simultaneous sign-ins
Premium, because it removes the need for any NTFS permissions on the share
questions.why: Premium shares run on solid-state disks and suit many simultaneous sign-ins, which matches a burst of 400 users at the same time.

questions.prompt: A contractor group is given the share-level role Storage File Data SMB Share Contributor on a file share that holds the profile folders for all staff. The contractors must not open anyone else's profile folder. Which control stops that?
choices: NTFS permissions on each folder, which limit access inside the share
Removing the contractor group's share-level role, since RBAC cannot be narrowed further
Moving the share to a premium tier, which encrypts each folder per user
Turning on identity-based authentication, which blocks all users by default
questions.why: The share-level role is a broad right, and NTFS permissions on individual folders are the inner layer that restricts each user to their own folder.

questions.prompt: A team creates a file share for FSLogix profiles, grants the user group the share-level role, and leaves out the NTFS step, while also leaving the share open on a public endpoint. What is the consequence the teaching text describes for this mistake?
choices: Each user shares one profile folder, so settings merge automatically at sign-in
Permissions are too broad or incomplete, so sessions may get a temporary profile that loses settings at sign-out
Users see faster sign-in because the share is reachable from anywhere
Users are charged more because public endpoints bill per user
questions.why: Skipping NTFS and opening the share publicly leaves access wrong, so a session host may fail to attach the profile and users get a temporary profile that loses their settings.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would set up storage for user profiles in an Azure Virtual Desktop pool, and name one limit or tradeoff of your choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would create a premium file storage account in the same region as the session hosts, because the profiles are read at every sign-in and latency there is what users feel. I would put one Azure file share on it, join it to identity-based authentication against our directory so the hosts authenticate as the signed-in user, and grant the user group the share-level SMB role. Then I would set NTFS permissions on the share so each user only controls their own profile folder, and the admins keep access for support. The tradeoff is cost: premium storage is billed on provisioned size and is more expensive than standard, so I would size it for the expected pool rather than guessing big. A second limit is that identity-based authentication needs the directory set up correctly first, so the share will not work until that dependency is ready.
rubricPoints: Names premium file shares in a storage account in the same region as the session hosts
Explains identity-based authentication so hosts access the share as the signed-in user
Separates share-level RBAC roles from folder-level NTFS permissions
States a real tradeoff such as cost of premium storage or the directory dependency

suggested.rationale: Choosing the right share type, authentication method and permission layers is a scenario decision that an exam-style situation to reason through teaches better than reading alone, and no existing mission covers Azure storage.

lessons.plain: An Azure Virtual Desktop user needs somewhere to keep files that survive when a session ends, and a shared folder on the network is the usual answer. Azure Files provides that folder in the cloud, reached over the same file-sharing protocol Windows already uses. Implementing a file share means creating the folder, deciding who may open it, and making sure the computers that run user desktops can reach it and sign in as the right person. Think of it as a shared drive many desktops can connect to, with a lock on the door and a guest list on the inside.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose 300 people share one file share that stores their desktop profiles. Would you give everyone the storage account key so they can connect, or let each person connect with their own identity? Why?
lessons.teach: A file share is a named folder served over SMB, the file-sharing protocol Windows uses. A storage account is the Azure resource that holds one or more file shares. A session host is a virtual machine that runs user desktops, and it is the computer that mounts the share on behalf of a signed-in user. Identity-based authentication means the share accepts each user's own directory identity, such as an Active Directory Domain Services or Microsoft Entra Domain Services account, instead of a shared secret. Access control works in two layers. The first is an Azure role assignment, such as a role that lets a user read and write data through SMB. The second is NTFS permissions, the file-level access lists that Windows enforces inside the share. Access is granted only when both layers allow it. Worked example: you enable identity-based authentication on the storage account and join it to your domain. You assign the Azure role to a group called AVD-Users. Ana signs in to a session host, and Windows presents her Kerberos ticket to the share. Azure checks her group's role and allows the connection. Windows then checks the NTFS list on the root folder. If that list lets users create subfolders, her profile folder is created; if not, she gets access denied. A common mistake is handing every session the storage account key, which gives full access to everyone and cannot be audited per person. The consequence on a running pool is serious: when the share refuses a user, that user gets a temporary profile or a failed sign-in, and the fault appears across many sessions at once.

questions.prompt: Northwind Clinic keeps roaming profiles in a share named profiles on the storage account nwclinicstore. The storage account is joined to the clinic domain, and the Azure role that allows SMB data access is assigned to the group Clinic-Staff. Priya, a member of that group, signs in to session host HP-02, and Windows presents her Kerberos ticket (a signed identity token from the domain) to the share. Step 1: Azure checks the role assignment and allows the connection. Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: Priya's profile folder cannot be created and she gets access denied. Which completion fills step 2?
choices: Azure grants Priya a second role assignment of her own so the connection succeeds
Windows checks the NTFS list on the share's root folder for Clinic-Staff, and that list lacks the right to create subfolders
The administrator hands the storage account key to HP-02 so the mount can bypass the NTFS list
Windows rejoins the storage account to the clinic domain so the Kerberos ticket is reissued
questions.why: NTFS permissions are the second layer, enforced by Windows after the Azure role has passed, and they decide whether a subfolder can be created on the root folder.

questions.prompt: In Azure Virtual Desktop, what does a file share served over SMB (the file-sharing protocol Windows uses) do?
choices: It is a named folder hosted in a storage account that session hosts can mount over SMB
It is a shared secret key that gives every session full access to stored files
It is the directory service that checks each user's password at sign-in
It is the virtual machine that runs users' desktops and mounts the share for them
questions.why: A file share is a named folder inside a storage account, and session hosts mount it over SMB; the other options describe a session host, a directory service, or a storage key.

questions.prompt: Northwind's storage account grants the group Clinic-Staff an Azure role that allows SMB data access. The root folder's NTFS list grants Clinic-Staff only read and execute. What happens when a Clinic-Staff member tries to create a new file in the root folder?
choices: Allowed, because the Azure role overrides the NTFS list
Denied, since the NTFS list blocks writing even though the Azure role allows it
Denied by Azure, since roles and NTFS lists never combine
Allowed, because the session host holds the storage account key
questions.why: Access requires both layers to allow it, so the NTFS list's refusal to grant write blocks the file creation even though the Azure role permits SMB access.

questions.prompt: A team needs an audit trail showing which named person opened a profile share on the storage account lakeside. Which access approach fits?
choices: A shared local password typed into each session host by an administrator
Identity-based authentication with a group role, so each person's own account is used
One storage account key copied to every session host so all sessions share it
A single machine account given full rights so every session uses it for the share
questions.why: Identity-based authentication makes each user present their own directory account, which can be recorded per person, while shared keys and shared accounts cannot be audited to an individual.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would let Azure Virtual Desktop users reach their profile file share securely. Name the two permission layers involved and one limit or tradeoff of the approach you choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would enable identity-based authentication on the storage account so each user signs in with their own directory identity, rather than sharing the storage account key. Then I would assign an Azure role that allows SMB data access to a user group, which covers the Azure layer. Next I would set NTFS permissions on the root folder so users can create their own profile folder but cannot read each other's, which covers the file layer. Both layers must allow access. The tradeoff is setup effort: the storage account has to be joined to the directory, and the Kerberos and NTFS configuration must match the domain. If it is wrong, users see access denied at sign-in, so I would test with a pilot user before rolling out to the whole pool.
rubricPoints: Identity-based authentication is preferred over sharing the storage account key, because it gives per-user access and auditing.
Access requires both an Azure role assignment and NTFS permissions on the folder inside the share.
Assign roles to groups rather than individual users to keep administration manageable.
Name a real tradeoff, such as directory join and permission setup effort or the need for a pilot test.
Explain the failure symptom users see when either layer is wrong.

suggested.rationale: Deciding whether a user can reach a share needs layered authorization checks that the planned policy evaluator would practise directly.

lessons.plain: Azure NetApp Files is a managed file storage service from Microsoft, built on the same kind of storage software that NetApp sells for data centres. Instead of running your own file server, you rent a pool of fast storage and carve out network drives, called volumes, from it. Azure Virtual Desktop uses shared storage like this so that user profiles and app data follow a person to any session host they log into. The main reasons to choose this service are high speed, steady performance under heavy load, and features like snapshots for quick recovery. It costs more than a basic file share, so teams choose it when performance or resilience really matters.
lessons.guessPrompt: Imagine 300 people sign in to a pool of virtual desktops at 9 a.m., and each sign-in reads a profile from one shared drive. What do you expect slows down first, and what would you check before the day starts to prevent it?
lessons.teach:
Azure NetApp Files is organised in three layers. A NetApp account is the container for everything. A capacity pool is a block of storage you provision at one service level (Standard, Premium or Ultra), and the service level sets how much throughput each tebibyte (TiB) of capacity can deliver. A volume is a network file share carved out of a pool, and its quota is the size limit you set on it. Because throughput depends on the volume quota and the service level, a bigger volume on a faster level performs better. Two more terms matter. A delegated subnet is a subnet in your virtual network reserved exclusively for this service, with no virtual machines in it. For SMB volumes, which FSLogix profile containers use, the volume must also connect to Active Directory Domain Services so users can authenticate.

Worked example: you need about 1 TiB of profile storage for 150 users with heavy sign-in traffic. Step 1, create a NetApp account. Step 2, create a Premium capacity pool large enough to hold the volume. Step 3, create a delegated subnet and place the pool there. Step 4, create an SMB volume with a 1 TiB quota and join it to your AD domain. Step 5, the volume gets Premium throughput scaled to its quota, and you pay for the provisioned pool. If sign-ins slow down, you raise the volume quota or move to a faster service level rather than adding more session hosts.

Common mistake: sizing only for total gigabytes and ignoring throughput, or putting the service in a subnet that already holds session hosts. Consequence: during a morning logon storm, profile reads queue up, sign-ins hang for minutes, and users see a frozen desktop even though the session host itself is healthy.

Azure NetApp Files gives predictable performance only when the capacity pool, the delegated subnet and the volume quota are sized together.

questions.prompt: A dental group with 40 staff needs 300 GiB (gibibytes, a unit of storage) of SMB file storage for Windows profile containers. SMB is the Windows file-sharing protocol, and a profile container is a file share holding each user's saved desktop profile. The group's only existing subnet already holds its session hosts, the virtual machines users sign in to. The admin follows these steps. Step 1: create a NetApp account. Step 2: create a Standard capacity pool of 1 TiB. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: create an SMB volume with a 300 GiB quota and join it to the Active Directory domain. What belongs in Step 3?
choices: Create a new delegated subnet with no virtual machines in it and place the capacity pool there.
Set the volume quota to 1 TiB so it matches the pool size.
Place the pool in the existing subnet so the session hosts and storage share one network.
Skip the Active Directory join, since the volume is small enough to open without authentication.
questions.why: The service needs a subnet reserved exclusively for it with no virtual machines, so an empty delegated subnet must be created and the pool placed there before the volume is made.

questions.prompt: A team has a 4 TiB capacity pool at the Standard service level and wants more throughput per TiB for its profile volumes. Which change controls that?
choices: Move the pool to a higher service level such as Premium or Ultra.
Connect the volume to a second Active Directory domain.
Add more address space to the delegated subnet.
Rename the NetApp account that holds the pool.
questions.why: The service level sets how much throughput each TiB of capacity can deliver, so raising the level is the control that changes it.

questions.prompt: A network engineer places a new Azure NetApp Files capacity pool in the subnet that already holds three session hosts, reasoning that it keeps all traffic local. What is wrong with this?
choices: Nothing is wrong, since subnets can be shared freely between any services.
Session hosts must sit in their own resource group, so the pool must be moved to another group.
The subnet must be delegated to this service and hold no virtual machines, and the shared subnet breaks that rule.
Capacity pools cannot be larger than 1 TiB, so the placement fails on size.
questions.why: A delegated subnet is reserved exclusively for the service with no virtual machines in it, so a subnet that already holds session hosts is the wrong place for the pool.

questions.prompt: A profile volume with a 2 TiB quota on the Standard service level shows slow sign-ins every weekday morning. Which response fits the teaching model best?
choices: Remove the Active Directory connection so profile reads skip authentication.
Raise the volume quota or move to a faster service level, rather than adding more session hosts.
Add more session hosts to the same pool so logons are spread across more machines.
Shrink the quota to 500 GiB so the volume is easier to manage.
questions.why: Throughput depends on the volume quota and the service level, so slow profile reads are fixed at the storage layer rather than by adding session hosts.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says we should just put FSLogix profiles on a cheap standard file share. In your own words, explain when Azure NetApp Files is worth its extra cost, and name one limit or tradeoff we would accept by choosing it.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would keep the standard share for light workloads and use Azure NetApp Files when many users sign in at once and profile reads are the bottleneck. The service gives high, steady throughput that scales with the volume quota and service level, so logon storms do not queue behind slow reads. The tradeoff is cost and setup: we pay for provisioned pool capacity whether or not it is used, the pool needs its own delegated subnet with no session hosts in it, and SMB volumes must join our Active Directory domain. So before choosing it we would size the quota for throughput, not just gigabytes, and check that the network design leaves room for the dedicated subnet.
rubricPoints: Names the service as managed file storage with capacity pools and volumes, and explains that volumes are sized by quota.
Explains that throughput depends on service level and quota, so performance is chosen by sizing, not only by capacity.
States the networking requirement: a dedicated delegated subnet that holds no session hosts.
Names a real tradeoff such as cost of provisioned capacity or the need for Active Directory connection for SMB.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine makes the learner provision and size Azure NetApp Files, so reading the concepts is the best fit for now.

lessons.plain: Azure is organised in layers, like folders inside folders. A management group is a folder that holds several subscriptions, so a rule set once there applies to all of them. A subscription is a billing and limits boundary: its spending, its quotas on how many virtual machine cores you can start, and its access rules all live there. A resource group is a folder inside a subscription that holds resources sharing a lifecycle. For Azure Virtual Desktop, deciding where host pools, session hosts and their supporting parts sit determines who can manage them, what they cost, and how easily you can remove an environment later.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company runs a test Azure Virtual Desktop environment and a production one that serves a different department. Which pair would you put in separate subscriptions, and which pair would you simply separate with resource groups? Give your gut reason in one sentence.
lessons.teach:
Definitions first. A management group is a container for subscriptions. Policies and role assignments made at a management group flow down to every subscription and resource beneath it. A subscription is a container for resources that also acts as a billing unit and a quota unit: each subscription has its own limits, such as how many virtual machine cores can run in a region. A resource group is a container inside one subscription that holds resources you intend to manage together. Deleting a resource group deletes everything in it, and access can be granted on that group alone.

Why it works: put shared rules where they apply to everything, and split things where they need separate money, limits or blast radius. Session hosts are virtual machines, so they consume compute quota. A busy production pool can exhaust the quota a test pool needs if both sit in one subscription. Separating production from test into different subscriptions keeps their limits and costs apart and lets you give a test team rights without giving them production.

Worked example. A team runs a production host pool for 400 users and a test host pool for validating images. Step one: both subscriptions sit under one management group, so a shared security policy applies to each. Step two: production and test go in separate subscriptions, because scaling test must not starve production of cores. Step three: inside each subscription, the host pool, application group, workspace and session host virtual machines go into one resource group per environment, since they are created, changed and retired together.

Common mistake: putting everything in one resource group because it looks tidy. Then deleting a test resource group also removes a workspace production depends on, or one broad role grant gives everyone rights over everything.

Consequence: without a subscription boundary, a runaway test scale-out can block production from starting new session hosts when users log on in the morning.

questions.prompt: A tutoring company runs a student pool for 90 learners and a separate pool where curriculum writers test new session host images. Step one: both subscriptions sit under one management group, so a shared data-residency policy applies to each. Step two: the student pool and the curriculum-writer pool go into separate subscriptions, because test scale-outs draw on the same virtual machine core quota that students need. Step three is missing: decide how the resources inside each subscription are grouped. Which completion of step three is correct?
choices: Create a separate management group for each pool, because management groups hold the workspace and the session host virtual machines.
Leave each resource in its own resource group so that deleting one never removes anything another part of the service depends on.
Group the host pool, application group, workspace and session host virtual machines for each pool into one resource group per pool, since they are created, changed and retired together.
Put every resource for both pools into one resource group in the student subscription, so a single role grant covers the whole service.
questions.why: Resources that are created, changed and retired together belong in one resource group per environment, inside that environment's subscription, which is the step the scenario leaves open.

questions.prompt: Which container is the right place for a security policy that must apply automatically to every subscription beneath it, including subscriptions created in the future?
choices: An individual session host virtual machine
A management group above those subscriptions
A resource group inside one of the subscriptions
An application group inside the host pool
