questions.why: A management group passes policies and role assignments down to every subscription and resource beneath it, so it is the level that covers current and future subscriptions.

questions.prompt: A development team's image-test pool scales out to 200 cores in the same subscription that hosts a production pool. On Monday morning, production cannot start new session hosts for users logging on. What best explains this?
choices: A management group policy blocked production from using the region it normally uses.
The subscription's virtual machine core quota is shared, and the test scale-out used up the cores production needed.
The production workspace was deleted when the test resource group was cleaned up.
Session hosts do not consume compute quota, so the failure must come from the network.
questions.why: A subscription has its own compute limits, and both pools drew on the same limit, so the test scale-out starved production of cores.

questions.prompt: A contractor needs to manage the session hosts of one host pool, and must have no rights over the production pool that shares the same subscription. Where should the access be granted?
choices: At the root of the whole tenant, so the contractor can see every resource that exists.
At the resource group that holds only that host pool's resources, since access can be granted on that group alone.
At the subscription, because the subscription is where session host quotas are managed.
At the management group above the subscription, so the rights are inherited consistently.
questions.why: Granting access on the resource group that holds only that pool's resources limits the contractor to those resources, whereas higher levels would extend rights beyond the pool.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide between a new subscription and a new resource group for an Azure Virtual Desktop environment, and name one limit or tradeoff of your choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start with what must be separated. If two environments need their own spending limits, their own vCPU quota, or different people allowed to change them, I give each its own subscription. Subscriptions are the boundary for billing and compute quota, so a busy pool in one cannot use up the cores another needs. If resources belong together and change together, such as a host pool, its application group and its session hosts for one environment, I put them in one resource group inside an existing subscription. Management groups sit above both, so a shared security policy reaches every subscription. The tradeoff is overhead: each extra subscription needs its own role assignments, quotas and monitoring, so I only split as far as the limits and access needs justify.
rubricPoints: Management groups hold subscriptions and pass policy and access down to them.
Subscriptions are the boundary for billing and compute quota, so split them when environments need separate limits or costs.
Resource groups hold resources that share a lifecycle and can be deleted or scoped together.
Session hosts and related AVD resources for one environment usually belong together in one resource group.
Each extra subscription adds administrative overhead, so splitting has a cost.

suggested.rationale: Choosing a placement for a given environment is a scenario to reason through, and no listed mission teaches it directly.

lessons.plain: Azure Virtual Desktop lets many people sign in remotely to a shared pool of virtual machines, called session hosts. Each session host runs an operating system, and that choice decides how many people can share one machine, which software and features are available, and what license you must pay for. Recommending an operating system means matching those three things to what the users and the business actually need, rather than picking the newest or most familiar option. It is like choosing between a shared office with many desks and a private room with one occupant.
lessons.guessPrompt: If 40 office workers need to run ordinary office apps on a small number of virtual machines, would you let one person sign in per machine or several at once, and what would you check before deciding?
lessons.teach:
A session host is the virtual machine that users connect to. The operating system (OS) is the software that runs on it. Two families matter here: Windows client editions, such as Windows 11 Enterprise, and Windows Server editions. A multi-session OS lets several users be signed in to the same machine at the same time, each in their own session. A single-session OS serves one user per machine.

Why this matters: sharing drives cost. A multi-session host serves many users, so you need fewer machines per user. A single-session host gives each user a dedicated machine. That suits people who need admin rights, special drivers, or a personal desktop, but it costs more per user.

The logic runs in order. Start with the workload. For standard office apps with shared capacity, Windows 11 Enterprise multi-session is the usual fit. For users who each need their own machine, use Windows 11 Enterprise single-session. Windows Server is chosen when an application or policy requires a server OS. It also supports multiple sessions, but it adds a licensing requirement for remote desktop client access licenses (RDS CALs) on top of the per-user Windows license, so check that before choosing it.

Worked example: 120 call-centre staff use standard apps and have no admin rights. Step one: they can share machines, so multi-session is the candidate. Step two: confirm their apps run on Windows 11 Enterprise. Step three: confirm they hold a qualifying per-user license for multi-session access. Result: Windows 11 Enterprise multi-session.

Common mistake: choosing single-session because it feels safer, then paying for many mostly idle machines. The reverse mistake is choosing Windows Server for convenience without budgeting for RDS CALs.

Consequence: the image you build later must match the chosen OS. Switching OS later means rebuilding the image and often the host pool, so a wrong early choice is expensive in a running system. The OS is settled before any image is built.

questions.prompt: A surveying firm has 15 field engineers. Each one must install a GPS device driver, which requires local admin rights, and each wants a personal desktop with their own saved settings. Step one: because they need admin rights and a dedicated machine, single-session is the candidate. Step two: confirm the surveying software runs on Windows 11 Enterprise. Step three is missing. Result: Windows 11 Enterprise single-session.
choices: Count how many engineers can share one host so you can cut the number of machines.
Check whether the GPS driver or a company policy requires a Windows Server edition, and stay on Windows 11 Enterprise if it does not.
Switch to Windows Server because it is the safer choice for dedicated desktops.
Buy RDS CALs for every engineer before deciding on the operating system.
questions.why: The logic runs in order, and Windows Server is chosen only when an application or policy requires a server OS, so this check confirms the choice of Windows 11 Enterprise.

questions.prompt: A company has 300 data-entry staff who use only standard office apps and have no admin rights. Which operating system choice fits best?
choices: Windows 11 Enterprise multi-session, with several users sharing each host
A single-session host for each user, since it feels safer
Windows 11 Enterprise single-session, one machine per user
Windows Server, chosen by default for any shared workload
questions.why: Standard apps with no admin rights and shared capacity point to Windows 11 Enterprise multi-session, because several users can share one host.

questions.prompt: A firm of 60 claims assessors uses only standard apps and needs no admin rights. Their architect proposes one single-session Windows 11 Enterprise host per assessor because it feels safer. What is the main consequence?
choices: The firm pays for many machines that sit mostly idle, when shared multi-session hosts would need fewer machines.
Users cannot reach their apps because single-session hosts block remote access.
The firm must buy RDS CALs for every assessor before the hosts can start.
The image must be rebuilt every week because single-session hosts cannot be updated.
questions.why: A single-session host gives each user a dedicated machine, which costs more per user, and these assessors do not need one, so shared hosts would be cheaper.

questions.prompt: A company of 40 users runs a line-of-business application that requires a Windows Server edition. Which licensing check must happen before choosing this operating system?
choices: Confirm that the hosts can use single-session mode, which Windows Server does not support.
Confirm that Windows 11 Enterprise is not already installed on the hosts.
Confirm that the images will be stored in a managed disk tier.
Confirm that each user holds RDS CALs on top of the per-user Windows license.
questions.why: Windows Server adds a requirement for RDS CALs on top of the per-user Windows license, so that must be checked before choosing it.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide between a multi-session and a single-session operating system for a new session host pool, and name one limit or tradeoff of the choice you would make.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with how the users work. If they run ordinary office apps and do not need their own admin rights, I would propose Windows 11 Enterprise multi-session, because several people share each machine and we need fewer hosts overall. Then I would check licensing: those users need a qualifying per-user Windows Enterprise or Microsoft 365 license for multi-session access. The tradeoff is that one heavy user can slow down neighbours on the same host, so I would size the hosts and monitor load. If an app needs its own machine, such as one that needs drivers or admin rights, I would put those users in a single-session pool and accept a higher cost per user. I would settle the OS before building the image, because the image has to match it.
rubricPoints: Matches the OS choice to the users' workload and whether they need a shared or dedicated machine.
Names multi-session Windows 11 Enterprise for shared capacity and single-session for dedicated desktops.
Checks license eligibility, including RDS CALs when Windows Server is the chosen OS.
States a tradeoff, such as cost per user against density, or load from heavy users affecting others.
Notes that the session host image must match the chosen OS, so the decision comes first.

suggested.rationale: This objective is a decision framework and product-catalogue knowledge, and no listed mission or planned engine practises it directly.

lessons.plain: Licensing is the paperwork that says who may use a piece of software and under what terms. Azure Virtual Desktop lets many people use Windows in the cloud, often sharing one machine, so before you build anything you must check two things: whether each user already holds an eligible Windows or Microsoft 365 entitlement, and whether the server operating system you choose is licensed for that kind of shared use. Recommending a licensing model means matching the users you have, the operating system you pick, and the cost to the rules that apply. It is like checking every guest has a valid ticket before you open the doors of a shared hall.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company has 200 office staff who each already have a Microsoft 365 subscription, and you plan to give them shared Windows desktops in Azure. Before looking anything up, what would you check first, and why would the Azure VM bill alone not answer the question?
lessons.teach:
A licence is a right to use software. Azure Virtual Desktop, often shortened to AVD, is a managed service that runs Windows desktops and apps for users from Azure virtual machines called session hosts. A session host is a virtual machine that users connect to. There are two broad choices. Windows client multi-session runs the desktop Windows client on a shared host, and it requires each user to hold an eligible per-user entitlement, typically through a Windows Enterprise or certain Microsoft 365 plans. Windows Server session hosts use the server operating system, and users connecting to it need RDS access rights, which come from Remote Desktop Services Client Access Licences (RDS CALs) or from Software Assurance, a paid maintenance add-on. Azure bills the virtual machine's compute, storage and sometimes the operating system, but it does not automatically grant every user the access right.

Worked example: 200 staff each hold an eligible Microsoft 365 plan. Step 1: list users and their current entitlements. Step 2: confirm the 200 are covered for multi-session Windows client. Step 3: a separate group of 30 contractors has no eligible plan, so they need a per-user entitlement or a different desktop model. Step 4: choose the host image and pool layout only after this matching is done.

Common mistake: assuming that because the virtual machine is running in Azure, every connecting user is covered. Consequence in a running system: unlicensed users can still connect, creating a compliance breach that surfaces at audit, and the cost of fixing it often arrives after the pool is already in production. Licensing rules change, so always confirm against current Microsoft terms before committing.

questions.prompt: Ridgeway Clinic plans an Azure Virtual Desktop pool on Windows Server session hosts for 90 reception and billing staff. Step 1: check each person's access right. 70 hold Software Assurance that covers Remote Desktop Services access, and 20 hold no access right at all. Step 2: the 70 are covered for these session hosts. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: choose the host image and pool layout only after the matching is done. Which statement correctly fills Step 3?
choices: Turn on Windows client multi-session so all 90 users share one host without further checks.
Assume the 20 are covered, since Azure bills the virtual machine compute for the pool regardless of who connects.
Remove the 20 accounts from the pool so only covered users remain, because Software Assurance is the only right.
Find the 20 uncovered staff and give each an RDS CAL or move them to another desktop model.
questions.why: Users without an access right must be matched to an RDS CAL or a different model before the image and pool layout are chosen, because Azure billing alone does not grant access.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm runs 12 dispatchers on Windows Server session hosts in Azure, and each dispatcher holds Software Assurance. Which statement is correct about whether these dispatchers can connect?
choices: They can connect, provided each holds an access right from Software Assurance or RDS CALs.
They can connect only if the firm also buys a Windows Enterprise plan for each of them.
They cannot connect, because Azure only allows Windows client multi-session users.
They can connect, because the Azure bill for the virtual machines covers every login.
questions.why: Windows Server session hosts require RDS access rights, which Software Assurance or RDS CALs provide, and the Azure compute bill does not grant that right.

questions.prompt: A small firm reasons that because its session hosts run in Azure and it pays for them, every user who logs in is covered. What is the most likely consequence?
choices: Azure blocks unlicensed users from connecting until the firm buys a licence.
The firm's virtual machines stop billing until the access rights are confirmed.
Unlicensed users can still connect, and a compliance breach may only surface at audit, often after the pool is in production.
Azure automatically reassigns unlicensed users to a free Windows client desktop.
questions.why: Running a virtual machine in Azure does not stop unlicensed users from connecting, so the breach can go unnoticed until an audit, when fixing it is costly.

questions.prompt: Which pairing correctly matches a desktop model to the access route its users need?
choices: Windows client multi-session needs an eligible per-user entitlement, such as certain Windows Enterprise or Microsoft 365 plans; Windows Server session hosts need RDS CALs or Software Assurance.
Both models are covered automatically by the Azure compute bill, so no per-user check is needed.
Windows client multi-session needs RDS CALs; Windows Server session hosts need a Windows Enterprise plan for each user.
Windows Server session hosts need a Microsoft 365 plan; Windows client multi-session needs Software Assurance.
questions.why: Each desktop model has its own access route: a per-user entitlement for multi-session Windows client, and RDS CALs or Software Assurance for Windows Server session hosts.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says, 'We will pick the cheapest Windows image and Azure will sort out the licensing.' Explain to them what licensing decisions an AVD design must settle before choosing a session host image, and name one limit of your own answer.
lessons.modelAnswer: That is not safe. Before choosing an image, you check who the users are and what entitlement each already holds. Windows client multi-session needs each connecting user to have an eligible per-user Windows entitlement, often included in certain Microsoft 365 or Windows Enterprise plans. Windows Server session hosts need RDS access rights for each user, from RDS CALs or Software Assurance. The Azure virtual machine price covers compute and sometimes the operating system, but it does not grant users their access rights automatically. So the image choice follows from the entitlements you already have. One limit of this explanation is that the exact rules for Azure-hosted Windows Server, and which plans count as eligible, change over time, so the team should verify them against current Microsoft terms before buying or deploying.
rubricPoints: Distinguish the operating system licence from the per-user access right that connecting users need.
Explain that Windows client multi-session requires an eligible per-user entitlement for each user.
Explain that Windows Server session hosts need RDS CALs or Software Assurance for users.
State that Azure compute billing does not by itself grant user access rights.
Name a limit: licensing rules and eligible plans change, so verify current terms.

suggested.rationale: Licensing eligibility, plan names and pricing are catalogue-style facts best learned by reading and checking current terms, which no listed mission or planned engine covers.

lessons.plain: A host pool is a set of remote desktop machines, called session hosts, that share the same settings, operating system image, and list of apps users can open. Before building one, you decide three things: what kind of pool it is, how many machines it needs, and how incoming connections are spread across those machines. Getting these wrong means users either wait for a free machine or pay for machines that sit idle. Planning a host pool is mostly about matching the number of machines to the number of people using them at the same time.
lessons.guessPrompt: You expect 200 people to use a remote desktop service, but at most 60 are online at the same moment. Roughly how many machines would you plan for if each machine can handle 12 people at once, and why did you not start from 200?
lessons.teach:
A host pool is a group of session hosts, the virtual machines that run user sessions, that share one configuration and one image. Planning one means choosing the pool type, sizing it, deciding how new sessions are spread across hosts, and choosing the image. A pooled pool lets many users share each host and gives them fresh sessions. A personal pool assigns each user a dedicated host that keeps their changes. Pooled pools cost less per user, so they suit shared workers.

Sizing starts from concurrent users, meaning sessions open at the same moment at peak, not the total number of accounts. Each host has a max session limit, the most sessions it will accept. Divide peak concurrency by that limit, then add spare hosts so one host failure does not remove capacity. Load balancing decides where a new session lands. Breadth-first spreads sessions across hosts, so one failed host affects fewer people. Depth-first fills one host before opening the next, so idle hosts can be shut down to save cost.

Worked example: 200 named users, peak 60 concurrent, max session limit 12. Step 1: 60 divided by 12 is 5 hosts. Step 2: add one spare for a total of 6. Step 3: with breadth-first, each host carries about 10 sessions at peak, leaving room for growth.

Common mistake: sizing from the 200 accounts, or putting finance and design users with different apps in one pool so no single image fits everyone. An undersized pool refuses new sessions at peak. A mixed pool forces one image to carry every app, so an update for one group can break another. Split pools by workload group.

questions.prompt: A call centre has 320 agent accounts and a peak of 95 agents signed in at the same time. Each session host accepts at most 16 sessions. Step 1: 95 divided by 16 is about 5.9. Step 2: [missing step]. Step 3: add one spare host for a total of 7, so one host failure does not remove capacity at peak. What belongs in the missing step?
choices: Keep 5.9 as the host count, because a fractional host can be treated as a partial host with no cost
Divide the 320 accounts by 16 to get 20 hosts, because sizing starts from total users
Round 5.9 up to 6 hosts, because rounding down leaves some sessions with no host to land on
Skip the division and set the host count to the session limit of 16
questions.why: Rounding up to 6 is the correct step because the sessions above 5 full hosts still need somewhere to go at peak, so rounding down would leave people refused.

questions.prompt: Which pool type gives each user a dedicated host that keeps that user's own changes between sessions?
choices: Personal, because each user is assigned a dedicated host
Depth-first, because it fills one host before opening the next
Breadth-first, because it spreads sessions across hosts
Pooled, because it shares each host across many users
questions.why: A personal pool assigns each user a dedicated session host that keeps their changes, while pooled pools share hosts and give fresh sessions.

questions.prompt: A team has 150 user accounts. At peak, 45 sessions are open at the same moment, and each host accepts at most 9 sessions. How many session hosts should the pool have, including one spare host?
choices: 4 hosts, from rounding the peak down and skipping the spare
6 hosts, from dividing 45 by 9 to get 5 and adding one spare
17 hosts, from dividing the 150 accounts by 9
5 hosts, from dividing peak concurrency by the session limit with no spare
questions.why: Peak concurrency of 45 divided by the limit of 9 gives 5 hosts, and adding one spare gives 6; the 150 accounts are not the sizing basis.

questions.prompt: A pool's cost target is the main priority, and the operator wants idle hosts to be shut down outside working hours. Which load-balancing method fits this goal?
choices: Breadth-first, because it spreads sessions so every host stays busy
Depth-first, because it fills one host before opening the next so the rest can be shut down
Round-robin across the account list, because it treats every user equally
Personal assignment, because each user keeps a dedicated host
questions.why: Depth-first load balancing concentrates sessions on as few hosts as possible, leaving others idle and eligible to shut down, which is the cost-saving behaviour described.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would size and split a host pool for a new remote desktop service, and name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start from peak concurrent sessions, not the total user count, and divide that by the max session limit for one host to get the minimum number of hosts. Then I would add at least one spare host so a single failure does not drop capacity. I would split users into separate pools by workload, so each pool runs one image that fits its apps and can be updated without affecting other groups. The tradeoff is cost and management: more pools mean more images to patch and more capacity to keep spare. Choosing depth-first load balancing saves money by letting idle hosts shut down, but it concentrates users on fewer machines, so one failure affects more people at once. I would say that clearly to the team before we commit to a setting.
rubricPoints: Sizes the pool from peak concurrent sessions and the max session limit, not total accounts
Adds spare capacity so one host failure does not remove all headroom
Splits pools by workload or app set so one image fits each pool
Names the tradeoff between breadth-first (spread, resilience) and depth-first (cost, concentration)

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine practises AVD host pool planning, so the learner should read the concepts and sizing arithmetic here.

lessons.plain: Designing an Azure Virtual Desktop setup for performance means choosing how the remote Windows desktops are built and shared, so people get a quick, smooth experience at the number of users you expect. Azure Virtual Desktop lets a company run Windows desktops and apps in Microsoft's cloud and stream them to laptops. Performance depends on the machines that run the sessions, how many people share each machine, and where those machines sit compared with the users. It is like planning a restaurant: the same kitchen can serve a quiet lunch or a packed dinner, but only if you planned staffing, seating, and location for the crowd you actually get.
lessons.guessPrompt: Imagine 50 people must all use one large shared computer at the same time. What happens to each person's speed when that computer is busy, and what could you change to fix it without buying a bigger machine?
lessons.teach:
A host pool is a group of virtual machines, called session hosts, that run user desktop sessions. A session is one user's logged-in desktop. Four settings shape performance. The pool type decides whether users share session hosts (pooled) or each user gets a dedicated one (personal). The max session limit is the number of simultaneous sessions allowed on one session host. The load-balancing setting decides where new sessions land: breadth-first spreads them across hosts, while depth-first fills one host before starting the next. The VM size sets the CPU and memory each host has, and whether it includes a graphics processor. Region sets how far the network traffic must travel between users and the hosts.

Why this works: every session on a host competes for the same CPU, memory, and disk. A limit set too high means every user slows down when the host is busy. A limit set too low wastes money on idle capacity. Breadth-first keeps load even, so one busy host does not hurt everyone, while depth-first lets scaling rules switch off empty hosts to save cost.

Worked example: a call-centre group of 60 users runs light office applications and needs steady responsiveness at 9:00. Step 1: choose a pooled host pool, because the users have similar light workloads. Step 2: load-test one host and set the max session limit to 10. Step 3: at 60 users that needs six hosts at peak, so add spare hosts for failures. Step 4: choose a VM size with enough memory for ten light sessions, and use breadth-first so no host reaches ten while others sit empty.

Common mistake: sizing from the average user instead of the peak hour, or copying a session limit from another pool without measuring it.

Consequence: when a host is oversubscribed, users see freezing and slow logons, and support tickets rise even while the pool itself looks healthy. A well-designed pool keeps the limit, the VM size, and the peak headcount in agreement.

questions.prompt: A law firm has 24 staff who run light document-review apps, so it uses a pooled host pool. Staff are on the system between 8:30 and 9:30, and the firm has measured a max session limit of 6 sessions per host. Step 1: the pool is pooled, because the workloads are similar. Step 2: the max session limit is set to 6, from measurement. Step 3: at 24 users at peak, four session hosts are needed. Step 4 is the missing one, and it must be filled in: choose the load-balancing setting. The firm wants no host to reach its limit while others sit idle, and it does not need scaling rules to switch hosts off overnight. What should Step 4 be?
choices: Raise the max session limit to 12 so fewer hosts run.
Pick a VM size that includes a graphics processor.
Breadth-first: spread new sessions across all hosts.
Depth-first: fill one host before starting the next.
questions.why: Breadth-first keeps load even across hosts, which matches the firm's goal of no host filling up while others sit empty.

questions.prompt: In an Azure Virtual Desktop host pool, what does the max session limit control?
choices: The number of host pools a single user may join.
The number of simultaneous sessions allowed on one session host.
The maximum CPU size of each session host's virtual machine.
The number of Azure regions the pool can span.
questions.why: The max session limit is defined as the number of simultaneous sessions allowed on one session host, so it caps sessions per host, not hosts or regions.

questions.prompt: A pooled host pool must serve 90 users at peak, and the measured max session limit is 12 sessions per host. What is the minimum number of session hosts needed at peak, before adding any spare hosts for failures?
choices: 8 hosts, because 90 divided by 12 is 7.5 and every session needs a host slot.
7 hosts, because 90 divided by 12 rounds down.
90 hosts, because each user needs their own session host.
11 hosts, because 90 divided by 8 gives the number of hosts needed.
questions.why: Dividing 90 by 12 gives 7.5, and since a partial host cannot be used you round up to 8, which is the minimum before spares are added.

questions.prompt: A pooled host pool uses depth-first load balancing and a max session limit of 15. Users on the first session host report freezing, while the other hosts sit almost empty. What is the most likely cause?
choices: Region is too far from users, which affects only the first host.
The limit of 15 is too high for this VM size, and depth-first packs sessions onto one host.
The pool is personal, so each host should only have one user.
Breadth-first is spreading load incorrectly and should be switched off.
questions.why: Depth-first fills one host to its limit before starting the next, so with a limit of 15 that host becomes oversubscribed while the others stay idle, and the limit or VM size needs adjusting.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would set up a host pool for 80 office users who need a responsive desktop at peak times. Name one limit or tradeoff of the choice you make.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with a pooled host pool, since office users share similar light workloads and pooling is cheaper than giving everyone a dedicated machine. I would size from the peak hour, not the average, so I would count how many users log on at once. Then I would load-test one session host to find a safe max session limit, maybe 8 to 10 sessions for light work, and divide peak users by that limit to get the host count, adding spare hosts for failures. I would use breadth-first load balancing so no single host gets crowded. The tradeoff is cost: more spare hosts means a higher bill, but fewer hosts means slow sessions when the pool is busy. I would accept a small amount of spare cost to protect the user experience.
rubricPoints: Chooses pooled or personal based on whether users have similar or specialised workloads
Sizes the pool from peak concurrent users, not the average
Sets the max session limit from measured load, not guessed
Names a real tradeoff such as cost versus responsiveness, or spare capacity versus density

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or engine covers host pool performance design, so an exam-style sizing scenario is the closest practice.

lessons.plain: Before you can give people a remote Windows desktop, you have to decide how much computing power to buy. A session host is a virtual machine that runs the desktops people connect to. Capacity planning means working out how many of those machines you need, how big each one should be, and whether your cloud account allows you to create that many. The main inputs are how many people are signed in at the same time at their busiest, and how many of them one machine can serve before it slows down. You then add spare room so a machine can be patched or fail without users being turned away. Get the numbers wrong and people either wait in line, or the platform refuses to build the machines at all.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team has 300 named users, but at most 90 of them are ever signed in at the same moment. Roughly what number should you plan the session hosts around, and why not 300?
lessons.teach:
A virtual machine (VM) is a computer simulated inside a cloud datacenter. Azure sells VMs in sizes, and each size has a fixed number of virtual CPUs (vCPUs, the processing units the VM can use) and a fixed amount of memory (RAM). A session host is a VM registered to a host pool, which is a group of such VMs that serve the same users. A session is one user's signed-in desktop running on one of those hosts. Concurrency is how many sessions are active at the same moment, and it is usually far lower than the number of named users. Density is how many concurrent sessions one host can carry before users notice slowness. Quota is the limit your subscription sets on how many vCPUs of a given VM family you may run in a region.

Capacity is worked out in three steps. First, estimate peak concurrent sessions for the busiest hour. Second, divide that by the density you have measured for a chosen VM size to get a host count. Third, add spare hosts so that a patch reboot or a failure does not drop capacity below peak. Then multiply the host count by vCPUs per host and compare the total with your regional quota for that VM family.

Worked example. Suppose there are 300 named users and a busiest-hour concurrency of 90 sessions. You choose an 8 vCPU size and plan 6 sessions per host. Ninety divided by six is 15 hosts. Add one spare, giving 16. Sixteen times 8 vCPUs is 128 vCPUs in one VM family and region. If your quota there is 100 vCPUs, the deployment fails partway through, so you request more quota before you build.

Common mistake. Sizing from the 300 named users, or from the concurrency of an average day instead of the peak.

Consequence. If there are too few hosts at 09:00, new sessions queue or fail, and that first wave of logons is the one users remember.

questions.prompt: A firm has 700 named users and a busiest-hour concurrency of 144 sessions. It chooses a 16 vCPU size and plans 12 sessions per host. Dividing 144 by 12 gives 12 hosts. It adds 2 spare hosts, so it has 14 hosts. Each host has 16 vCPUs, so the total is 224 vCPUs in that VM family and region. The firm's regional quota for that family is 200 vCPUs. What is the one remaining step before building?
choices: The 700 named users are the base, so 700 divided by 12 gives the host count and the quota check is unnecessary.
The two spare hosts should be removed, since 200 divided by 16 is 12 hosts and that is enough.
224 exceeds the 200 quota by 24 vCPUs, so the firm must request more quota before building.
The 224 vCPUs fit under the 200 quota, so the deployment can proceed as planned.
questions.why: The last step is to compare the planned vCPU total with the regional quota, and 224 is 24 more than 200, so quota must be raised first.

questions.prompt: A school has 420 named users, a busiest-hour concurrency of 105 sessions, and a measured density of 7 sessions per host. Before adding spare hosts, how many hosts does the first step of sizing give?
choices: 13 hosts, from dividing 105 by 8 as if density were fixed
60 hosts, from dividing the 420 named users by 7
15 hosts, from dividing the 105 peak concurrent sessions by 7
105 hosts, from treating each session as its own host
questions.why: Sizing divides peak concurrent sessions by measured density, so 105 divided by 7 is 15 hosts, and named users are not the base.

questions.prompt: A team sizes its pool from an average-day concurrency of 40 sessions instead of the busiest-hour peak of 110. It measured density at 10 sessions per host and plans 4 hosts. What is the most likely result at the morning peak?
choices: Sessions run normally because the spare host count covers the gap.
The quota is exceeded before any user signs in, so the host pool cannot be created at all.
Users get more vCPUs than planned, so no logon is affected.
Four hosts cannot carry 110 sessions at 10 per host, so about 70 sessions at peak cannot be placed and logons queue or fail.
questions.why: Four hosts at 10 sessions each carry 40 sessions, leaving 70 of the 110 peak sessions without a host, which is the failure case the sizing method is meant to prevent.

questions.prompt: A subscription's quota for a VM family is described as a limit on what, within a region?
choices: vCPUs of a given VM family you may run in that region
Hosts allowed in each session host image
Sessions allowed per host pool
Named users in the tenant
questions.why: Quota caps the number of vCPUs of one VM family you can run in a region, so it is checked by multiplying hosts by vCPUs per host.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would size the session hosts for a new host pool, and name one limit or tradeoff in your method.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with peak concurrent sessions, not total users, because the hosts only need to carry what is active at the busiest moment. I would divide that peak by the number of sessions one VM size can carry at the density we have measured, which gives a host count. I would add one spare host so that a patch reboot or a failure does not push us over capacity. Finally I would multiply hosts by vCPUs per host and compare the total with the regional vCPU quota for that VM family, requesting more quota early if it falls short. The tradeoff is that density is an estimate: a heavier workload or a different VM size changes it, so the numbers need re-checking against real usage data, and a larger spare margin costs money every hour the hosts run.
rubricPoints: Sizes the pool from peak concurrent sessions, not total named users
Divides peak by measured density for a chosen VM size to get host count
Adds spare capacity so patching or failure does not drop below peak
Checks total vCPUs against the regional VM family quota before deploying

suggested.rationale: Sizing a host pool against peak concurrency, density, spare capacity and quota is best learned by reasoning through an exam-style scenario rather than a single console step.

lessons.plain: A host pool is a group of identical virtual machines that people connect to for a remote desktop, somewhat like several identical checkout lanes serving one shop. Each machine in that group is called a session host. In a pooled pool, many people share each session host at once, while in a personal pool each person gets one dedicated machine. Creating a host pool means deciding how many lanes the shop has, what each lane looks like, and how customers are spread across them. Azure lets you do this through a guided form in its web console, which creates the group and its machines together. The form is quick, but each choice you make in it affects capacity, cost, and what users experience later.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose 40 people need to be using a remote desktop at the same moment, and each machine can comfortably handle 10 of them. How many machines would you start with, and what is your reasoning?
lessons.teach:
A host pool is the container for a set of session hosts, which are Windows virtual machines in Azure that users reach over a remote desktop connection. A pooled host pool lets many users share the same session hosts, while a personal host pool assigns one dedicated machine to each user. In the Azure portal you create the pool with a guided wizard. The first part asks for basics such as the subscription, the resource group (a named folder that holds related resources for billing and access control), the region, and the host pool type. It then asks for a max session limit, which caps how many user sessions one host will accept, and a load balancing setting that decides where new sessions go. Breadth-first spreads new sessions across hosts, while depth-first fills one host before opening the next. The session host step then asks for an image, a VM size, how many hosts to create, a naming prefix, the virtual network and subnet, and how the machines join your identity directory. The wizard deploys the pool and its hosts together.

Worked example: you need 40 concurrent users. You set the max session limit to 10 and deploy 4 session hosts. Capacity is 4 times 10, which is 40 sessions. With breadth-first, new sessions land on different hosts, so load stays even.

Common mistake: sizing the pool from total users instead of concurrent users, or forgetting that the region must have enough quota for the VM size you chose. If quota runs out partway through, some hosts deploy and others fail, leaving a half-built pool that users cannot yet reach. Check quota and the image before you press Create.

The sizing choices made in this wizard determine how many sessions the pool can hold, and changing them later usually means rebuilding machines.

questions.prompt: A dental practice called Harbor Dental expects 50 concurrent users and sets the max session limit to 8 sessions per host. Step 1: take the concurrent user count, 50. Step 2: divide 50 by 8, which gives 6.25. Step 3 is missing and you must supply it: turn 6.25 into a whole number of session hosts that still covers all 50 sessions. Which completion is correct?
choices: Round up to 7 hosts, because 7 times 8 is 56, which covers the 50 sessions.
Deploy 8 hosts, because the max session limit is the number of hosts to create.
Round down to 6 hosts, because 6 is the nearest whole number to 6.25.
Deploy 50 hosts, one for each user, because the limit only caps a host and does not reduce the count.
questions.why: Hosts must be whole machines, and rounding up to 7 gives enough capacity (7 times 8 is 56) for 50 concurrent sessions, while rounding down would leave 2 users without a slot.

questions.prompt: In a pooled host pool, what does the load balancing setting called breadth-first do with each new user session?
choices: It sends every new session to the most recently added host.
It spreads new sessions across the hosts so that load stays even.
It holds new sessions in a queue until an administrator assigns a host.
It fills one host up to its max session limit before opening another.
questions.why: Breadth-first places new sessions on different hosts to keep load even, which is the opposite of depth-first, where one host is filled first.

questions.prompt: You create a host pool that should deploy 6 session hosts. The region's quota runs out after 4 hosts are created, and the other 2 fail. What is the most likely state of the pool, and why does it matter?
choices: All 6 hosts deploy anyway, because quota is only checked after the pool has been created.
Users can reach the pool immediately through the 4 hosts that succeeded, at reduced capacity.
The wizard quietly lowers the host count to 4, and the pool serves all users normally from then on.
A half-built pool: some hosts exist but users cannot reach it yet, so quota and the image must be checked before retrying.
questions.why: Quota shortfalls part way through leave a half-built pool that users cannot yet reach, which is why the common mistake warns to check quota and the image before pressing Create.

questions.prompt: Your team wants new sessions to fill the first session host completely before a second host is used, so that spare hosts can be drained and patched during quiet hours. Which load balancing setting fits this goal?
choices: Breadth-first, because it spreads sessions evenly and leaves no host idle.
Personal host pool type, because each user then has a dedicated machine to patch.
A max session limit raised to a very large number, so that one host can take everyone.
Depth-first, because it fills one host before opening the next, leaving the rest free.
questions.why: Depth-first fills one host before opening the next, which leaves the remaining hosts with few or no sessions so they can be drained, whereas breadth-first would spread sessions across all of them.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a host pool and its session hosts relate, and name one limit or tradeoff of creating a pool through the portal wizard rather than through repeatable automation.
lessons.modelAnswer: A host pool is the group, and session hosts are the virtual machines inside it that users actually connect to. Capacity comes from the number of hosts multiplied by the max session limit on each one, so the pool is sized by concurrent users, not total headcount. The portal wizard is quick and good for a first build, and it is easy to see every setting on screen. The limit is repeatability: clicking through the form is hard to record, review, and reproduce exactly, so a second environment or a rebuild may drift from the first. For anything you will need to recreate, the same settings are better captured in a template or script. Also remember that a failed deployment, often caused by quota, can leave a partly built pool, so verify the hosts before handing the pool to users.
rubricPoints: A host pool is a group of session hosts, and users connect to the session hosts
Capacity is hosts multiplied by max session limit, sized on concurrent users
The portal wizard is fast and visible but hard to repeat exactly
A partial deployment, for example from insufficient quota, can leave a broken pool

suggested.rationale: This objective is console steps and wizard settings, which are best learned by reading the choices, and no listed mission or planned engine covers it.

lessons.plain: Instead of clicking through a web portal to build each virtual desktop machine and its group, you can write the setup down as instructions a computer follows. Some tools run a list of commands one after another, like a recipe you follow step by step. Others describe the finished result you want, and the platform works out what to create. This lesson covers the common ways to automate this for Azure Virtual Desktop and when each suits a job. Knowing the difference matters because a repeatable setup is much easier to rebuild, review, and fix after something goes wrong.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you must build the same ten shared desktop machines every month, would you rather keep a list of commands to run by hand each time, or a written description of the finished result that you give to a tool? Which would you trust more after a run fails halfway, and why?
lessons.teach:
A host pool is a group of identical session host virtual machines that users connect to, and a session host is one of those machines. Automating their creation means writing the setup down so a tool can build it. There are two broad styles. Imperative tools, PowerShell and the Azure CLI (a command-line tool), run commands in order: create this, then create that. You control every step, but if the script stops halfway, you must work out what already exists. Declarative tools, ARM templates and Bicep files, describe the wanted end state: one host pool, one application group, four session hosts. ARM is Azure Resource Manager, the service that builds resources, and its templates are JSON files. Bicep is a simpler language that compiles to ARM templates, so Azure processes the same kind of deployment either way. Declarative deployments are repeatable: running the same file again compares the desired state with what exists and changes only what differs. This property is called idempotence.

Worked example. A template takes a parameter, sessionHostCount, set to 4, and you deploy it. Azure creates the host pool, the application group, and four VMs. Next you change the parameter to 6 and deploy again. The engine finds four existing hosts, leaves them alone, and creates two more. A script that loops to create four VMs would instead try to create VMs with names that already exist, fail, or create duplicates.

Common mistake: treating the registration token as permanent. A session host joins a pool using a registration token, which expires, so automation must generate a fresh token when it runs.

Consequence: a host that cannot register sits unusable while still costing money, and users see no desktop. Declarative templates make that drift visible on the next deployment.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm keeps a Bicep file that describes a host pool named hp-depot-west with a desired count of 3 session hosts. Last week 3 hosts were deployed. Someone then deleted one host by hand, so 2 hosts remain. The team runs the same deployment again. Step 1: the engine reads the desired count of 3. Step 2: the engine counts the existing hosts and finds 2. Step 3: [missing step: the engine works out the difference, which is 1 host, and creates exactly one new VM]. Step 4: the two existing hosts are left unchanged. What fills the missing step?
choices: The engine deletes both remaining hosts and rebuilds all three from scratch.
The engine creates three new VMs, because the script always starts the loop from zero.
The engine creates one new VM, because that is the difference between desired and existing.
The engine stops with an error, because a host was removed outside the template.
questions.why: A declarative deployment compares the desired state with what exists and changes only the difference, so one missing host means one new VM.

questions.prompt: A bakery chain writes a PowerShell script that creates a host pool first and then creates five session host VMs one after another. Which description best fits this approach?
choices: It is idempotent by default, so running it again never changes anything that already exists.
It is imperative: the commands run in order, and the author must work out what already exists if the script stops partway.
It compiles to an ARM template before it runs, so it behaves the same as a Bicep file.
It is declarative, so the file describes the end state and the tool works out the steps on its own.
questions.why: A PowerShell script is an imperative tool that runs commands in sequence, so if it stops halfway the author must check what was already created.

questions.prompt: A clinic deploys a declarative template that defines six session hosts. The first run fails after creating four hosts. The team runs the same template again without changing it. What is the most likely outcome?
choices: The engine creates six new hosts, and the four old ones are renamed so the names do not clash.
The engine creates a second host pool with six hosts, because existing resources are never reused.
The engine compares six desired hosts with four existing ones and creates the remaining two, leaving the four alone.
The engine fails immediately, because the template cannot be run twice.
questions.why: Declarative deployments are idempotent, so rerunning the template creates only the missing two hosts and leaves the existing four unchanged.

questions.prompt: A law firm runs a nightly pipeline that creates new session hosts. The pipeline reads a registration token stored in a variable that was created three weeks ago. The new hosts never appear as available in the pool. What is the right fix?
choices: Increase the VM size so the hosts have more memory to register.
Rotate the local administrator password on each new VM.
Make the pipeline generate a fresh registration token each time it runs, before the hosts are created.
Delete the host pool and recreate it, reusing the same old token.
questions.why: Registration tokens expire, so automation must request a new token on every run; the old token is the cause, not the VM size or password.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would use a PowerShell or Azure CLI script rather than a Bicep file to build a host pool, and name one limit of the script approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I'd use a script when the job is a one-off or needs steps a template can't express easily, such as calling an API to fetch a token or running a custom check between steps. A Bicep file is my default for anything I'll rebuild, because it describes the end state and running it again only changes what differs. The limit of a script is that it is imperative: it runs commands in order, so if it fails halfway, the next run may collide with resources that already exist unless I write checks for each one. Scripts also don't record what the environment should look like, so drift can go unnoticed. A template avoids both problems, but it is harder to use for a quick custom step, so I'd combine them when needed.
rubricPoints: Imperative scripts run ordered commands and give full control over each step.
Declarative templates describe the desired end state and suit repeatable rebuilds.
Scripts are fragile on partial failure because re-running may collide with existing resources.
Choosing a tool depends on whether the job is one-off or something to rebuild and review.

suggested.rationale: Choosing between imperative scripts and declarative templates for a given rebuild situation is best practised by reasoning through a scenario, and no listed mission covers it directly.

lessons.plain: A host pool is a named group of identical virtual machines that serve remote desktops or apps to users. Each machine in the group is called a session host. When someone connects, the service picks a machine for them. Configuring the pool means deciding how users share machines and how new connections are spread across them. Configuring each session host means setting how many people it can take, whether it accepts new connections, and what happens when it starts. It works like a hotel front desk: you decide whether guests share rooms or get their own, and how the desk assigns rooms when guests arrive.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company has 40 office workers who all need the same desktop, but only about 10 of them are online at any one time. Would you give each worker a dedicated desktop or share a smaller set of desktops among everyone, and what would you check before deciding?
lessons.teach:
A host pool is a group of session hosts, which are virtual machines that run user sessions. There are two kinds. A pooled host pool lets many users share the same machines, and a personal host pool gives each user a machine of their own. Inside a pooled pool, you choose a load balancing type. Breadth-first spreads new sessions across all available hosts. Depth-first fills one host up to its limit before it moves to the next, which lets idle hosts be switched off to save cost. The max session limit is the number of sessions one host accepts before the service stops sending it new users. In a personal pool, the assignment setting decides whether a user gets a machine automatically on first connect or whether an administrator assigns one directly.

Why does this matter? Each choice trades density against cost and performance. Depth-first packs users tightly, so fewer machines run, but one busy host can slow everyone on it.

Worked example: a pool has three hosts, a max session limit of five, and breadth-first. Session 1 goes to host A, session 2 to host B, session 3 to host C, and session 4 back to host A. Under depth-first, sessions 1 to 5 all land on host A, and host B only receives users once A reaches five.

Common mistake: setting a high max session limit without considering host size. Five heavy users on a small machine can leave all five sessions sluggish.

Consequence in a running system: a session host in drain mode keeps its current sessions but accepts no new ones. This is how you take one host out of rotation for maintenance without cutting off people already working.

Choose the pool type and load balancing method before users arrive, because changing them later changes where every new session lands.

questions.prompt: Fill in the missing step. A pool has hosts W, X and Y, a max session limit of three, and depth-first load balancing. Sessions 1, 2 and 3 land on host W. Session 4 lands on host X. Sessions 5 and 6 also land on host X, so X now holds sessions 4, 5 and 6. Session 7 arrives next. Which host receives it, and what is the step that decides this?
choices: Host Y, because X already holds three sessions, which is its max session limit, so Y is the only host with room
Host X, because depth-first keeps filling the host that received the most recent session
The pool refuses session 7, because depth-first never opens a third host
Host W, because it holds sessions 1 to 3 and depth-first always goes back to the first host
questions.why: Depth-first fills a host up to its max session limit before moving on, and X is already at three, so the next session must go to Y, the only host with a free slot.

questions.prompt: A training company runs a personal host pool with one machine per instructor, 25 instructors in total. Each instructor should get a machine automatically on their first connection, without an administrator choosing one in advance. Which setting fits this need?
choices: Direct assignment by an administrator
Automatic assignment
Breadth-first load balancing
Depth-first load balancing
questions.why: Automatic assignment in a personal pool gives each user a machine on first connect, whereas load balancing settings only apply to pooled pools and direct assignment requires an administrator to choose the machine.

questions.prompt: A pooled host pool uses breadth-first load balancing with six hosts, each of which is a two-core machine. The max session limit is set to 12 on every host. Users report that every session feels slow, even though the pool has plenty of total capacity. What is the most likely cause in the setup?
choices: Personal assignment is set to automatic
Breadth-first spreads sessions too widely across hosts
The max session limit ignores host size, so each small host is overloaded
Drain mode is switched on for all hosts
questions.why: A high max session limit that does not account for host size lets a small machine accept more sessions than it can run well, which is the common mistake the teaching text describes.

questions.prompt: An administrator puts session host HX-07 into drain mode to patch it. One user is already connected to HX-07, and a second user tries to connect. What happens?
choices: Both users are moved to another host immediately
The host leaves the pool, and the connected user loses access to it
The connected user keeps working, and the new user is sent to a different host that has room
The connected user is logged off, and the new user is sent to HX-07
questions.why: Drain mode keeps existing sessions running but stops the host from accepting new ones, so the new user is routed to another host in the pool.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between a pooled host pool with breadth-first load balancing, a pooled pool with depth-first load balancing, and a personal host pool for a call centre of 200 staff who share 60 seats across shifts. Name one limit or tradeoff of your choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with a pooled host pool, because 200 staff sharing 60 seats means people are not using a seat all day, so a dedicated machine per person would waste capacity. Between breadth-first and depth-first, I would pick depth-first if cost is the main concern, since it packs sessions onto fewer hosts and lets empty hosts be shut down. The tradeoff is that a busy host can slow the users on it, so I would set the max session limit with the host size in mind. If each agent needed their own customised setup, I would consider a personal pool instead, but that costs more because every seat needs its own machine. I would also use drain mode before taking any host down for maintenance, so current calls are not cut off.
rubricPoints: Explains that pooled pools share machines when usage is less than seat count.
Distinguishes breadth-first (spread) from depth-first (fill one host first).
Names the tradeoff of depth-first: density and cost versus performance on busy hosts.
Links the max session limit to host size.
Mentions drain mode for maintenance without cutting off current sessions.

suggested.rationale: Choosing a pool type and load balancing method for a stated workload is a reasoning task that a short exam-style scenario teaches better than a reading alone.

lessons.plain: Before people can sign in to a shared desktop that runs in the cloud, the company must have the right to use the Windows software on that machine. Licensing is the set of rules and paperwork that grants that right. For Windows client machines, the main question is whether each user already holds an eligible per-user Windows license, such as an enterprise edition bundled with certain Microsoft 365 plans. For Windows Server machines used as shared desktops, there is a second layer: each person or device connecting also needs a Remote Desktop client access license, often called an RDS CAL. Think of it like a venue needing both a building ticket and a seat ticket for each guest.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company wants twenty staff to share a few cloud desktops running Windows Server. Before any teaching, what do you think each staff member needs in addition to a normal Windows sign-in, and what would you check first?
lessons.teach:
A session host is a virtual machine that users connect to and run their desktop or applications on. Licensing for session hosts answers two questions: does the operating system on the host have the right to be used this way, and does each connecting user or device hold the access right it needs?

Windows client eligibility means the Windows edition on the host is licensed for multi-user or cloud-hosted use. Per-user subscription plans that include an enterprise edition of Windows are the usual route. The license follows the person, so a user covered by a qualifying plan can connect to the shared host without an extra purchase for that host.

RDS CAL stands for Remote Desktop Services client access license. When session hosts run Windows Server, each user or device that connects to the Remote Desktop Session Host role needs an RDS CAL. The server side may also need its own licensing terms, such as Software Assurance or a subscription. Access licenses are counted per user or per device, so you choose the model that matches how people share machines.

Worked example: a company has 40 office staff on a qualifying Microsoft 365 plan and 10 contractors with no Windows license. Step one: list everyone who will connect. Step two: check each person's existing license. Step three: the 40 staff are covered for Windows client hosts under their plan, while the 10 contractors need either a qualifying license or RDS CALs if the hosts run Windows Server.

Common mistake: assuming that an Azure subscription by itself covers every Windows host. The subscription pays for infrastructure, but it does not automatically grant every user the right to connect. Consequence: an unlicensed host or user is found during a compliance review, after the desktops are already in use, which can force a rushed purchase or a rebuild.

Licensing terms change, so the rule you apply is the one stated in the current official licensing documentation.

questions.prompt: Northwind Dental runs Windows Server session hosts with the Remote Desktop Session Host role. Its 18 clinic staff each hold a qualifying per-user Windows plan and connect from their own laptops. Four shared reception thin clients are used all day by different temporary staff, and 3 locum dentists with no Windows license connect from personal devices. Worked steps: Step 1, list everyone and every device that connects: 18 staff, 4 shared thin clients, 3 locums. Step 2, check existing licenses: the 18 staff are covered by their plan for Windows client eligibility, and the 4 thin clients and 3 locums are not. Step 3: ____ . Which completion correctly fills the missing step?
choices: Assume the Azure subscription that pays for the hosts also grants the 4 thin clients and 3 locums the right to connect.
Buy RDS CALs for the 18 staff as well, since a qualifying plan does not cover connecting to a Windows Server host.
Choose the access model that matches the sharing: the thin clients are shared among many people, so count them as devices, and the locums need access licenses counted per user.
Count the 3 locums as a single shared device so only one access license is needed for the whole group.
questions.why: RDS CALs are counted per user or per device, so the choice of model should match how people share machines, which is the step that completes the trace.

questions.prompt: In your own words, what does the Windows client eligibility part of session host licensing attach to?
choices: The RDS CAL count on the Remote Desktop Session Host role.
The Azure subscription that is billed for the host's compute and storage.
The physical hardware of the virtual machine, so moving the host to a new region moves the right with it.
The person, so a user covered by a qualifying plan can connect to a shared host without an extra purchase for that host.
questions.why: The teaching text says the license follows the person under a qualifying per-user plan, not the hardware or the subscription.

questions.prompt: A company runs Windows Server session hosts. Twelve outside consultants connect from personal laptops that have no Windows license. What does the teaching text say these consultants need in order to connect?
choices: RDS CALs counted per user or per device, plus any server-side licensing terms the server needs.
Nothing, because the consultants are not employees of the company that owns the subscription.
A Windows client plan purchased for each host they connect to, since the host is the licensed unit.
Only a server-side Software Assurance agreement, because that covers every connecting device.
questions.why: The text states that Windows Server session hosts need an RDS CAL for each connecting user or device, and the server may also need its own licensing terms.

questions.prompt: A team lead says: our Azure subscription pays for the virtual machines, so every Windows host we run is fully licensed for anyone to connect. What is the flaw in this reasoning?
choices: The subscription pays for infrastructure but does not automatically give each connecting user the right to connect, so each user's license still has to be checked.
The lead is correct, because a paid subscription always covers every user who connects to a Windows host.
Subscriptions only cover Linux hosts, so the Windows hosts must be licensed separately by the operating system vendor.
Windows Server hosts never need any licensing, so the subscription is irrelevant either way.
questions.why: The teaching text warns that an Azure subscription alone does not grant every user the right to connect, which is why each user's license must be checked.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how licensing for shared cloud desktops differs between Windows client session hosts and Windows Server session hosts. Name one limit or tradeoff the team must check before deploying.
lessons.modelAnswer: With Windows client session hosts, the main check is whether each user holds a qualifying per-user Windows license, usually an enterprise edition included in certain Microsoft 365 or similar plans. With Windows Server session hosts, the server edition needs its own licensing, and each user or device that connects to the Remote Desktop Session Host role needs an RDS CAL. The tradeoff is that a client-based design can be simpler when staff already hold eligible plans, while a server-based design adds a per-connection cost and more paperwork. Before deploying, the team should count connecting users or devices, confirm which licenses each already has, and check the current licensing terms, because a host that is out of license can fail a compliance review after users are already relying on it.
rubricPoints: Windows client hosts depend on each user holding a qualifying per-user Windows license
Windows Server session hosts need RDS CALs for each connecting user or device
Subscription costs for infrastructure do not automatically grant user access rights
The team must count connections and check current licensing terms before deployment

suggested.rationale: Licensing eligibility and CAL rules are catalogue-style facts and terms that are best read directly, and no listed mission or planned engine covers them.

lessons.plain: A session host image is a saved master copy of a computer's disk. Azure Virtual Desktop uses it to build many identical remote desktop machines, called session hosts, that people connect to. Making one by hand means you set up a machine the way you want, tidy it so it can be copied, and save it. It's like preparing one perfect laptop and then making a clean backup that new laptops can be installed from. You do it yourself in steps rather than with an automated recipe, which is useful for learning but slower to repeat.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you set up one remote desktop computer perfectly and then want ten identical copies, what would you need to do to the first one before copying it, and why might copying it as-is cause problems?
lessons.teach:
A session host is a virtual machine (VM) that users sign in to remotely. An image is a reusable template built from a VM's disk. A manual image is one you build step by step yourself rather than with an automated pipeline. The process has four ideas. First, a VM starts from a base image, such as a Windows multi-session image from the marketplace. Second, you customise it by installing applications, the FSLogix profile agent, and updates. Third, you generalise it: a tool called Sysprep removes machine-specific identity such as the computer's unique security ID and hardware details, so copies can boot as fresh machines. Fourth, you capture it: after the VM is shut down and deallocated, you save its disk as a managed image or into an image gallery.

Worked example. (1) Deploy a multi-session Windows VM into a test subnet. (2) Sign in, install the line-of-business app, add FSLogix, and apply all updates. (3) Run Sysprep with the generalize, OOBE and shutdown options. (4) Wait until the VM stops, then deallocate it so it is no longer billed for compute. (5) Capture the VM as an image. (6) Create new session hosts from that image in the host pool.

Common mistake: joining the VM to the domain, or restarting it normally after Sysprep, before capture. That can bake in the machine's identity, so copies conflict or fail to finish setup. Consequence in a running system: new session hosts can come up broken, and users are sent to machines that refuse sessions until someone rebuilds the image.

A manual image is only as current as the day it was captured, so every patch cycle means repeating these steps.

questions.prompt: Brightwater Logistics builds a manual session host image for its dispatch team. A manual image is one you build step by step yourself rather than with an automated pipeline. The engineer's trace so far: (1) deploy a multi-session Windows VM from the marketplace base image into test subnet 10.40.2.0/24; (2) sign in, install the dispatch app, install the FSLogix profile agent, and apply all June updates; (3) [step missing]; (4) shut the VM down and deallocate it so compute billing stops; (5) capture the disk as a managed image in the image gallery; (6) create three new session hosts from that image in the host pool. The missing step is the one that removes machine-specific identity, such as the unique security ID, so that copies can boot as fresh machines. What belongs in step (3)?
choices: Restart the VM normally to confirm the June updates have finished installing
Join the VM to the corporate domain so the dispatch app can authenticate users
Run Sysprep with the generalize, OOBE and shutdown options to remove machine identity
Resize the VM to a larger size so the three session hosts have enough memory
questions.why: Sysprep with generalize, OOBE and shutdown is the step that strips the machine's unique identity before capture, and skipping it lets copies conflict when they boot.

questions.prompt: In a manual session host image, what does the generalize step of Sysprep remove, and why does that matter for copies?
choices: It removes the FSLogix profile agent so profiles are not cached twice
It turns off the image gallery so the managed image cannot be shared
It removes machine-specific identity such as the unique security ID, so copies can boot as fresh machines
It deletes the installed applications so the image stays small
questions.why: Generalize strips per-machine identity such as the unique security ID and hardware details, which is what lets each copy from the image come up as a distinct, working machine.

questions.prompt: A team at Crestview Insurance finishes Sysprep on its image VM, then the admin restarts the VM normally to check the claims app before capturing it. Three new session hosts built from the image later fail to accept user sessions. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The claims app needs a higher-performance disk than the marketplace base image provides
The FSLogix profile agent was installed before the updates were applied
The image gallery was not in the same region as the host pool
The normal restart after Sysprep baked the machine's identity into the image, so copies conflict or fail to finish setup
questions.why: Restarting normally after Sysprep and before capture can bake the machine's identity into the image, so copies conflict or fail setup, which leaves session hosts that refuse sessions.

questions.prompt: A manual image was captured on the first day of the month. The security team now asks whether that image still needs to be rebuilt for the next patch cycle. Which statement is correct?
choices: Yes, a manual image is only as current as the day it was captured, so each patch cycle means repeating the build steps
Yes, but only the FSLogix agent needs repeating, because Windows updates are kept in the host pool instead
No, a captured image stays current indefinitely because the base image is updated automatically
No, updates can be applied to running session hosts without touching the image at all
questions.why: A manual image reflects the patch level at capture time and is not refreshed by itself, so each new patch cycle means rebuilding it by repeating the steps.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a manually created session host image is, why the generalisation step is needed before capture, and one limit or tradeoff of building the image by hand compared with an automated approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: A manual session host image is a master disk we build by hand: we deploy a VM from a base Windows multi-session image, install our apps, the FSLogix agent and updates, then shut it down and save it. Before saving, we run Sysprep with generalize so the machine-specific identity is removed; otherwise every host built from the image would carry the same identity and can fail during first boot or conflict on the network. The limit is repeatability. The image is only as current as the day we captured it, and every patch cycle means repeating the steps, which is error-prone and slow. For a team that rebuilds often, an automated image pipeline is usually worth the effort, while the manual route suits learning or a one-off build.
rubricPoints: Describes a manual image as a VM customised by hand, generalised with Sysprep, then captured
Explains that generalisation removes machine-specific identity so copies boot cleanly
Names the tradeoff of manual builds: repeatability, speed and staleness after updates
Mentions that the VM must be stopped and deallocated before capture

suggested.rationale: The steps are console and tool workflow with no listed mission that builds a VM image, so reading the sequence and then explaining it fits best.

lessons.plain: A session host image is the saved template that every shared Windows desktop in a virtual desktop pool starts from. Azure VM Image Builder is a managed Azure service that builds that template for you. You describe a starting image, list the steps that customize it, and say where the finished result should be stored. The service creates a temporary build machine, runs your steps, prepares the machine to be copied, and publishes the image. You get the same result every time instead of a hand-built machine nobody can reproduce.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you install an app and apply Windows updates by hand on one machine, then build ten more machines from it, what could go wrong with those ten, and how would you prevent it?
lessons.teach:
Start with the terms. A session host is a Windows virtual machine that users connect to and share. A session host image is the template those machines are created from. Azure VM Image Builder is the managed service that produces that image from a recipe called an image template. The template has three parts. The source is the starting Windows image, taken from the marketplace or from a gallery. Customizers are ordered steps, such as running a PowerShell script, installing applications, applying Windows updates and restarting. Distribution is where the finished image is published, for example as a version in an Azure Compute Gallery, which is a library that stores and versions images.

Why it works: the build runs on a temporary virtual machine that the service creates and later deletes. Because every step is written down and runs in the same order, rebuilding the template gives the same result, and each result is a version you can keep and roll back to.

Worked example. Step 1: the service creates a build machine from the source Windows image. Step 2: a script installs the line-of-business app. Step 3: updates are applied and the machine restarts. Step 4: a final step runs Sysprep, the Windows tool that generalizes the machine by removing its unique identity so it can be copied. Step 5: the result is published as version 1.0.0 in the gallery. Session hosts built later from that version are identical.

Common mistake: skipping the generalize step, or running the build with an identity that lacks permission to write to the gallery, so the build fails late or copies one machine's identity into every host.

Consequence: if a faulty image is published and new hosts are created from it, every new session host inherits the fault. That is why versions are kept and the previous one stays available for rollback.

The image builder lets a team change the session host image on purpose, in one defined place, and reproduce it exactly.

questions.prompt: A regional insurance firm, Harbor Claims, builds its session host image with Azure VM Image Builder. The image template has four steps so far. Step 1: the source is version 3.0.2 of a Windows 11 multi-session image from the firm's gallery. Step 2: a PowerShell customizer installs the claims tool, version 4.8. Step 3: a customizer applies Windows updates and restarts the build machine. Step 4: a final customizer runs Sysprep to generalize the machine. Step 5 is missing.
