The team wants the finished image published as version 2.1.0 in the Azure Compute Gallery named gal-claims-eu, so new session hosts can be created from it.
choices: Publish the finished image as version 2.1.0 in the Azure Compute Gallery named gal-claims-eu, which is the distribution part
Create a session host directly from the build machine and skip distribution, since a running machine can be copied
Delete the build machine's disk and keep only the running virtual machine, so hosts can be cloned from it
Run Sysprep a second time after publishing so the version number is reset to 1.0.0
questions.why: Step 5 is distribution, the part of the template that publishes the finished result as a stored, versioned image in the gallery, which is what the team asked for.

questions.prompt: In an image template, which part names the starting Windows image that the build machine is created from?
choices: Customizers, the ordered steps that install and configure software
The build identity, which controls who can write to the gallery
The source, which is taken from the marketplace or a gallery
Distribution, the place where the finished image is published
questions.why: The source is defined in the teaching text as the starting Windows image, taken from the marketplace or a gallery, while the other options describe different parts of the template or the build identity.

questions.prompt: A team publishes version 4.0.0 of its session host image and then finds a fault in it. Which practice from the teaching text lets them recover quickly?
choices: Keep the previous version available so the team can roll back to it
Stop creating new session hosts until the fault is fixed by hand
Delete all earlier versions to avoid confusion in the gallery
Rebuild version 4.0.0 in place so the fault is overwritten
questions.why: The teaching text says versions are kept and the previous one stays available for rollback, which limits the damage from a faulty published image.

questions.prompt: A build of a session host image finishes, but every host created from it reports the same machine identity, causing conflicts. Which omitted step most likely explains this?
choices: Applying Windows updates and restarting the build machine
Installing the line-of-business application with a script
Running Sysprep to generalize the machine before it is copied
Choosing a marketplace source instead of a gallery source
questions.why: Sysprep generalizes the machine by removing its unique identity, so skipping it causes copies to inherit one machine's identity, as the common mistake in the teaching text describes.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why we build the session host image with a managed build pipeline instead of by hand on one VM, and name one limit or tradeoff of doing it this way.
lessons.modelAnswer: A hand-built VM is hard to reproduce. Someone remembers which patches and apps went on, and the next build drifts. A managed build defined as a template runs the same ordered steps each time, produces a versioned image in a gallery, and lets us roll back to an earlier version if a release is bad. The main tradeoff is that the build depends on the right permissions and on the template being correct. A missing permission makes the build fail, and a missed generalize step can copy one machine's identity into every host. Builds also take time and cost money while the temporary build machine runs, and anything installed by a script must be tested again whenever the template changes.
rubricPoints: Names the managed service and the image template as the defined, repeatable recipe
Explains that the result is a versioned image that can be rebuilt and rolled back
States a concrete limit such as build permissions, generalization, or build time and cost
Connects a bad image to every new session host created from it

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a failed build or a drifting image adds more than reading the steps, and no listed mission covers image building directly.

lessons.plain: A session host is a virtual machine that people connect to and work on remotely. Its image is the saved template the machine is built from: the operating system plus any software and settings. Modifying an image means changing that template, for example adding security updates or a new app, so every future machine starts with the change already in place. You cannot simply edit the template in place, so the usual route is to start a machine from it, change it, prepare it to be copied, save a new copy, and point new machines at that copy. Think of it like updating a master recipe card and cooking from the new version rather than scribbling on the old one.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose every desktop in a pool was built from one master image that is now missing a security patch. Before any teaching, what would you change first: the running desktops directly, or the master image, and why?
lessons.teach:
Terms first. A session host is a virtual machine in a host pool that users sign in to remotely. A host pool is a group of identical session hosts. An image is the saved disk template that a new machine is created from. A generalized image is one whose machine-specific identity, such as the computer name and security identifiers, has been stripped out with the Windows preparation tool called sysprep, so copies can boot cleanly. Capturing means saving the disk of a prepared machine as a new image or a new version of an image. Draining means letting existing sessions finish while no new sessions are sent to a host.

Why it works: a running session host accumulates its own state and small differences over time, so changing it by hand leaves each machine slightly different. Changing the template once and building new hosts from it keeps the pool consistent, and the old version stays stored, so you can roll back.

Worked example. Goal: add a line-of-business app to a pool. Step 1: create a temporary VM from image version 1.0. Step 2: install the app and apply the latest Windows updates. Step 3: run sysprep with the generalize and shutdown options. Step 4: capture the VM as version 1.1 in the image gallery. Step 5: point the host pool's deployment at version 1.1, build new session hosts from it, then drain and replace the old hosts.

Common mistake: editing a live session host and assuming the pool now has the change. New hosts will not have it, and any host you forgot about keeps the old state.

Consequence in a running system: a pool that mixes version 1.0 and 1.1 hosts can behave differently for the same user, which makes problems hard to reproduce. Modifying the image through a new version is the controlled way to make the change everywhere.

questions.prompt: A dental clinic group, Harbor Dental, runs a pool of 8 session hosts built from image version 3.0 in its own image gallery. Staff need a newer scheduling client, version 7.2, on every host. The team follows the standard change path. Step 1: create one temporary VM from image version 3.0. Step 2: install scheduling client 7.2 on that VM and apply the latest Windows updates. Step 3: ___ (missing). Step 4: capture the temporary VM as image version 3.1 in the gallery. Step 5: point the host pool at version 3.1, build 8 new session hosts from it, then drain and replace the old hosts. The missing Step 3 is the one that strips the machine-specific identity from the temporary VM so copies can boot cleanly before capture. Which action fills Step 3?
choices: Sign in to the temporary VM as the pool's test user and leave the session running so the profile is warm
Restart the host pool so existing sessions drain before the capture starts
Delete the temporary VM's disk so the capture has less data to store
Run sysprep on the temporary VM with the generalize and shutdown options
questions.why: Sysprep with generalize and shutdown removes machine-specific identity and stops the VM, so the captured version can be copied into clean new hosts.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does it mean to drain a session host?
choices: Stop the host's virtual machine so it no longer uses compute charges
Disconnect every signed-in user immediately and delete the host from the pool
Let existing sessions on the host finish while sending no new sessions to it
Copy the host's disk into a new image version so it can be reused
questions.why: Draining is defined as letting current sessions finish while the host accepts no new sessions, which is what makes a safe replacement possible.

questions.prompt: A team runs a pool of 20 session hosts from image version 4.2 and must add a finance reporting tool. Which approach fits the course's controlled method?
choices: Install the tool only on the hosts that users complain about most, since the rest are working
Create image version 4.3 from a prepared temporary VM, build new hosts from it, then drain and replace the old hosts
Install the tool by remote desktop on each live host and restart them one at a time
Export the user profiles from the pool and import them into a fresh Windows machine outside the pool
questions.why: Making the change in a new image version and replacing hosts keeps every host identical and keeps the older version available for rollback.

questions.prompt: A pool has some hosts built from version 2.0 and some from version 2.1 of its image. A user reports a bug on one host that cannot be reproduced on another. What is the most likely cause?
choices: Draining has permanently locked the sessions on the 2.0 hosts so they cannot be reached
The pool has too many hosts, which makes the sign-in service overloaded on some machines only
Sysprep on version 2.1 deleted the user's profile, causing a random failure
The hosts are running different image versions, so they do not share the same installed state and behavior
questions.why: Hosts built from different image versions differ in installed software and settings, which is why the same user can see different behavior and problems are hard to reproduce.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks how we change the desktop image for our Azure Virtual Desktop pool without breaking users. In your own words, walk them through the modification workflow and name one limit or tradeoff of it.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would explain that we never fix the image in place. We start a temporary VM from the current image version, apply the updates and the app, then generalize it with sysprep so its machine identity is removed, shut it down, and capture it as a new version in the image gallery. The host pool is then pointed at the new version, and existing session hosts are drained and replaced over time so users are not cut off mid-session. The tradeoff is time and cost: every change means a rebuild cycle, testing, and a rollout, so urgent fixes are slower than editing a machine directly, and while a rollout is in progress the pool runs mixed versions until it finishes.
rubricPoints: Changes are made to a temporary VM built from the current image, then captured as a new image version.
Sysprep generalization removes machine-specific identity so the image can be copied safely.
The host pool is pointed at the new version and old hosts are drained and replaced, not edited live.
A tradeoff such as slower urgent fixes or mixed versions during rollout is named.

suggested.rationale: The core skill is explaining the image change workflow and its tradeoffs back in your own words, and no listed mission or planned engine practises this image lifecycle directly.

lessons.plain: A session host image is the saved template that a shared remote desktop machine is built from. Lifecycle management means handling that template over its whole life: making the first version, changing it, applying security and app updates, storing each numbered version safely, and replacing the machines that run older versions. Think of a recipe card in a bakery. You keep versioned copies, test a new one before anyone eats from it, and retire the old one once customers have moved on. Doing this well keeps every shared desktop identical and patched without disturbing live users more than necessary.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you update a shared desktop template and fifty users still log in to machines built from the old one, what would you expect to differ between those machines, and how would you move everyone to the new version without breaking anyone's session?
lessons.teach:
A session host is a virtual machine that users connect to for a remote desktop. A host pool is a group of session hosts that serve the same desktop setup. An image is a saved, reusable copy of a machine's disk, and new session hosts are created from it. Lifecycle management means controlling each image version from creation to retirement.

Why it works: a machine built from an image starts identical to every other machine built from that image, so you fix the template once instead of repairing many live machines by hand. Before a Windows machine is captured as an image, it is generalised, meaning its machine-specific identity is stripped out (a tool called sysprep does this), so each copy gets a unique identity when it boots. Azure Compute Gallery is the store that holds image definitions and their numbered versions, and it can copy versions to other regions. VM Image Builder is a managed service that runs a repeatable pipeline: it starts from a source image, runs customisation steps such as installing updates or applications, generalises the result, and writes a new version to the gallery.

Worked example: version 1.0 is live. A new build starts from 1.0, installs the month's security updates, and writes version 1.1 to the gallery. You create a test host pool from 1.1 and check it. Then you create new session hosts from 1.1 in the production host pool, put the old 1.0 hosts into drain mode (no new connections, existing sessions finish normally), and remove them as users log off.

Common mistake: patching a live session host by hand and never recording the change. The next host built from the image lacks the fix, so machines in one pool behave differently.

Consequence: mixed image versions inside one host pool mean users see different applications and settings depending on which machine they land on, which makes support problems hard to reproduce.

questions.prompt: A pharmacy chain keeps its desktop image as version 5.2 in its Azure Compute Gallery. An engineer sets up a VM Image Builder pipeline to start from 5.2, install a label-printer driver, and write version 5.3. The run goes like this: (1) the pipeline starts a temporary VM from 5.2; (2) it installs the printer driver; (3) ______; (4) it writes 5.3 to the gallery; (5) a test host pool is built from 5.3 and checked. Which step belongs in the blank?
choices: The pipeline copies version 5.3 to every other Azure region before any test runs.
The pipeline hand-patches the live 5.2 session hosts so they match the new driver.
The pipeline puts the 5.2 session hosts into drain mode so no new connections reach them.
The pipeline generalises the customised machine, stripping its machine-specific identity so each future host gets a unique identity when it boots.
questions.why: Generalising must happen before the machine is captured as a version, so that copies built from 5.3 do not share one identity; the other choices are either done to live hosts or happen at a different point in the lifecycle.

questions.prompt: What does it mean that a Windows machine is generalised before it is captured as an image?
choices: The image is copied automatically to every region that holds the gallery.
Its installed applications are locked so that users cannot change them later.
Its machine-specific identity is removed, so each machine built from the image gets a unique identity when it boots.
All session hosts later built from the image are placed in drain mode.
questions.why: Generalising strips out machine-specific identity before capture so that every copy can receive its own identity at boot, which is the defining purpose of that step.

questions.prompt: A host pool has 12 session hosts built from version 3.1. An engineer patches one live host by hand, fixing a login problem, and does not record the change anywhere. Which outcome is most likely over the next few weeks?
choices: Nothing changes, because gallery images are read-only once written.
The patched host automatically becomes the new template in the gallery.
Users are blocked from connecting until the image is regenerated from scratch.
Hosts built later from version 3.1 lack the fix, so machines in the same pool behave differently.
questions.why: A fix applied by hand to one live machine is not part of the stored image, so new machines built from that image do not have it and the pool drifts apart.

questions.prompt: A small firm wants every new session host to start identical, and wants old hosts retired without cutting off users mid-session. Which approach fits lifecycle management of session host images best?
choices: Let each host fetch its own application list at login.
Build every new host from one numbered gallery version, then move old hosts into drain mode until their users log off.
Remote into each live host and install updates by hand.
Clone one VM's disk by hand each time a new host is needed.
questions.why: Building from one numbered version gives identical starting points, and drain mode lets existing sessions finish while preventing new connections, which is the controlled retirement the lifecycle approach relies on.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says we should just patch the live session hosts in place each month instead of building a new image. Explain to them how image versioning works and name one limit or tradeoff of building new hosts from a new image.
lessons.modelAnswer: Patching in place looks quicker, but the machines drift apart and nothing records what changed. With versioning, the update goes into a new image version, such as 1.1, built from the previous version and stored in the gallery. We test a host pool made from that version, then create new session hosts from it and drain the old ones as users log off, so every machine in the pool matches the record. The tradeoff is time and cost: building, testing and replacing hosts takes longer than a quick in-place patch, and while old and new hosts run side by side you pay for extra capacity. Keeping old versions also uses storage. Still, the record of exactly what each host contains is what makes problems traceable and rollback possible.
rubricPoints: Explains that each change becomes a new numbered image version built from the previous one.
Explains that new hosts are created from the new version and old hosts are drained and removed.
Names the cost or time tradeoff of replacing hosts instead of patching in place.
Notes that in-place changes cause drift that is hard to track or reproduce.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine covers building and versioning machine images, so reading the workflow and catalogue facts is the best available route.

lessons.plain: A session host is a virtual machine that users connect to and work on. Many session hosts are built from one master copy called an image, so every new machine starts out identical. Over time that master falls behind, because security patches are released and applications get new versions. Applying OS and application updates means changing that master copy, testing it, and then using it to build new session hosts, so the whole pool moves to the new version together instead of each machine being patched by hand.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your pool has 20 session hosts, all built from one image, and an urgent security patch has just been released. Would you log into each running host and install the patch, or would you change the image and build new hosts from it? Why?
lessons.teach:
A session host image is the master copy of the operating system and applications that a host pool's virtual machines are built from. Updating it means producing a new version of that master that contains the latest OS updates and application releases. The usual workflow is this: create a temporary build VM from the current image, apply the OS updates and install or upgrade the applications, test the result, then generalize the VM. Generalizing means removing machine-specific details such as the computer name and security identifiers, which is done with the Windows sysprep tool. Finally, capture the VM as a new image version. A store such as Azure Compute Gallery keeps each version with a name, so you can replicate it to other regions and roll back to an older one if needed. New session hosts are then built from the new version. Old hosts are put into drain mode, which stops new user sessions from being assigned to them, and then removed once their sessions end.

Why this works: the image is the single source of truth. Every host built from it is identical, so you test once and know what users will get. Patching live hosts one at a time causes drift, where machines end up with different patch levels and nobody is sure what is actually running.

Worked example: a pool runs image version 1.0 on eight hosts. A fix is released on Tuesday. Step 1: deploy a build VM from version 1.0. Step 2: install the OS updates and the application upgrade. Step 3: run sysprep and capture the result as version 1.1. Step 4: build one pilot host from 1.1 and check it with a test user. Step 5: drain the old hosts and replace them gradually.

Common mistake: patching the live session hosts and assuming the image is now updated. The next scale-out creates machines from the old image, so the fix disappears and the pool runs mixed versions.

Consequence: with mixed versions, some users have the fix and others do not, and troubleshooting becomes slow and confusing.

questions.prompt: Harbor Dental runs a pool of six session hosts built from image version 3.2. A new browser release and Windows patches are ready, and the team follows the same process as the reference workflow. Step 1: deploy a build VM from version 3.2. Step 2: install the Windows updates and upgrade the browser on that build VM, then test it. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: capture the build VM as image version 3.3 in the gallery. Step 5: build one pilot host from 3.3 and have a test user check it. Which action belongs in the missing Step 3?
choices: Put the six live hosts into drain mode so that no new sessions are assigned to them
Delete the build VM so that the browser upgrade is not copied into the new image
Run the Windows sysprep tool to remove machine-specific details such as the computer name and security identifiers
Copy version 3.2 to a second region so that a rollback is available
questions.why: Generalizing the build VM with sysprep must happen after the updates are installed and before the VM is captured, because it removes machine-specific details that should not be baked into the image.

questions.prompt: In a host pool, what does putting an old session host into drain mode do?
choices: It deletes the host's operating system disk so the host cannot boot again
It copies the host's image into a gallery so that it can be used in another region
It stops new user sessions from being assigned to that host while existing sessions are allowed to continue
It immediately signs out every user who is currently connected to that host
questions.why: Drain mode blocks new session assignments on a host without forcing out users already connected, which is why old hosts can be removed gradually once their sessions end.

questions.prompt: A team patches the eight live session hosts in their pool one at a time and assumes the image is now updated. A week later the pool scales out and the new hosts do not have the fix. What is the root cause?
choices: Drain mode was left on, which stopped the patched hosts from receiving the new sessions
The gallery replicated the image to too many regions, which overwrote the patches
The sysprep tool was not run on the live hosts, so the patches were discarded during scale-out
The team never created a new image version, so new hosts are still built from the old version and the fix is missing
questions.why: Patching live hosts does not change the image that new machines are built from, so scale-out recreates the old version and the fix disappears, leaving the pool with mixed versions.

questions.prompt: Why does an image store such as Azure Compute Gallery keep several named versions of a session host image instead of only the latest one?
choices: So that every version can be deleted automatically after its first pilot host is built
So that each older version can be used to roll back if a newer version causes problems
So that drain mode can be turned on without removing any session hosts from the pool
So that sysprep only needs to run once for all versions of the image
questions.why: Keeping named versions lets you roll back to a known older image if a newer one has a problem, which is one of the reasons the store is used rather than overwriting a single master copy.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why you would update a session host image and build new hosts from it, rather than patching the running session hosts. Name one limit or tradeoff of the image approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: We update the image rather than the live hosts because the image is what every new host is built from. If we patch only the running machines, any host added later from the old image lacks the fix, and the pool ends up with mixed patch levels that are hard to track. So we build a temporary VM from the current image, apply the OS and application updates, generalize it with sysprep, and capture it as a new version. We test that version on a pilot host, then drain and replace the old hosts. The tradeoff is time and cost: building, testing and capturing takes a maintenance window, and replacing hosts disrupts users unless sessions are drained first and the rollout is staged.
rubricPoints: Explains that the session host image is the master copy from which new hosts are built.
Describes the workflow: build a temporary VM, apply updates, generalize with sysprep, and capture a new image version.
Says running hosts should be drained and replaced rather than patched in place, to avoid drift between machines.
Names a tradeoff such as maintenance window time, testing effort, or user disruption during rollout.

suggested.rationale: Choosing how to roll a new image version out to a pool (staged replacement, drain, and rollback) is best practised in the planned deployment strategies engine.

lessons.plain: When you need more remote desktops for people to use, you can copy a ready-made computer instead of building each one by hand. A custom image is that ready-made master: an operating system already set up with the apps and updates your team needs. This lesson is about creating new session hosts, the computers people log into to do their work, from that saved master. Think of a rubber stamp: every new host comes out identical to the original, so people get the same desktop each time, and new capacity can be added quickly.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you need ten identical remote desktops ready by the morning, would you rather install and configure each one by hand, or build one good master and copy it? Why?
lessons.teach:
A session host is a virtual machine that users connect to and run their desktop or apps on. A custom image is a prepared operating system disk, with your apps, settings, and updates already included, that you save so new virtual machines start from that same state. Creating a session host from a custom image means deploying new session hosts into a host pool using that saved image instead of a plain operating system from the marketplace. A host pool is the group of session hosts that share the same configuration. In Azure, saved images are often kept in an Azure Compute Gallery, a library where images are stored as named definitions with numbered versions, so you can pick one exact version to deploy.

Why it works: the image is a template. Each new session host is a copy, so every host in the pool matches, which keeps the user experience consistent and makes scaling out fast. Before the image is captured, the source machine must be generalized. Generalizing removes machine-specific identity, such as the computer security identifier and machine name, so each copy gets a fresh identity when it first boots.

Worked example: a team builds a virtual machine with a line-of-business app, applies Windows updates, runs the generalize step, stops the machine, and captures it as version 1.0.0 of an image definition in the gallery. Next they start a host pool deployment, select that gallery image version, set the VM size and a count of five, and let the deployment create the hosts. Each host boots from its own copy, receives its own name, joins the domain, and registers with the pool.

Common mistake: capturing a machine that was never generalized, or leaving a stale registration or old machine identity inside the image. Copies then share an identity, so domain joins or pool registration fail or hosts collide with each other.

Consequence: a broken image passes its fault to every new host, so scaling out adds broken capacity all at once. Keeping numbered image versions lets the team roll the pool back to a known good version.

questions.prompt: Harbor and Lowe, a small accounting firm, runs a pool of four session hosts built from the image definition fin-apps in its Azure Compute Gallery. Version 2.1.0 of fin-apps added a broken tax-app build, but version 2.0.0 is still in the gallery and worked well. The admin's rollback plan is: (1) stop deploying new hosts from 2.1.0; (2) start a new host pool deployment with a count of two and VM size D4s_v5; (3) the missing step; (4) once the new hosts register, drain and remove the four hosts built from 2.1.0. Which choice belongs in step 3?
choices: Select the fin-apps definition without a version number so the gallery chooses the newest build, which is 2.1.0.
In the deployment's image source, select fin-apps and pin version 2.0.0 explicitly so that exactly that numbered version is used.
Run the generalize step on the four running 2.1.0 hosts so they can serve as the source for the new deployment.
Delete version 2.1.0 from the gallery, then capture the broken VM again and label it 2.0.0.
questions.why: Pinning the exact numbered version 2.0.0 makes the new hosts copies of the known good state, which is the point of keeping numbered versions for rollback.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, why does each session host created from a custom image get its own identity when it first boots?
choices: Azure copies the image's stored machine name and security identifier to every host without changes.
The source machine was generalized before capture, which removed its machine-specific identity so each copy generates a fresh one on first boot.
The gallery stores a separate identity record for each numbered version, and the host reads its record at boot.
The host pool assigns a new domain account to each host during registration, overriding the image.
questions.why: Generalizing strips machine-specific identity such as the computer security identifier and machine name, so each copy gets a fresh identity when it first starts.

questions.prompt: A team captured a configured VM as an image without running the generalize step, then deployed five session hosts from it. What is the most likely result?
choices: The hosts automatically rename themselves and recover, so no visible problem occurs.
Each host gets its own identity and joins the pool normally, with only the apps running more slowly.
The copies carry the same machine identity, so domain joins or pool registration can fail or the hosts can collide with each other.
The hosts fail to start because Azure refuses to boot any VM built from an image that was not generalized.
questions.why: Without generalizing, the copies keep the source machine's identity, which causes domain join or registration failures and host collisions.

questions.prompt: A retail chain needs six kiosk session hosts in a new host pool. The gallery holds the image definition retail-kiosk with versions 3.3.0 and 3.4.1, and 3.4.1 is the approved build. Which deployment choice best fits this requirement?
choices: Deploy six hosts from the plain Windows marketplace image and install the kiosk app on each host by hand after boot.
Copy the disk of an existing kiosk host into six new VMs, skipping the gallery entirely.
Select the retail-kiosk definition only, and let the deployment use whichever version is first in the list.
Select retail-kiosk version 3.4.1 explicitly as the image source and set the count to six.
questions.why: Choosing the exact approved version from the gallery and setting the count to six creates identical hosts from the same known state, which is what the requirement calls for.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what happens when a new session host is created from a custom image, and name one limit or tradeoff of using that approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: A custom image is a saved master disk that already contains the operating system, apps, and updates. When we create session hosts from it, the deployment builds new virtual machines, each starting as a copy of that image. Each copy then gets its own name, joins the domain, and registers with the host pool. The main benefit is consistency and speed: every host matches, and adding capacity is just a larger count. The tradeoff is that the image is frozen at the moment it was captured. Any fix or update means building a new image version, testing it, and then moving the pool onto that version. If the master has a fault, every new copy inherits it, so we keep numbered versions and can roll back. The master must also be generalized first, or the copies will share an identity and fail to join cleanly.
rubricPoints: A custom image is a saved master that new session hosts are copied from.
Each new host gets its own identity and joins the domain and host pool at deployment.
The benefit is identical hosts and fast scale-out.
The tradeoff is that the image is frozen, so changes need a new version and testing.
The source machine must be generalized, or copies will share identity.

suggested.rationale: A scenario about which image version to deploy and how to roll back adds the most, since no current OpsForge mission covers AVD image deployment.

lessons.plain: Think of a shared cookbook for computer setups. When you need many identical virtual desktops, you do not want to install Windows and every app by hand each time. Instead you prepare one finished setup, save it as a master copy, and keep a numbered history of updated copies. Azure Compute Gallery is Azure's storage library for those master copies. It holds them in organised groups, lets you publish a new numbered version when you update the setup, and can copy versions into the regions where you need them. This lesson covers why that library exists and how to plan where it lives and where its copies go.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you build one golden desktop setup and then need 50 identical desktops in two different Azure regions, what would you want stored centrally, and what would go wrong if every new desktop were built by hand?
lessons.teach:
An image is a saved copy of a virtual machine's disk, prepared so new machines can start from it. In Azure Virtual Desktop, the session host image is the operating system plus apps and settings that every session host in a host pool begins with. Azure Compute Gallery, previously called Shared Image Gallery, is the service that stores these images in a library. The library has three layers. A gallery is the container. An image definition inside it describes one kind of image, such as a multi-session Windows setup, including its OS type, its Hyper-V generation, and whether it is generalized, meaning machine-specific identity was removed so it can be cloned. An image version is one numbered release of that definition, such as 1.0.0 or 1.1.0.

Why it works: each published version is treated as fixed, so you never edit a released image. You publish a new version after applying updates, and a host pool can reference a specific version. Versions can also be replicated to other Azure regions, so a host pool in one region does not pull a large image across the world at deploy time. Each replica is stored with a storage type and a replica count that you choose.

Worked example: a team has version 1.0.0 in East US with one replica. They patch the image and publish 1.1.0 with replicas in East US and West Europe. Step one, the patched machine is generalized and captured. Step two, a new version number is created in the definition. Step three, replicas are placed in both target regions. Step four, the host pool scales out in West Europe, and the new hosts deploy from the local replica.

Common mistake: treating the gallery as a backup. It holds deployable images, not point-in-time recovery of user data, and deleting an image version removes what new hosts can deploy from.

Consequence: if a scale-out event needs a region with no replica, the deployment is slower or fails at the exact moment capacity is needed most.

questions.prompt: Lakeside Clinic keeps a multi-session Windows image definition named win11-ms inside a gallery named clinicimages. The current version is 3.2.0, with three replicas in Canada Central. On Monday an engineer patched a reference machine and generalized it, meaning machine-specific identity was removed so it can be cloned. The team then worked through this plan. Step 1: capture the generalized disk. Step 2: create version 3.3.0 under the win11-ms definition from that capture. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: scale out the host pool in Australia East so new hosts deploy from the local copy of 3.3.0. Which step belongs in the gap?
choices: Delete version 3.2.0 to free storage before any new hosts deploy.
Back up the user profile data from the session hosts into the gallery as a recovery point.
Edit version 3.3.0 in place to add the Australian regional settings after it is published.
Place a replica of version 3.3.0 in Australia East and wait until it finishes before scaling out.
questions.why: Scale-out in Australia East can only use a local copy if a replica of the new version exists there, and that copy must be ready before the hosts are deployed.

questions.prompt: A host pool must always start from the exact image a team tested, even after newer versions are published. Which setting in the gallery makes this happen?
choices: Reference the specific image version number that was tested.
Point the host pool at the image definition name and let it choose the newest version automatically.
Edit the tested version in place so its contents stay current with the latest patches.
Copy the whole gallery into a second subscription so the tested image is kept there.
questions.why: Each published version is fixed, so naming its version number pins the host pool to that exact tested image, whereas the definition name alone does not.

questions.prompt: Northwind Logistics has image version 5.0.1 stored with one replica in Brazil South. It plans a scale-out next week in Japan East, where no copy exists yet. What should the team do before the scale-out?
choices: Export version 5.0.1 to a backup file and restore it in Japan East on the day of the scale-out.
Add a replica of version 5.0.1 in Japan East and let it finish before scaling out.
Raise the replica count in Brazil South to five so that more hosts can be deployed from there.
Rename version 5.0.1 to 5.0.2 so the Japan East deployment treats it as a new release.
questions.why: Hosts in Japan East deploy fastest and most reliably from a replica placed in that region ahead of time, and more replicas in Brazil South do not help there.

questions.prompt: Harbor Dental deleted image version 2.0.0 last month, believing it was an old backup nobody used. This week a scale-out in a second region failed because the host pool referenced 2.0.0. What is the lesson?
choices: A gallery replicates deleted versions automatically, so the failure must come from the region's network.
A gallery stores deployable images, so deleting a version removes something new hosts may still need, and it is not a backup of user data.
Version numbers must be kept in order, so the deletion broke the numbering that the scale-out relies on.
Versions should be deleted only after every replica has been removed, which would have kept 2.0.0 available.
questions.why: The gallery holds images that new hosts deploy from, not recovery copies of user data, so deleting a version can break any host pool that still references it.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what Azure Compute Gallery is for when building Azure Virtual Desktop session hosts, and name one limit or tradeoff of replicating image versions into several regions.
lessons.modelAnswer: Azure Compute Gallery is the library where we keep the master images our session hosts are built from. We keep one image definition per desktop type, and each update becomes a new numbered version, because a published version does not change. That makes rollback simple: we point new hosts back at the previous version. We replicate versions into the regions where our host pools run, so new hosts start from a nearby copy and scale-out is quicker and more reliable. The tradeoff is cost and effort. Every replica is storage we pay for, and every new version has to be copied again, so replicating to many regions takes time and money. We should replicate only where we deploy, and remove old versions only after confirming no host pool still references them.
rubricPoints: Describes the gallery, image definition and image version layers in plain terms
Explains that published versions are fixed, so updates become new numbered versions
States that replicas in target regions speed up and secure session host deployment there
Names a real tradeoff such as replica storage cost or copy time across many regions

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine practises image library planning, so reading the concepts and reasoning through the worked example is the best fit.

lessons.plain: When you set up a virtual desktop service, every person who signs in needs an account, and the desktop computers (session hosts) need to trust those accounts. Choosing an identity scenario means deciding where those accounts live and how the session hosts are tied to them. There are three common choices: a traditional directory your company already runs on its own servers, a cloud directory that handles sign-in over the internet, and a managed copy of a traditional directory hosted in the cloud for older apps. Picking the wrong one means users either cannot sign in or cannot reach the file shares and apps they need.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company already keeps staff accounts in a directory on servers in its own office, and some older apps need classic Windows domain logins. Before reading further, which identity option would you guess keeps those logins working with the least change, and why?
lessons.teach:
An identity scenario is the arrangement that answers two questions: where do user accounts and computer accounts live, and how do session hosts (the Windows machines users work in) join a trust relationship with them? Three options matter here.

Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS) is the traditional Windows directory, usually run on domain controllers (servers that answer login requests) in your own data center or on virtual machines you manage. Session hosts join the domain, so Kerberos (the ticket-based login protocol Windows domains use) and group policy (central settings pushed to machines) work as they always have. The catch is that session hosts need a network path to the domain controllers, typically a VPN or private link.

Microsoft Entra ID is the cloud identity service that handles sign-in for web and Microsoft 365 apps. Session hosts can be joined directly to Entra ID with no domain controllers at all. This suits cloud-only organisations, but apps that require traditional domain authentication may not work without extra design.

Microsoft Entra Domain Services gives you a managed domain in Azure, kept in sync with Entra ID. Cloud users get domain join, Kerberos and group policy without you running domain controllers. It fits when you need legacy domain features but have no on-premises directory.

Worked example: a firm has 300 staff in an on-premises AD DS and runs a line-of-business app that requires domain login. Step 1: the existing accounts live in AD DS, so that is the starting point. Step 2: the session hosts join that domain over a private link. Step 3: users sign in with the same credentials they already use, and the app's domain check passes.

Common mistake: choosing Entra ID join because it is newer, then discovering the legacy app needs domain authentication that the session hosts cannot provide.

In a running system, a mismatched scenario appears at sign-in time, so the identity decision must be made before the host pool is built.

questions.prompt: A design agency has 80 staff whose accounts exist only in Microsoft Entra ID, with no on-premises directory. One legacy stock-control app needs Kerberos login and group policy on the session hosts. Step 1: there is no on-premises directory, so keeping accounts in AD DS as their home is ruled out. Step 2: the app needs domain authentication, which session hosts joined only to Entra ID cannot provide. Step 3: [missing]. Which completion finishes the reasoning?
choices: Stand up two domain controllers in the agency's office and connect the session hosts to them over a VPN
Create local accounts on each session host and copy the staff passwords into them so the app can check them
Keep Entra ID join, since staff already sign in with Entra ID and the app will still pass its domain check
Join the session hosts to a managed domain that stays synchronised with the agency's Entra ID accounts, so Kerberos and group policy work without running domain controllers
questions.why: A managed domain kept in sync with Entra ID gives cloud users domain join, Kerberos and group policy without the agency running its own domain controllers, which is exactly what the app needs.

questions.prompt: A nonprofit has 25 staff whose accounts exist only in Microsoft Entra ID. It runs no servers of its own and uses only web and Microsoft 365 apps. Which identity scenario fits best?
choices: Active Directory Domain Services on a virtual machine the nonprofit manages itself
Microsoft Entra ID join for the session hosts, with no domain controllers needed
A VPN from the session hosts to a domain controller in a head office
Microsoft Entra Domain Services, because it supplies a domain the session hosts can join
questions.why: Entra ID join suits a cloud-only organisation whose apps use web sign-in, so no domain controllers or domain features are required.

questions.prompt: A logistics company has 500 users in an on-premises AD DS. An engineer proposes Entra ID joined session hosts because they are simpler to build. One internal tool requires Kerberos login. What is the most likely result?
choices: Sign-in to that tool fails or is blocked at sign-in time, because joined-only hosts cannot provide the domain authentication the tool needs
Users must create a second password, but the tool still works once they do
Group policy is applied automatically from the Entra ID tenant, so nothing breaks
The tool works, because Entra ID join supports Kerberos for every application
questions.why: Entra ID joined hosts cannot provide traditional domain authentication, so an app that depends on it fails at sign-in rather than quietly working.

questions.prompt: A team built its session host pool first and chose the identity scenario afterwards. Later they found a legacy app's domain check failing. According to the teaching, what should have happened?
choices: The identity choice only affects cost, so it can be changed after the pool exists with no consequence
The team should have added more session hosts to fix the domain check
The identity scenario should have been chosen before the host pool was built, because a mismatch shows up at sign-in time
The team should have switched the app to web sign-in, because host pools cannot use domain login at all
questions.why: The teaching states the identity decision must be made before the host pool is built, since a mismatched scenario appears at sign-in time.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks why we cannot just use Entra ID join for every new virtual desktop. Explain to them, in your own words, how you would choose between AD DS, Entra ID and Entra Domain Services, and name one limit or tradeoff of the option you would not pick.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with two questions: where do our user accounts live today, and does any app need traditional domain login such as Kerberos or group policy? If accounts are already in on-premises AD DS and an app needs domain membership, I would keep AD DS and connect the session hosts over a private network. The tradeoff is that we then depend on domain controllers and on that connectivity. If we are cloud-only and need no legacy domain features, Entra ID join is simpler. It does not give us traditional domain services, so an app that needs them would fail. If we are cloud-only but still need domain features, Entra Domain Services fits, though it is a managed service with its own cost and sync behaviour to plan. Entra ID join is not automatically the answer just because it is newer.
rubricPoints: Names the three options and where each one's directory lives.
Links the choice to whether existing accounts and legacy apps need domain authentication.
States a tradeoff: AD DS needs network connectivity and domain controllers, Entra ID join lacks traditional domain features, and Entra Domain Services adds cost and sync considerations.
Notes that the identity decision is made before the host pool is built.

suggested.rationale: Choosing a scenario from a stated requirement is best practised by reasoning through exam-style situations, and no listed mission or planned engine covers identity scenarios directly.

lessons.plain: When many people connect to a shared remote desktop computer over the internet, that computer has to know who each person is and whether they are allowed in. Identity is the system that answers those questions. Before you build the machine, you write down which identity system holds the users, whether the machine must join a directory, and what it needs to reach on the network. Those written requirements decide how the machine joins its directory, how its network is set up, and how people sign in. If they are wrong, users are locked out or the machine cannot reach the services it needs, even when the hardware is fine.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company keeps all its staff accounts in an old on-premises directory, and you want people to sign in to shared remote desktops. Before you build anything, what three things would you need to find out about that directory and the network to decide how the desktop machines should be set up?
lessons.teach:
A session host is a virtual machine that users connect to and work on. A directory is a database of user accounts and computer accounts. Joining a machine to a directory registers it, so the directory can vouch for the people who log on to it. Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS) is the classic on-premises directory, organised into domains. Microsoft Entra ID is a cloud directory. Microsoft Entra Domain Services is a managed service that gives cloud machines a domain to join, without you running domain controllers yourself. A hybrid join registers a machine in both AD DS and Entra ID.

So the requirements start with the question: where do the users live? Then you ask whether the session host must join that directory, what network path it needs to reach the directory's servers, and how name lookups must resolve so the domain can be found.

Worked example. Users live in on-premises AD DS, connected to Azure by a private network link. Step 1: the directory is AD DS. Step 2: the session host must join that domain, so you pick a domain join type that fits. Step 3: the subnet must route to the domain controllers. Step 4: the virtual network's DNS must point at those domain controllers. Step 5: a join account with permission to create computer accounts must be available. Step 6: join the machine, then sign in as a test user to confirm.

Common mistake: leaving the virtual network on its default DNS. The domain name then cannot be resolved, the join fails, and the machine looks healthy in the portal while nobody can sign in.

In a running system, a session host with the wrong join or DNS settings stays listed as available, so users are routed to it and then fail at sign-in.

questions.prompt: A design studio keeps all of its staff accounts only in Microsoft Entra ID, the cloud directory, and has no domain controllers of its own. It wants its session hosts in a virtual network named vnet-studio-west to join a domain, so it enables Microsoft Entra Domain Services, a managed domain service that gives cloud machines a domain to join. The team's requirement steps so far are: Step 1: the directory the users live in is Entra ID. Step 2: the session hosts will join the Entra Domain Services domain, because no on-premises domain exists. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: the virtual network's DNS servers are set to the managed domain's DNS addresses. Step 5: a join account with permission to create computer accounts is available. Which entry correctly fills Step 3, before the join is attempted?
choices: Skip any network check, because a managed domain is always reachable from any subnet
Point the session hosts' local hosts file at the domain name so lookups succeed
Confirm the session host subnet has a network path to the managed domain's servers
Deploy a domain controller virtual machine into the subnet so the join has a local server
questions.why: The session host must be able to reach the managed domain's servers over the network, and that path is confirmed before DNS and the join are set up, even though the domain itself is managed.

questions.prompt: Which description best defines a hybrid join for a session host?
choices: The machine is registered only in Microsoft Entra ID and never in a domain
The machine is registered in Entra Domain Services and in a local workgroup
The machine keeps a local account and is not registered in any directory
The machine is registered in both AD DS and Microsoft Entra ID
questions.why: A hybrid join registers the machine in both the on-premises AD DS directory and the cloud Entra ID directory, as the teaching text states.

questions.prompt: A team builds session hosts in a virtual network whose DNS is left on the default setting. The domain join fails, yet the machines still show as healthy and available in the portal. What is the most likely consequence for users?
choices: Users are routed to the hosts, then fail at sign-in because the domain name cannot be resolved
Users sign in normally but their profiles are stored on the wrong disk
Users see an error only after the host is removed from the host pool
Users are blocked from the portal until the join succeeds, so no sessions are ever routed
questions.why: Default DNS prevents the domain name from resolving, so the join fails, but the host still appears available, so users are sent to it and fail when they try to sign in.

questions.prompt: A company's staff accounts exist only in Microsoft Entra ID and it needs its session hosts to join a domain. Which question should it answer first when specifying the requirements?
choices: Which monitoring dashboard should display the session host health?
Which screen resolution the remote app should default to?
Where do the users live, meaning which directory holds their accounts?
How many disks each session host image should contain?
questions.why: The requirements start by identifying the directory the users live in, which then determines whether and how the session hosts must join a domain.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a session host built for users in on-premises AD DS needs different identity requirements from one built for users who exist only in Microsoft Entra ID. Name one tradeoff of the AD DS approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: The join target depends on where the accounts live. For on-premises AD DS users, the session host has to join that domain, so it needs a network route to the domain controllers, DNS pointing at them, and a join account with rights to create computer objects. For users who exist only in Microsoft Entra ID, the session host joins Entra ID directly and needs no domain controllers, so the network and DNS requirements are much simpler. One tradeoff of the AD DS route is that it adds a dependency: if the link to the on-premises network or the domain controllers fails, new sign-ins can fail even though the virtual machines are running. That is why the requirements have to name the directory, the join type, and the network path together, not treat them as separate tasks.
rubricPoints: Identifies the user directory first, since it determines the join target
Explains that AD DS joins need a network route and DNS pointing at domain controllers
Notes that Entra-only designs need fewer network dependencies
Names a concrete tradeoff, such as dependence on connectivity to on-premises domain controllers

suggested.rationale: Choosing the right join target and network requirements from a described situation is best practised as an exam-style scenario, and no listed mission covers it directly.

lessons.plain: Role-based access control is a way of deciding who can do what to a set of resources by giving people a named bundle of permissions, called a role, and attaching that role to a person or group at a particular place in the system. Think of a building where a visitor badge opens the lobby but not the server room, while a facilities manager key opens everything on one floor. In Azure Virtual Desktop, this decides who can manage the service itself, such as creating host pools, and who can simply be given a desktop or app to use. It is a separate layer from the permissions inside the Windows machines themselves, which are handled elsewhere.
lessons.guessPrompt: A support engineer needs to see and restart the session hosts in one host pool, but must not be able to delete the whole resource group or change who has access. Would you give her a broad role across the entire subscription, or a narrow role on just that host pool? Why?
lessons.teach:
A role definition is a named list of allowed actions, such as reading a resource or starting a virtual machine. A role assignment connects a role definition to a security principal, which is a user, a group, or an application identity. The scope is the place where that connection applies: a management group, a subscription, a resource group, or one single resource. Scopes nest, and an assignment made at a higher scope is inherited by everything below it. Azure RBAC is additive: a principal gets the combined set of actions from every assignment that reaches it, and a lower scope cannot take away a permission granted above it.

Why it works: you grant the smallest set of actions at the narrowest scope that still lets the job be done, so a mistake or a stolen account affects less. For Azure Virtual Desktop, the built-in roles are split by job. Desktop Virtualization User lets someone connect to a published desktop or app, and it is normally assigned on the application group rather than the whole subscription. Contributor-style roles, such as Desktop Virtualization Host Pool Contributor, let administrators change the pool and its settings at that pool's scope.

Worked example: a group called Finance-Users must reach the Finance app group. Step 1, identify the principal: the Finance-Users group. Step 2, pick the role: Desktop Virtualization User, which covers access. Step 3, pick the scope: the Finance app group resource only. Result: members can open the Finance desktop, and nothing else in the subscription changes.

Common mistake: assigning a broad Contributor role at subscription scope because it is quicker than finding the right role. That allows changes to every resource in the subscription, and the risk stays hidden until something is deleted or reconfigured.

Consequence: when users cannot see a desktop they should reach, the usual cause is a missing user role at the application group scope, not a failed network connection. Narrow assignments make that kind of fault quick to find and quick to fix.

questions.prompt: Harbor Dental has a pool called Clinic-Pool-West in its own subscription. The group Dental-Ops must be able to change that pool's settings, but must not be able to change anything else in the subscription. Here is the reasoning so far. Step 1, identify the principal: the Dental-Ops group. Step 2, pick the role: this is missing and needs to be filled in. Step 3, pick the scope: the Clinic-Pool-West host pool resource only. What belongs in Step 2?
choices: Contributor, assigned on the whole subscription
Owner, assigned on the management group above the subscription
Desktop Virtualization Host Pool Contributor, assigned on the host pool
Desktop Virtualization User, assigned on the host pool
questions.why: A host pool contributor role lets administrators change the pool at that pool's scope, which matches the goal without reaching anything else, whereas the user role only grants connection rights and the broad roles reach far beyond the pool.

questions.prompt: In Azure RBAC, what does it mean that the system is additive?
choices: A principal's effective permissions are the combined actions from every assignment that reaches it, and a lower scope cannot remove a permission granted above it.
Only the most specific assignment a principal holds is applied, and broader assignments are ignored once a narrower one exists.
Assignments made at a subscription cancel out any group-based assignments that a user also holds.
Each role definition adds time limits to the actions it lists, so permissions expire unless they are renewed.
questions.why: Additive means the actions from all reaching assignments are unioned together, and nothing at a lower scope can subtract a permission that was granted higher up.

questions.prompt: At Northwind Imaging, the group Radiology-Staff needs to open the desktop published in the Imaging app group, which sits in the Med-Prod subscription. Which assignment fits the requirement with the least access?
choices: Owner on the Med-Prod subscription
Desktop Virtualization User on the Imaging app group
Desktop Virtualization Host Pool Contributor on the Imaging app group
Desktop Virtualization User on the whole Med-Prod subscription
questions.why: The user role covers connecting to a published desktop or app, and assigning it on the app group alone grants that access without changing anything else, while the other options are either the wrong job or far too broad.

questions.prompt: At a training company, members of the group Lab-Students are assigned the Desktop Virtualization Host Pool Contributor role on the pool Lab-Pool-3. Students report they cannot see the desktop Lab-Desktop-2, although network tests to the session hosts succeed. What is the most likely fix?
choices: Assign Desktop Virtualization User to Lab-Students at the scope of the application group that publishes Lab-Desktop-2.
Give Lab-Students Contributor at the subscription scope so they can see every resource.
Remove the host pool contributor role, because pool administrators are blocked from seeing desktops.
Open more ports in the network security group attached to the session hosts.
questions.why: The likely cause is a missing user role at the application group scope, since the pool contributor role is for changing the pool and does not grant the connection right, and the successful network tests rule out a connectivity fault.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between a role definition, a role assignment, and a scope, using Azure Virtual Desktop as the example. Then name one limit or tradeoff of granting access at a broad scope.
lessons.modelAnswer: A role definition is the list of allowed actions, like the Desktop Virtualization User role that lets someone connect to a published desktop. A role assignment is the act of giving that role to a principal, such as a user group, and the scope is where it applies, such as one application group or a whole subscription. In Azure Virtual Desktop, if I assign the user role at the application group, only that group's members can open those desktops. The tradeoff of a broad scope is that the assignment is inherited by everything beneath it, so access reaches resources nobody meant to expose, and because Azure RBAC is additive, you cannot carve out an exception at a lower level. The fix is to keep scopes as narrow as the job allows and review them regularly.
rubricPoints: Defines role definition as a set of allowed actions and role assignment as connecting a role to a principal
Explains that scope determines where the assignment applies and that it is inherited downward
Gives an Azure Virtual Desktop example such as the user role on an application group
Names a limit or tradeoff, such as broad scopes exposing unintended resources or additive permissions that cannot be reduced below

suggested.rationale: Deciding whether a principal's combined role assignments allow an action at a given scope is exactly what a planned authorization policy evaluator would let the learner practise.

lessons.plain: Think of a building with a security desk. Anyone can ask to come in, but the desk checks a short list of rules first: is this person who they say they are, are they using a company laptop, are they connecting from an expected place, does the sign-in look risky. A Conditional Access policy is one of those rules, written down for a cloud service. For Azure Virtual Desktop, it decides whether a user may open a remote desktop at all, and what extra proof they must give first, such as a second factor. The policy changes who gets in and under what conditions. It does not change what they can do once they are inside.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company wants people to connect to remote desktops only from company-managed laptops, but still lets them connect from home. Without looking anything up, what kind of rule would you write, what would it check, and what would it do when the check fails?
lessons.teach:
A Conditional Access policy in Microsoft Entra ID (the cloud directory that holds user accounts and sign-in rules) is an if-then rule. Its assignments say who and which application the rule covers. Its conditions describe the situation of the sign-in, such as device state, location, or sign-in risk. When the conditions match, the policy applies grant controls, which either block the sign-in or require something first, such as multifactor authentication or a compliant device. Session controls shape what happens after access is granted, such as how often the user must sign in again.

For Azure Virtual Desktop, the target is the Azure Virtual Desktop cloud application, so the rule runs when a user signs in to get a session. This works because the identity service evaluates the rule at sign-in, before the user reaches the remote desktop. A failed check stops the connection early instead of starting a session and cleaning it up afterwards.

Worked example: a policy assigns all users in a Sales group to the Azure Virtual Desktop application. The condition is any location except the corporate network. The grant control requires multifactor authentication. Step 1: a salesperson signs in from home. Step 2: the condition matches, because the location is not the corporate network. Step 3: the grant control requires a second factor, so the user is prompted. Step 4: once the prompt succeeds, the session opens.

Common mistake: turning a new policy straight on in enforced mode without testing it. Report-only mode records what would have happened, so you can find users who would be blocked before anyone is actually locked out.

Consequence: a block applied to a broad group stops all of those users' connections at once, so a wrong assignment affects the whole service for them, not one machine.

questions.prompt: Northwind Dental assigns its Billing group to the Azure Virtual Desktop application. One policy condition is 'sign-in risk is high', and the grant control is 'block'. Trace a sign-in. Step 1: a billing clerk starts a sign-in to the app. Step 2: the identity service flags the attempt as high risk, so the condition matches. Step 3: the grant control is block. Step 4 is missing: complete it by stating what happens to the sign-in and what the clerk sees.
choices: The session opens, and the policy is checked again only when the clerk next signs in to the app.
The session starts, and the service ends it after the sign-in limit is reached.
The clerk is prompted for multifactor authentication, and the session opens once that succeeds.
The sign-in is refused at the identity service, so no remote desktop session is created.
questions.why: A block grant control stops the sign-in during the identity check, before any remote desktop session is created.

questions.prompt: In a Conditional Access policy, which element describes the situation of the sign-in, such as device state, location, or sign-in risk?
choices: Session controls
Assignments
Grant controls
Conditions
questions.why: Conditions describe the circumstances of the sign-in, while assignments name the users and application and grant controls state what is required.

questions.prompt: Riverside Logistics turns a new policy straight to enforced mode for 60 contractors without testing it. What is the safer first step?
choices: Delete the policy and recreate it with a shorter name
Add a session control that signs users out every hour
Set the policy to report-only mode to see who would be blocked
Widen the assignment to all users so the test covers everyone
questions.why: Report-only mode records what would have happened without blocking anyone, so affected users can be found before enforcement.

questions.prompt: A Northwind Health rule should apply only when a clinician's device is not compliant. Which element holds the trigger that decides when the rule applies?
choices: Session controls, because they set how often sign-in is required
Grant controls, because they block or require something
Conditions, because they describe the sign-in situation
Assignments, because they name the application
questions.why: The device state that decides whether the rule runs belongs in conditions, while grant controls only state the requirement once the conditions match.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a Conditional Access policy does for Azure Virtual Desktop connections, and name one limit or tradeoff of switching a new policy to enforced mode straight away.
lessons.modelAnswer: A Conditional Access policy is an if-then rule that is evaluated when a user signs in to Azure Virtual Desktop. We define who it applies to, then conditions such as location, device state, or sign-in risk. If the conditions match, the grant controls either block the sign-in or require something first, like a second factor. It controls access at the front door. It does not control what the user can do inside the session, which is handled by permissions and host settings. The tradeoff is that a wrong rule can lock people out. So I would first run it in report-only mode, check the sign-in logs to see who would be affected, and only then enforce it. I would start with a small pilot group and keep emergency admin accounts excluded, so we cannot lock ourselves out of fixing the problem.
rubricPoints: Says a policy has assignments (who and which app) plus conditions and grant or session controls.
Explains that it is evaluated at sign-in, before the desktop session starts.
Gives a concrete example, such as requiring MFA or a compliant device for off-network sign-ins.
Notes that it governs access at the front door, not permissions inside the session.
Names a tradeoff such as lockout risk, with a mitigation like report-only mode or an emergency account exclusion.

suggested.rationale: Working out which rule matches a given sign-in and what it decides is exactly the practice the planned authorization policy evaluator would give.

lessons.plain: When someone connects to a remote Windows desktop, the system has to be sure who they are. Authentication is that proof step. For Azure Virtual Desktop, you choose how people prove identity before a session starts. The options include a password plus a second check (multifactor authentication, or MFA), a passwordless method such as a fingerprint or face unlock on a trusted device, or a smart card, which is a physical card holding a certificate that a reader checks. Each option fits different users, devices and rules, so planning means matching the method to the requirement.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company wants staff to connect to remote desktops without typing a password, but still wants a strong check that the person really is who they say they are. Before reading on, what kind of method would you pick, and what would worry you about it?
lessons.teach:
Authentication means proving who you are. Multifactor authentication (MFA) means the proof uses at least two different kinds of factor: something you know (a password or PIN), something you have (a phone or security key), or something you are (a fingerprint or face). Passwordless authentication removes the password and relies on a key pair or biometric bound to one device. Examples are Windows Hello for Business, which uses a PIN or biometric unlocking a device-held key, and a FIDO2 security key, a physical USB or NFC token that signs a challenge from the sign-in service. A smart card is a physical card holding a certificate and a private key. The user inserts it into a reader and enters a PIN, and the certificate proves identity. These methods work because the secret never travels across the network as a reusable password, so a stolen or typed-in password is not enough.

Worked example: a support engineer, Dana, signs in to a remote session with a FIDO2 key. Step 1: the sign-in service sends a one-time challenge. Step 2: the key signs the challenge with a private key that never leaves the key. Step 3: the service checks the signature against the public key registered to Dana's account. Step 4: if the check passes, the session is issued. A phished password would gain nothing here, because there is no password to type.

Common mistake: believing that passwordless means MFA is no longer needed, or that a password plus an SMS code is the same as a passwordless method. A passwordless method already counts as multifactor, because it combines a device with a PIN or biometric.

Consequence: if a smart card reader fails or a certificate expires, the user cannot start any session, so planning needs a fallback path and a renewal process.

The method you choose must match the identity scenario and the devices your users actually have.

questions.prompt: Omar, a bookkeeper at a branch office, signs in to his remote desktop with a smart card. Step 1: he inserts his card into the reader. Step 2: he types his PIN, which unlocks the private key stored on the card. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: the sign-in service issues his session. Which step belongs in place of Step 3?
choices: The card copies its private key onto the reader so the key can be stored there for later sessions.
The sign-in service sends a one-time SMS code to Omar's phone for a second check.
Omar is asked to type his account password again so the service can compare it with the directory.
The certificate on the card is presented to the sign-in service, which uses it to prove Omar's identity.
questions.why: A smart card proves identity through the certificate it holds, which the sign-in service checks, so presenting that certificate is the step that completes the proof before the session is issued.

questions.prompt: A sign-in asks for a password and then a six-digit code sent to the user's phone. Which kinds of factor does this combine?
choices: Two things you know, because the code is also a secret typed in by the user.
Something you are and something you have, because the phone identifies the person.
Something you know and something you are, because the code is tied to the user's face.
Something you know and something you have, which makes it multifactor authentication.
questions.why: A password is something you know and a phone that receives a code is something you have, so the two factors are different kinds, which is the definition of multifactor authentication.

questions.prompt: A field service company has engineers who share a pool of laptops with no fingerprint sensor and no smart card reader. Each engineer carries a personal USB security key. The company wants passwordless sign-in that follows the engineer rather than the laptop. Which method fits best?
choices: Windows Hello for Business enrolled on each laptop, since the key is created on the device.
A FIDO2 security key, since the engineer's own physical token signs the sign-in challenge on any laptop with a USB port.
A smart card with a PIN, since every laptop can read the card once a reader is attached.
A password combined with a code sent by SMS, since the phone travels with the engineer.
questions.why: A FIDO2 security key is a portable physical token the engineer carries, so it matches both the available hardware and the requirement that sign-in follow the person.

questions.prompt: A company moved its smart card users to a new certificate set. All certificates expired on a Sunday, and on Monday no user could start any session. Which planning gap caused this?
choices: The company used multifactor authentication, which blocks sessions whenever a certificate has expired.
The company had no renewal process for certificates and no fallback path for when smart card sign-in fails.
The company did not require a PIN on the smart cards, so the sign-in service rejected them.
The company should have switched to a password plus SMS code, which never depends on certificates.
questions.why: Smart card sign-in depends on a valid certificate, so without a renewal process and a fallback path, an expiry stops every session, which is the failure the planning must prevent.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between MFA, passwordless sign-in and smart card authentication for an Azure Virtual Desktop deployment. Name at least one limit or tradeoff of the option you would not choose by default.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with the requirement. If users have company laptops and a cloud identity, and the main goal is removing passwords, I would choose passwordless sign-in such as Windows Hello for Business or FIDO2 keys, since each sign-in needs a device plus a PIN or biometric. The limit is that it depends on enrolled devices, so unmanaged or shared machines cannot use it. If users have no suitable devices, I would use a password with MFA as the default. Its weakness is that it still relies on a password that can be phished, and an SMS code can be intercepted. A smart card is my choice when a regulation or existing PKI requires certificate-based sign-in.
