Step 3: a claims worker signs in to any host in the pool, and at sign-in or the next refresh the wallpaper rule applies to that worker.
choices: Under Computer Configuration, set the wallpaper path to Enabled so every host in the pool carries the same image.
Create a second GPO linked to each individual user account and leave the hosts alone.
Under User Configuration in the administrative templates, set the wallpaper setting to Enabled with the image path, because the rule must follow the signed-in worker.
Set the wallpaper only in the local registry of the first host, since the GPO will copy it to the others.
questions.why: A user configuration applies to the person who signs in, so placing the wallpaper setting there lets it follow each worker across pool hosts, while the other choices scope to the machine, link to accounts rather than containers, or use local edits the GPO does not manage.

questions.prompt: In a Group Policy Object, what is the difference between a user configuration and a computer configuration?
choices: The user one applies to the machine; the computer one applies to the signed-in person.
A user configuration is only for Intune and a computer configuration is only for Group Policy.
They are the same setting shown in two menus, and choosing one only changes the display order.
The user one applies to the signed-in person; the computer one applies to the machine itself.
questions.why: The teaching text defines a user configuration as applying to the person who signs in and a computer configuration as applying to the machine itself.

questions.prompt: A setting will not stick on a host because it is set in both a Group Policy Object and an Intune policy. What should you check first?
choices: Rebuild the session host image so the value is baked in.
Delete the Intune policy, because Group Policy always removes it.
Check which source, Group Policy or Intune, actually applies to that setting before troubleshooting further.
Restart the broker service to force the value to reapply.
questions.why: The teaching text says that when Group Policy and Intune set the same value one source wins by precedence, so you must first confirm which one applies.

questions.prompt: A computer configuration is set on a pooled host that several staff members share. Which result is expected?
choices: It follows each user to every host they sign in to, because the rule is stored with the user account.
It applies to that host, so anyone who signs in there gets it, but it does not carry over to other hosts.
Only the first user to sign in gets the setting for the rest of the day.
It applies only to administrators who sign in to the host.
questions.why: A computer configuration applies to the machine itself, so every user on that host receives it, but it does not follow a user to a different host.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide whether a per-user setting for your session hosts belongs in Group Policy or in Intune. Name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start by asking how the session hosts are joined to identity and whether they are managed by Intune, because that decides which tool can actually reach them. If the hosts are domain joined and already governed by Group Policy, I keep user settings there so there is one rulebook and one place to check. If the hosts are managed by Intune, I use Intune configuration policies for the same kind of setting. The main tradeoff is that two sources can set the same value, and the winner depends on precedence, so a setting may not stick even though the policy looks correct. To avoid that, I record which tool owns each setting and check the effective result on a test host before rolling it out to the pool.
rubricPoints: Explains that the choice depends on how hosts are joined and managed
Distinguishes user scope from computer scope and where each applies
Names the risk of conflicting sources and precedence
Gives a practical check, such as testing the effective result on one host

suggested.rationale: Choosing between Group Policy and Intune for a given host and scope is best practised by reasoning through an exam-style situation rather than by memorising either tool's steps.

lessons.plain: A host pool is a group of virtual machines that serve remote desktop sessions to users. RDP properties are the settings that travel with a host pool and tell the remote connection how to behave, such as colour depth, which local devices may be shared into a session, and whether a screen can be captured. Think of them as house rules posted at the door of a shared office, read by every visitor before they walk in. Changing a rule changes how new visitors are let in, so you need to know what each rule does before you edit it.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you change one RDP property on a host pool while users are already connected, do you expect their open sessions to change immediately? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
Definitions first. A host pool is a set of session host virtual machines that users connect to. A session host is one such machine. An RDP property is one named setting in the remote connection configuration for a host pool. The platform passes these settings to the client that opens the connection. Each property is written as a name, a type letter and a value, separated by colons, and properties are separated by semicolons. The type letter tells the client how to read the value: i means integer, s means string, and b means boolean.

Why it works: the client reads the whole list when a connection starts and applies every setting it understands. The host pool therefore holds one shared set of behaviour for everyone who connects through it, instead of each user configuring their own session.

Worked example. Suppose the host pool list contains session bpp:i:32; Step 1: the name is session bpp. Step 2: the type letter i says integer. Step 3: the value 32 is the colour depth. Step 4: a user connecting afterwards gets a 32-bit colour session. If someone wrote session bpp:s:32; instead, the type letter says string, and the client may not read it as a number, so the setting may be ignored. The error is the wrong type letter, not the value.

Common mistake: assuming an RDP property overrides everything. Other controls, such as a group policy on the session host or a setting on the user's client, can restrict the same behaviour. When two rules conflict, the stricter one usually wins.

Consequence in a running system: properties apply to connections made after the change. Sessions already open keep the settings they started with, so a fix can look as if it did nothing until users sign out and back in. Test the change with one user before rolling it out to the whole pool.

questions.prompt: A managed desktop pool for a small accounting firm called Ledgerline must stop clipboard sharing for everyone who connects. The administrator builds one entry for a setting named redirectclipboard, which is either on or off, and uses the value 0 for off. Worked so far: Step 1: the name is redirectclipboard. Step 3: the value 0 means off. Step 2 is missing: the type letter for a setting that is only on or off is ___. Step 4: the finished entry is redirectclipboard, then the type letter, then a colon and 0, with the parts joined by colons.
choices: b, because on and off values are booleans
c, because the type letter should match the first letter of the name
s, because on and off are written as words
i, because on and off values are numbers
questions.why: The teaching text says the type letter b means boolean, which is the type for a setting that is only true or false, so the entry is redirectclipboard:b:0.

questions.prompt: In an RDP property such as scale:i:1, what does the middle letter tell the client?
choices: The name of the host pool the setting belongs to
How to read the value that follows, such as whole number, text or true-or-false
The order in which the client should apply the settings
Whether the setting can be changed by the user during a session
questions.why: The type letter tells the client how to read the value: i for integer, s for string and b for boolean.

questions.prompt: A host pool list contains the entry autoreconnect:s:1 for a firm that wants automatic reconnection turned on. Users report the setting has no effect. What is the most likely cause, based only on the format rules?
choices: The semicolons separating entries should have been commas
The type letter s says string, so the client may not read 1 as a number and may ignore the setting
The value 1 is too small to be read by the client
The list was saved before users signed in for the day
questions.why: The error is the wrong type letter for the value; the client may ignore a setting whose type does not match how it is written.

questions.prompt: An administrator changes an RDP property on a host pool at 9 a.m. A user whose session was already open at that time reports no change, but a user who signs in at 10 a.m. sees the new behaviour. Why?
choices: The property was not saved and the 10 a.m. user saw an older setting
Sessions already open keep the settings they started with, and new connections read the updated list
The change applies only to the first user who connects after it is made
The platform only applies changes to sessions that have been open for more than an hour
questions.why: The client reads the list when a connection starts, so properties apply to connections made after the change while open sessions keep their original settings.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how RDP properties on a host pool work, including one limit or tradeoff of changing them on a pool that already has users.
lessons.modelAnswer: RDP properties are a semicolon-separated list of named settings stored on the host pool. Each entry has a name, a type letter and a value, such as session bpp:i:32. The connecting client reads the list when a session starts and applies the settings it understands. So one change to the host pool affects everyone who connects afterwards, which is useful for consistency. The limit is timing: sessions already open keep their old settings, so an edit will not help people who are signed in right now. Also, a group policy or client setting can narrow the same behaviour, so the effective result is usually the stricter of the two. On a live pool, I would change one setting, have a pilot user sign out and back in to confirm it, and only then roll it out more widely.
rubricPoints: RDP properties are named settings stored on the host pool and read by the client when a connection starts.
Each entry uses a name, a type letter (i, s or b) and a value, separated by colons and semicolons.
A wrong name or type letter can cause a setting to be ignored without an obvious error.
Changes apply to new connections; sessions already open keep their previous settings.
Other policies can restrict the same behaviour, so the stricter rule usually determines the result.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine covers host pool RDP property configuration, so reading the settings reference and console steps is the most direct route.

lessons.plain: A remote desktop session is a user's work running on a shared computer in the cloud. A session timeout is a rule that decides how long that session can stay open when the user is not actively using it. Think of a hotel room that gets cleaned after the guest has been away too long. These timeouts free up the computer for other people and stop unused sessions from quietly holding resources. Setting them well means balancing user convenience against wasted capacity and data that stays open longer than it should.
lessons.guessPrompt: A user closes their remote window at 10:05 without signing out, and never comes back. Their work is still open on the shared server. What do you think should happen to that session, and after how long, and why might the answer differ from a user who is still typing?
lessons.teach:
A session timeout is a rule that limits how long a remote desktop session may remain open in a given state. In Azure Virtual Desktop these rules are set on the session hosts, the virtual machines that run user sessions, usually through a policy, which is a group of settings applied centrally to many machines. There are three timers. The active session limit caps how long a connected session that is in use can run. The idle session limit starts when the user stops giving input such as keyboard or mouse activity, and applies once that quiet period passes. The disconnected session limit covers a session the user has left without signing out, so it keeps running on the host with no window attached. A separate setting decides whether reaching a limit ends the session completely or only disconnects it.

Why it works: each session uses memory, processor time and, importantly, a user profile. Timers return that capacity without waiting for someone to remember to sign out.

Worked example: idle limit is 30 minutes, disconnected limit is 2 hours, and sessions end when limits are reached. Maya stops typing at 10:00. At 10:30 the idle timer fires and her session ends, so the host frees its resources. Now suppose she instead closed her window at 10:05 without signing out. The session becomes disconnected, the disconnected timer starts, and it ends the session at 12:05.

Common mistake: assuming a disconnected session is harmless. It still holds the user's profile open, so a second session for the same user on another host may be unable to load that profile.

In a running system, short timers protect capacity, while very long disconnected limits leave orphaned sessions consuming resources and blocking the user's next login.

questions.prompt: Ledgerline Clinics runs session hosts for front-desk staff. Its policy sets the idle limit to 20 minutes, the disconnected limit to 90 minutes, and turns on the setting that ends sessions when a limit is reached. Trace Ines, who closes her window at 15:00 without signing out. Step 1: the session becomes disconnected and the disconnected timer starts with a 90-minute limit. Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: at 16:30 the disconnected timer ends the session and releases the profile. Which statement correctly fills Step 2?
choices: At 15:20 Ines signs in on Host B and gets a fresh copy of the profile, which restarts the disconnected timer on Host A.
At 15:20 signing in on Host B ends the Host A session at once, releasing the profile.
At 15:20 the idle limit on Host A starts and ends her session at 15:40.
At 15:20 Ines signs in on Host B, where Host A still holds the profile open, so that logon may be blocked or slowed.
questions.why: While the session is still disconnected on Host A, it keeps the user's profile open, so a second logon on another host can be blocked or slowed, as the teaching text describes.

questions.prompt: A warehouse clerk minimises the session window at 09:00 and never signs out. Which timer governs what happens next?
choices: The setting that chooses between ending and disconnecting
The idle session limit
The active session limit
The disconnected session limit
questions.why: A session left open with no window attached is disconnected, and the disconnected session limit is the timer that governs it.

questions.prompt: A reporting team's scheduled script sends a keystroke to every analyst session each minute, so the session never goes quiet. Which limit can still end the session?
choices: The idle session limit, which never starts because input keeps resetting the quiet period
The disconnected session limit, which applies only after a window is closed
The active session limit, which caps how long a connected session in use can run
The setting that decides whether a limit ends or disconnects, which itself starts no timer
questions.why: Continuous input prevents the idle timer from ever starting, but the active session limit caps a connected session in use regardless of input, so it still applies.

questions.prompt: Hollis Dental wants user profiles not to stay held open for long after staff leave a session without signing out. Which configuration fits this requirement?
choices: Turn off the setting that ends sessions, so reaching a limit only disconnects them
Set a short disconnected limit and enable the setting that ends sessions when a limit is reached
Remove the idle limit so that no session is ever timed out
Lengthen the disconnected limit to 14 days so users keep their open work
questions.why: A short disconnected limit combined with the end-session setting frees the host and the profile sooner, whereas the other options leave sessions or profiles held open longer.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what the three session timeout timers measure, and name one tradeoff in choosing how long the disconnected session limit should be.
lessons.modelAnswer: The active limit caps how long a connected session that is in use can run. The idle limit counts from the last keyboard or mouse input and applies once a user has been inactive for that long. The disconnected limit applies when someone closes the window without signing out, and it controls how long that session keeps running on the host before it ends. The main tradeoff is in the disconnected limit. A long value lets users return to their open work after a network drop, but it keeps resources and the user's profile tied up, which can stop a new session from loading that profile. A short value frees capacity and avoids profile conflicts, but users may lose unsaved work more often. Choosing it means weighing the cost of lost work against the cost of blocked logins and wasted capacity.
rubricPoints: Distinguishes the active, idle and disconnected timers by what each one measures
Explains that a disconnected session keeps running and holding resources
Names the tradeoff between user convenience or lost work and capacity or profile conflicts
Notes that the end-session setting decides whether a limit ends or only disconnects the session

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through which timer fires in a realistic idle-then-disconnected scenario builds the decision skill better than reading the settings alone.

lessons.plain: Start VM on Connect is a cost-saving setting for a remote desktop pool. Session hosts are the virtual machines that users log into remotely. When nobody is using them, they can be switched off so the team stops paying for idle computing time. With this setting turned on, a user who tries to connect to a switched-off machine causes the platform to power it on automatically, so nobody has to wake machines by hand. The idea is simple: keep machines off until someone needs them, then start them on demand.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a team keeps twenty remote desktop machines running all night even though nobody uses them, what could it change to pay less, and what would a user notice when they sign in the next morning?
lessons.teach:
A session host is a virtual machine in a host pool that users connect to. A host pool is a group of these session hosts. A deallocated machine is one that has been shut down at the platform level, so its compute is no longer billed, although its attached disks still are. Start VM on Connect is a host pool setting. When it is on, the broker, which is the part of the service that matches users to machines, can power on a stopped session host at the moment a user tries to connect and no suitable machine is already running.

Why it works: the broker already sees the connection attempt, so the setting lets it act at that exact moment instead of keeping every machine running all day. The service also needs permission to do this. Its own identity must be allowed to start virtual machines in the subscription or resource group where the hosts live. Without that permission, the setting has no effect.

Worked example: a pool has ten hosts, all deallocated at 18:00. At 08:55 a user opens the client and signs in. First, the broker receives the connection request. Second, it finds no running host with free capacity. Third, because the setting is on and the service has permission, it starts one deallocated host. Fourth, the user waits a few minutes while the machine boots, then gets a session. Only the machines that are actually needed run during the day.

Common mistake: assuming the setting also shuts machines down. It does not. It only powers machines on. Something else, such as an automation schedule or a shutdown policy, must turn them off, or they stay on all night and the saving disappears.

Consequence: users see a delay on their first connection, and the first person in the morning waits longest. Cost falls, but startup latency rises, which matters for a team that needs instant access.

Keeping idle machines off saves money, and Start VM on Connect makes that practical by starting them only when a user actually connects.

questions.prompt: A small legal firm has a host pool called Harbor-Legal with six session hosts, all deallocated (shut down at the platform level, so compute is not billed) at 19:00 the night before. The broker, the part of the service that matches users to machines, is the component that handles connection requests. Start VM on Connect is on, and the service identity has permission to start VMs in the resource group. At 07:40 a paralegal connects and follows this sequence: (1) the broker receives the connection request; (2) it checks for a running host with free capacity and finds none; (3) [missing step]; (4) the paralegal waits a few minutes for the machine to boot, then gets a session. Which choice correctly fills step 3?
choices: The broker starts all six hosts at once so that capacity is ready before any further user connects.
The broker emails an administrator and holds the request until someone starts a host by hand.
The broker starts one deallocated host, because the setting is on and the service has permission to do so.
The broker deletes the five unused deallocated hosts so that the remaining host is cheaper to run.
questions.why: With the setting on and the service permitted to start VMs, the broker starts one deallocated host at the moment of connection, which is exactly the action the feature is designed to take.

questions.prompt: A team turns on Start VM on Connect in their host pool, but users sign in and no deallocated host ever starts. The hosts stay off. Based on how the feature works, which gap is the most likely cause?
choices: The users' passwords have expired and must be reset in the identity provider.
The client app version is too old to display the session list.
The service's own identity has not been given permission to start virtual machines where the hosts live.
The hosts do not have enough memory to run a user session once they boot.
questions.why: The feature needs the service identity to be allowed to start VMs in the subscription or resource group; without that permission the setting has no effect.

questions.prompt: A pool of eight session hosts has Start VM on Connect enabled. Every evening at 19:00 the team expects the hosts to shut down, but they are still running at midnight and the compute bill is high. Which statement best explains this?
choices: The broker keeps all hosts running for twenty-four hours whenever the setting is enabled.
Start VM on Connect only powers machines on; a separate shutdown schedule or policy must turn them off.
The feature only deallocates hosts when the pool has fewer than two users connected.
Start VM on Connect shuts down any host that has no signed-in users after working hours.
questions.why: The setting is one-directional: it starts deallocated machines when a connection needs them but does not stop running machines, so something else must shut them down.

questions.prompt: In a finance team's pool of four session hosts with Start VM on Connect enabled, the first user each morning waits several minutes to get a session, while later users connect almost instantly. What explains the pattern?
choices: Later users bypass the broker and connect directly to a running host, which is faster.
The first connection has to start a deallocated host and wait for it to boot, while later users reach a host that is already running.
The broker only assigns the first user to a host that has been running for at least an hour.
The first user's client is always updated at startup, which delays the connection.
questions.why: A deallocated host needs time to boot after the broker starts it, so the first connection of the day absorbs that delay while later users find machines already running.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what Start VM on Connect does, how it saves money, and one limit or tradeoff the team should weigh before turning it on.
lessons.modelAnswer: Start VM on Connect lets a host pool keep its session hosts switched off when nobody is using them. When a user tries to connect and no running host has room, the broker powers on a stopped host for them, so we only pay for compute while people are working. The service needs permission to start the virtual machines in the resource group, or the setting does nothing. The main tradeoff is startup delay: the first user of the day waits for a machine to boot, which may be several minutes. It also does not turn machines off, so we still need a shutdown schedule or policy, otherwise the savings never happen. Before enabling it, I would check whether the team can tolerate that wait and whether the shutdown side is in place.
rubricPoints: States that the setting powers on a stopped or deallocated session host when a user connects and no suitable host is running
Notes that the service needs permission to start the virtual machines, or the setting will not work
Names the tradeoff of a boot delay on first connection
Points out that the setting does not shut machines down, so a separate shutdown mechanism is needed to save money

suggested.rationale: A situation to reason through, such as a pool where users complain about waiting or costs stay high, tests which setting fits and why better than a listed mission does.

lessons.plain: Some desktops in a cloud virtual desktop setup are personal: one machine belongs to one person, much like a laptop on a desk. Assigning a personal desktop means recording that a particular user owns that machine, so when they sign in they land on their own computer and nobody else is sent there. Unassigning means removing that link so the machine is free for someone else. The idea is simple, but timing matters, because pulling the link while someone is still working on the machine can cut them off mid-task.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company gives each of 20 engineers a personal virtual desktop from a shared pool of 20 machines. One engineer leaves, and a new hire starts Monday. What has to happen to the old machine before the new hire can use it, and why might the old assignment still be in place after the engineer has gone?
lessons.teach:
A host pool is a group of virtual machines that users connect to remotely. Each machine in the pool is called a session host. In a personal host pool, each session host is dedicated to one user at a time rather than shared among many. The link between a session host and its user is called an assignment.

Assignment can happen in two ways. With automatic assignment, the first time a user connects, the service picks a free session host and records that the user now owns it; that link stays in place after the user signs out. With direct assignment, an administrator chooses the user and the machine ahead of time. Either way, the user also needs permission to reach the desktop through its application group, which is the list of what a user is allowed to open.

Unassigning removes that link so the session host becomes free for someone else. It does not delete the machine, and it does not by itself remove files the user saved on the machine's local disk, which is why user data is usually handled separately.

Worked example: a pool of ten personal desktops. Dana connects on Monday. Automatic assignment finds desktop 4 free and records Dana as its owner. Dana leaves in June, but desktop 4 still shows Dana as owner, so the pool has only nine usable machines. An administrator first puts desktop 4 into drain mode, which stops new sessions from starting on it. They confirm Dana's session has ended, then unassign Dana. Desktop 4 returns to the free list and can serve the next user.

Common mistake: unassigning while the user still has an open session or unsaved work. The session can be cut off and the work lost. Drain the session host and end sessions first.

In a running system, stale assignments quietly shrink capacity. New users arrive, find no free desktop, and cannot sign in, even though the pool looks full of machines.

A personal desktop is therefore only as available as its assignment record is accurate.

questions.prompt: A dental clinic runs a personal host pool of four desktops, PC-A to PC-D, using direct assignment, meaning an administrator picks the user and the machine ahead of time. Nurse Priya moves to another branch on Friday, and new hire Omar starts Monday and should get PC-C. On Friday the administrator put PC-C into drain mode (a setting that stops new sessions from starting on a machine) and confirmed that Priya's session had ended. The administrator then directly assigned Omar to PC-C. Missing step: what should happen between confirming that Priya's session ended and assigning Omar?
choices: Turn drain mode off so the machine can accept Omar's first sign-in
Unassign Priya, which removes her link to PC-C and frees the machine
Delete PC-C and create a fresh desktop for Omar so no old record remains
Remove Priya from the application group so her access to PC-C ends
questions.why: Unassigning is the step that removes the existing user-to-machine link and makes the session host free, so it must happen before a new user is linked to it.

questions.prompt: A colleague says that unassigning a personal session host deletes the virtual machine and everything on its disk. Which statement corrects this?
choices: Unassigning only changes the password the previous user needs to sign in
Unassigning converts the machine into a shared host that many users can reach at once
Unassigning removes the link between the machine and its user so the machine is free, while the machine itself and its files stay in place
Unassigning deletes the machine, so a new one must be built for the next user
questions.why: The teaching text says unassigning removes the link, does not delete the machine, and does not by itself remove files saved on the local disk.

questions.prompt: A personal pool has 15 desktops. Four of them still show owners who left months ago, and none of those owners has an open session. How many desktops can new users actually be given, and why?
choices: 15, because the pool size is the only number that matters
15 minus the links, which new users can clear by signing in
11, because the four stale links still hold their machines until they are unassigned
4, because only the stale owners appear on the list
questions.why: Each stale assignment keeps its machine tied to someone who is no longer using it, so only the remaining 11 are free for new users until those links are removed.

questions.prompt: Jin was automatically assigned a personal desktop yesterday, and the desktop still shows Jin as owner. Today Jin's connection is refused. Drain mode is off on the desktop. Which cause fits the teaching text best?
choices: The owner link is stale, so unassigning Jin and letting automatic assignment run again is the fix
Automatic assignment only works for the first day, so Jin needs a direct assignment instead
Jin is not listed in the application group, so permission is missing even though the owner link is correct
Signing out deleted the machine, so the desktop record no longer exists for Jin
questions.why: The teaching text says a user needs permission through the application group in addition to the assignment, and the assignment here is still valid, so the missing permission is the likely cause.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between automatic and direct assignment of personal desktops, and name one limit or tradeoff of automatic assignment when people leave the company.
lessons.modelAnswer: Automatic assignment means the first sign-in picks a free desktop and records that user as its owner, so setup is quick and nobody has to plan in advance. Direct assignment means an administrator chooses who gets which machine beforehand, which suits cases where a specific person needs a specific machine or configuration. The tradeoff with automatic assignment is that the link is sticky: when someone leaves, their desktop stays assigned to them until someone unassigns it. If nobody does, the pool quietly loses usable machines, and new users are turned away even though the machines exist. A leaver process should therefore include draining the session host, ending any open sessions, and then unassigning it.
rubricPoints: Personal pools dedicate one session host to one user at a time.
Automatic assignment links a user to a free session host at first sign-in and keeps that link afterward.
Direct assignment has an administrator choose the user and machine in advance.
Unassigning frees the session host for others without deleting the machine or its local data.
Unassign only after draining the host and ending the user's session, so work is not cut off.

suggested.rationale: Choosing an assignment approach for a given staffing situation is a reasoning task that an exam-style scenario builds better than reading alone, and no listed mission covers it directly.

lessons.plain: When a team wants a program to run for people working on a remote desktop in the cloud, someone has to decide how that program gets onto the machines those people use. Picture a shared computer lab. You could install the software on every machine before anyone sits down, you could add it to a machine after it is already in use, or you could keep it in a central store and let each machine borrow it when someone needs it. Each choice trades off speed, upkeep, and how alike the machines stay. This lesson is about weighing those trade-offs against a stated requirement.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company has 300 staff on a remote desktop service, and one accounting program gets a monthly update that every user must have. Would you rather put that update into the master copy that new machines are built from, or update each running machine by hand? Say why.
lessons.teach:
A session host is a virtual machine that users sign in to and run their work on. A host pool is a group of session hosts that serve the same users. An image is the master template a machine is built from, so every machine created from it starts with the same software. Deploying an app means getting it onto the session hosts in a way users can reach. There are three common methods. The first is to install the app into the image itself, so every new host starts with it. The second is to install it on hosts that are already running, either by hand or with a script. The third is dynamic delivery, called App attach here, where the app is packaged once into a disk image file that is attached to a host when a user needs it, without being installed in the base image.

To choose, ask how often the app changes, how many hosts need it, and whether every user needs it. A stable app that everyone uses suits the image. An app that changes monthly is costly to bake in, because each change means rebuilding the image and replacing hosts. A one-off fix on a few hosts suits a manual install, but only if you accept that the hosts may drift apart.

Worked example: 300 users need an accounting app updated monthly. Step one, baking it into the image means a new image and new hosts every month. Step two, installing by hand means 300 users' hosts must each be touched, and a host added later may miss the update. Step three, packaging it for dynamic delivery means you rebuild only the package each month and attach the new version. The choice is dynamic delivery.

The common mistake is installing an app by hand on running hosts and assuming future hosts will match. They will not, and users then report that the app works on one machine but not another. The consequence in a running system is inconsistent behaviour across a host pool that is hard to diagnose.

The right method is the one whose cost of change matches how often the app changes and how widely it must be identical.

questions.prompt: A design studio has 25 users, and every one of them needs a drawing viewer. The vendor releases a new viewer version every six weeks. Step one: baking the viewer into the image means building a new image and replacing all 25 session hosts each time a version ships. Step two: installing the viewer by hand on the running hosts means touching all 25 hosts each release, and any host added later may miss the update. Step three is missing. What should the studio do next, and why?
choices: Keep the manual installs, because 25 hosts is a small enough number to update by hand without drift.

Package the viewer for dynamic delivery so that only the package is rebuilt at each release and the new version is attached to hosts when users need it, because the cost of each change then matches how often the viewer changes.
Bake the viewer into the image but delay the rebuild until the next scheduled host refresh, so the hosts are replaced less often.
Install the viewer by hand on one host, copy that host's disk to the others, and skip the image entirely.
questions.why: Packaging the viewer for App attach means each six-week change rebuilds only the small package rather than the image or every host, which matches how often the app changes.

questions.prompt: Which description best fits App attach as used for deploying an app to Azure Virtual Desktop?
choices: The app is installed into the master image so every new session host starts with it.
The app is installed by a script on hosts that are already running, and each host is checked by hand afterwards.
The app is packaged once into a disk image file that is attached to a session host when a user needs it, without being installed in the base image.
A separate host pool is created for each app, and users are moved to that pool when they open it.
questions.why: App attach packages the app into a disk image file that is attached on demand rather than installed in the base image or on running hosts.

questions.prompt: A team installs a line-of-business app by hand on 10 running session hosts. The next month they add 5 new hosts built from the unchanged image. What is the most likely result?
choices: The app stops working on the original 10 hosts until the image is rebuilt.
All 15 hosts run the app identically, because the image and the running hosts share the same disk.
The new hosts are rebuilt automatically with the app, because a manual install always updates the image.
The 5 new hosts may lack the app or run a different version, so users see it working on some machines but not others.
questions.why: A manual install on running hosts is not carried into the image, so hosts added later may miss it and drift apart, which causes inconsistent behaviour across the pool.

questions.prompt: A company has 500 users who all need a stable company utility. The utility changes about once every two years. Which method best matches how often the app changes and how widely it must be identical?
choices: Install the utility into the master image, because a rare change is cheap to absorb through an occasional image rebuild and every host stays identical.
Install the utility on one host only and send users to it, because a single host avoids drift entirely.
Use App attach for the utility, because any app used by every user must be packaged separately.
Install the utility by hand on each host as users sign in, because rare changes never need to be tracked centrally.
questions.why: A stable app that everyone uses suits the image, since its rare changes make a periodic rebuild cheap and every host starts identical.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide between installing an app into the session host image, installing it on running hosts, and delivering it with App attach. Name one limit or tradeoff of the method you would be least likely to pick.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start with three questions: how often the app changes, how many hosts and users need it, and whether every host must match exactly. If the app is stable and everyone uses it, I bake it into the image, so every new host starts identical. If it changes often, baking it in is the wrong choice, because each change means rebuilding the image and replacing hosts. In that case I would use dynamic delivery with App attach, where a packaged app is attached when needed and I can replace the package without rebuilding the image. The tradeoff is that packaging takes effort and the app has to suit that approach. I would least likely install by hand on running hosts. It is quick for a single fix, but hosts drift apart and any host added later misses the change, which is hard to diagnose.
rubricPoints: Names the three methods: image, running hosts, and dynamic delivery with App attach
Ties the choice to how often the app changes and how many hosts need it
Explains that changing the image means rebuilding and replacing hosts
States a limit of one method, such as drift on hand-installed hosts or packaging effort for App attach

suggested.rationale: Choosing a delivery method is best practised by reasoning through a scenario with competing requirements, which no current mission covers directly.

lessons.plain: An application group is a named set of things that a remote desktop service can offer to users. Picture a shared office with a room of computers that many people can borrow. The application group is the label on the door that says what can be used in that room: either the whole computer desktop, or just a few specific programs. Creating the group means choosing which computers it draws from, deciding whether it offers the full desktop or individual apps, and placing it where users can find it. Who is allowed in is handled as a separate step that this lesson does not cover.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company has one pool of remote computers. Some staff should get the full desktop, while others should see only one accounting program. What would you expect to create to separate these two experiences, and why would one group not be enough?
lessons.teach:
A host pool is a collection of remote computers, called session hosts, that run user sessions in a virtual desktop service. An application group is the object that sits on top of a host pool and defines what users receive from it. There are two common kinds. A desktop application group offers the full remote desktop. A RemoteApp application group offers selected individual programs, which appear to the user almost as if they were installed locally. A workspace is the list or feed a user sees when they sign in, and an application group must be registered to a workspace before its contents are visible there.

Why it works: the host pool supplies the computing power, and the application group decides the shape of what is delivered. One host pool can feed several groups, so the same machines can serve different audiences without being duplicated.

Worked example: a finance team needs one accounting program on the pool named finance-pool. Step 1: create a RemoteApp application group and link it to finance-pool. Step 2: add the accounting program to that group (publishing is covered elsewhere). Step 3: register the group with the corporate workspace so it appears there.

Common mistake: creating a second desktop application group for a host pool that already has one. A host pool can hold only one desktop application group, so the creation fails or the new group is not usable as intended. Another frequent error is forgetting workspace registration, which leaves a correctly built group invisible to everyone.

Consequence: if the group is linked to the wrong host pool, users receive programs installed on machines that lack them, and sessions fail in ways that look like application faults.

An application group is the decision point that turns a pool of computers into the specific desktops or apps a user actually sees.

questions.prompt: Harbor Dental runs its front-desk and imaging tools on a host pool named dent-pool-02 in its own Azure subscription. Step 1: an administrator creates a RemoteApp application group named hygiene-apps, links it to dent-pool-02, and adds the X-ray viewer program to it. Step 2: the administrator registers hygiene-apps with the Harbor workspace so hygienists can see it at sign-in. Step 3 is the one left to you: the office manager needs a full remote desktop, and dent-pool-02 already has its single desktop application group. What is the correct action for Step 3?
choices: Create a second desktop application group on dent-pool-02 and register it with the Harbor workspace
Put the office manager's desktop on a different host pool, because dent-pool-02 cannot hold a second desktop application group
Link the existing RemoteApp group to a new desktop group so both share one registration
Create a RemoteApp group on dent-pool-02 that contains the full desktop
questions.why: A host pool can hold only one desktop application group, so the manager's full desktop must come from a different host pool, not a second group on this one.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does an application group decide?
choices: Which user profile containers are attached at sign-in
Whether a user's sign-in is allowed by the identity service
How much processor and memory each user session is given
What users receive from a host pool: the full desktop or selected individual programs
questions.why: An application group sits on a host pool and defines the shape of what is delivered, either a full desktop or chosen programs.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm has a host pool named lg-pool-west. Staff need three invoicing tools, but nobody needs a full desktop. Which setup fits best?
choices: Create a desktop application group on lg-pool-west and remove the tools from view
Create a second host pool just for the invoicing tools and link it to a desktop group
Create one desktop application group and install the three tools on every session host
Create a RemoteApp application group linked to lg-pool-west, add the three tools, then register the group with the workspace
questions.why: Selected individual programs call for a RemoteApp application group, linked to the pool that has the programs, and it must be registered to a workspace to be visible.

questions.prompt: An administrator builds a RemoteApp application group correctly, links it to the right host pool, and adds the programs. Staff still do not see it when they sign in. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The host pool needs a larger number of session hosts
The programs were added before the group was linked to the pool
The group is a desktop group, which users cannot see
The group has not been registered to a workspace
questions.why: A correctly built application group stays invisible until it is registered to a workspace, which is the list users see at sign-in.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what an application group is in a remote desktop service, how it relates to a host pool and a workspace, and one limit or tradeoff they should keep in mind when creating one.
lessons.modelAnswer: An application group is the layer that decides what users get from a host pool. The host pool is the set of remote computers doing the work, and the application group says whether users receive the full desktop or selected RemoteApp programs. When I create one, I first link it to the correct host pool, because that pool is where the programs must be installed. Then I register it with a workspace, since users only see groups that are registered there. The main limit is that a host pool can contain only one desktop application group, so if I want a full desktop for a new audience I have to reuse the existing one or use a separate pool. RemoteApp groups have no such limit, so I can create several on one pool to serve different teams from the same machines.
rubricPoints: Defines an application group as the object that sets what a host pool delivers, either a full desktop or individual apps
States that the group is linked to a host pool and that the programs must exist on that pool's session hosts
Explains that the group must be registered to a workspace before users can see it
Names the limit that a host pool holds only one desktop application group, while RemoteApp groups can be several

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine practises creating application groups, and the core material is product-specific configuration facts that a reading serves best.

lessons.plain: Assigning users to application groups means deciding who can see and open a particular set of apps or desktops published from an Azure Virtual Desktop host pool. Think of an application group as a shelf of apps in a shared office and the assignment as the list of people allowed to walk up to that shelf. Someone who is not on the list does not see those apps in their client, even when the apps are installed on the machines. The skill is matching the right people, usually through a group they already belong to, to the right shelf, so that access follows roles instead of hand-picked individuals.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company installs an accounting program on ten shared computers. Only the finance team should see it in their launcher. Before reading anything, how would you decide who gets to see that program, and where would you record that decision?
lessons.teach:
A host pool is a set of session host virtual machines that users connect to. A session host is one of those machines. An application group is a named collection of resources published from a host pool. A desktop application group offers a full remote desktop, and a RemoteApp application group offers individual programs that appear to run on their own. An assignment is a grant that lets a user, or a user group stored in Microsoft Entra ID (the Azure directory that holds user accounts and groups), see one application group. The client reads the assignments for the signed-in user and shows only the matching resources, so the check happens when the feed is built. A host pool holds one desktop application group, but it can hold several RemoteApp groups.

Worked example. The host pool HP-Prod has a RemoteApp group called RA-Finance that publishes Excel. The Entra group grp-finance has twelve members. Step one: assign grp-finance to RA-Finance. Step two: a finance member signs into the client. Step three: the client sees the membership and shows Excel. Step four: a user who is not in grp-finance signs in and sees no Excel icon, even though Excel is installed on the same session hosts.

Common mistake: people assume an assignment also grants licences, network reach or permission to files inside the app. It does not. An assignment only controls visibility of the published resource. Licensing, network rules and file permissions are separate controls.

Consequence: if you remove a user from an assignment, the icon can remain in their client until the feed refreshes, and a session they already opened keeps running until it ends. Assign through groups so the list stays current as people join and leave teams, and treat each assignment as a visibility control, not a security boundary.

questions.prompt: Northwind Clinic publishes its appointment tool from the host pool HP-Clinic. Step one: create a RemoteApp application group called RA-Scheduling that publishes the Practice Scheduler app. Step two is missing from this sequence. Step three: a receptionist who is a member of the Entra group grp-reception signs into the client, the client reads that user's assignments, and it shows Practice Scheduler. Step four: a nurse who is not in grp-reception signs in and sees no scheduler icon, even though the app is installed on the same session hosts. Which action completes the missing step two?
choices: Assign the Entra group grp-reception to the RemoteApp group RA-Scheduling
Buy a per-seat licence for Practice Scheduler and attach it to grp-reception
Grant grp-reception read access to the scheduler's database share
Create a second desktop application group in HP-Clinic that holds the scheduler
questions.why: An assignment is what lets a user or Entra group see an application group, so assigning grp-reception to RA-Scheduling is the step that makes the icon appear for receptionists and not for the nurse.

questions.prompt: In the client, what does an assignment decide?
choices: How much licence the user consumes when an application starts
Which folders an application is allowed to open once it is running
Whether the user is allowed to reach the session host over the network at all
Which published resources the client shows to a given user or group when it builds their feed
questions.why: The teaching text says an assignment is a grant of visibility, and the client checks it when building the feed, so it decides which resources appear, not network, licence or file rights.

questions.prompt: An administrator removes a user from an assignment while that user has a session open. Which outcome matches how assignments behave?
choices: The file permissions on the application's data are reset to their default values for everyone
The icon may stay in the client until the feed refreshes, and the open session keeps running until it ends
The licence is revoked at once and the user cannot reopen the application until a new licence is bought
The session is ended immediately, the user is signed out of the whole client, and any unsaved work in every open application is lost
questions.why: The teaching text notes that the icon can linger until the feed refreshes and that an already-opened session continues until it ends, so removal does not cut off a running session.

questions.prompt: A host pool named HP-Lab already contains one desktop application group. An engineer needs a full desktop for a second team. Which approach fits the rules in the teaching text?
choices: Create a second desktop application group in HP-Lab and assign the second team to it
Remove the existing desktop group, then create two RemoteApp groups for the new team
Create a separate host pool for the second team, because one host pool holds only one desktop application group
Assign the second team to the existing desktop group, since assignments can point at any group
questions.why: A host pool holds one desktop application group but can hold several RemoteApp groups, so a second full desktop needs a different host pool.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says the finance team cannot see the Excel app, even though Excel is installed on the session hosts. In your own words, explain how application group assignment works, what it does and does not control, and one limit or tradeoff of assigning access through a user group.
lessons.modelAnswer: Assignment is what decides which users see an application group in their client. The client gets the signed-in user's assignments and shows only the resources in those groups. So installing Excel is not enough, because the finance people also need an assignment to the RemoteApp group that publishes it. The assignment does not change anything on the session host, and it does not give licences, network access or file permissions. Those are separate. The tradeoff of using a user group is convenience and fewer manual changes. The limit is timing: when someone leaves the group, the icon can linger in their client until the feed refreshes, and an open session keeps running until it ends. So group membership should be reviewed, and the group should not be treated as a security boundary on its own.
rubricPoints: Assignment controls which users see an application group in their client feed
Installing an app on session hosts is not enough; the published group must be assigned to the user
An assignment does not grant licences, network access or file permissions
Assigning a user group is convenient, but removal takes effect with delay, and open sessions persist

suggested.rationale: The core skill is explaining what assignment controls and its limits, which is best practised by explaining it back to a teammate.

lessons.plain: Publishing an application as a RemoteApp means making one program available to a remote user as if it were installed on their own computer, without giving them the whole remote desktop. The program actually runs on a shared server in your cloud environment, and only its window appears on the user's screen, alongside their local apps. Think of a restaurant that lets a customer order one dish from the kitchen without giving them a seat in the kitchen. Teams use this when a user needs just one tool, such as an accounting program, because it keeps the experience focused and exposes less of the server to the user.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a shared server runs a program for many remote users, and each user should see only that program's window rather than a full desktop, what do you think the administrator has to set up, and what would go wrong if the program were installed on only one of several identical servers?
lessons.teach:
A session host is a virtual machine that runs user sessions. A host pool is a group of identical session hosts, usually built from one image, which is a saved template of an operating system with software already installed. An application group is a container that decides which programs a user can reach. A RemoteApp application group publishes individual programs, while a desktop application group publishes the whole desktop. A published app is a program a session host offers to the remote client as its own window. The client receives a list of these published apps, and launching one starts that program on the session host, streaming only its window back to the user.

Why it works: each session host has a start menu listing the programs installed on it. The administrator picks a program from that list, and the platform records how to launch it. The user never sees the rest of the server.

Worked example: a team needs a ledger program called Ledger Pro. Step 1: install Ledger Pro into the session host image and confirm it launches from the start menu. Step 2: create a RemoteApp application group in the host pool and add Ledger Pro from a session host's start menu list. Step 3: a user who has access to this group sees Ledger Pro in their client and launching it opens only that window.

Common mistake: installing the program by hand on one running session host rather than in the image. New hosts added to the pool later will not have it, so the published app fails on some sessions and works on others.

Consequence: because users are spread across hosts, this inconsistency looks like a random fault. Publish only programs that exist in the image the whole pool is built from.

questions.prompt: Harbor Legal runs a host pool named hp-legal, built from image version 3, for about 40 paralegals. The admin follows these steps for a document comparison tool called RedlineView. (1) Installs RedlineView into image version 3 and confirms it opens from the start menu. (2) Creates a RemoteApp application group in the hp-legal host pool. (3) The step that is missing. (4) Assigns the paralegal user group to the application group. Afterwards, some paralegals report that RedlineView opens and others get an error. Which action fills step (3)?
choices: Publish the full desktop of a session host in the same application group so RedlineView is reachable from it
Copy the RedlineView program file into the paralegal group folder so the client can find it
Install RedlineView by hand on one running session host so the group can read it from there
Add RedlineView from the start menu list of a session host into the RemoteApp application group
questions.why: A RemoteApp group publishes a program chosen from a session host's start menu list, which is the step that records how the platform launches RedlineView.

questions.prompt: A firm wants a single payroll calculator to appear as its own window on a user's laptop, with no visible remote desktop around it. Which application group type and publishing approach fits, based on how published apps work?
choices: A desktop application group, because it shows the full desktop of the session host
A host pool with no application group, because the client reads programs straight from the host folder
A RemoteApp application group with the calculator typed in as a path, because the start menu list is only for administrators
A RemoteApp application group with the payroll calculator picked from a session host's start menu list
questions.why: A RemoteApp group publishes individual programs, and the admin picks the program from the start menu list so the platform knows how to launch it.

questions.prompt: A pool of 8 session hosts is built from one image. An admin installs a timesheet tool by hand on 3 running hosts and publishes it. Some users open it fine and others get a launch failure. What is the most likely cause and fix?
choices: The tool was not in the image, so new or other hosts lack it; install it in the image and rebuild hosts from that image
The users lack permission to the host, so the fix is to grant local admin rights on all hosts
The application group type is wrong, so the fix is to switch it to a desktop group
The client cache is corrupt, so the fix is to clear it on each laptop
questions.why: Hosts built from the image lack the hand-installed tool, so only some sessions work; the durable fix is to put the program in the image the whole pool uses.

questions.prompt: A user launches a published app from a RemoteApp group and sees only that program's window, not the session host desktop. What explains this behaviour?
choices: The client hides the desktop by default, and the host still runs the full desktop behind it
The program was published as a single window, and the platform streams only that program's window while the rest of the host stays out of view
The session host shuts down all other programs at login to save memory
The user's profile limits the start menu to one item for security
questions.why: A published app is streamed as its own window, and the platform records how to launch just that program, so the user never sees the rest of the host.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has only used a full remote desktop how publishing an application as a RemoteApp differs, and name one limit or tradeoff of publishing a single app.
lessons.modelAnswer: With a full remote desktop, the user gets the whole session host desktop, with its taskbar, file system view and every installed program. With a RemoteApp, the administrator publishes one program into a RemoteApp application group, and the user sees only that program's window, which can sit next to their local apps. The program still runs on the shared session host, so the processing and the data stay in the cloud environment. One limit is that the published program depends entirely on the image: if it is missing or broken on some session hosts, users get intermittent failures that look random. Another tradeoff is that a user who needs several tools may end up with several separate windows, so a desktop group is sometimes simpler for them.
rubricPoints: A RemoteApp shows only one program's window, while a desktop application group shows the whole desktop.
The program runs on the session host, not on the user's own device.
The app must be installed in the image that all session hosts in the pool are built from.
A limit or tradeoff is named, such as inconsistent behaviour across hosts or several windows for several tools.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine walks through publishing apps to a session host pool, so the learner should read the teaching text and check the explanation prompt.

lessons.plain: Microsoft 365 Apps is the Office suite: Word, Excel, Outlook and the rest. On Azure Virtual Desktop, many people share one remote Windows machine at the same time, called a session host. Installing and licensing the suite there differs from a laptop, because one copy of the software must serve many people who each sign in with their own account. This lesson explains the three choices you make: how the apps are installed on the shared machine, how each user is activated, and how updates are kept consistent across all the hosts in a pool.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company has 40 staff sharing four remote Windows session hosts. Should Microsoft 365 Apps be installed once for the whole machine or separately for each user, and why?
lessons.teach:
Definitions first. A session host is a Windows virtual machine that users connect to remotely. A host pool is a group of identical session hosts. A multi-session host lets several users work on the same machine at once. Microsoft 365 Apps is the Office suite, delivered by subscription, and it has an update channel that sets how often new features arrive. Shared computer activation is the licensing mode for a machine used by many people, where each user signs in with their own licensed account instead of the machine holding a license for one person.

Why it works: on a single-user PC, the suite installs for one person and activates against that person's account. On a multi-session host, one installation is shared by everyone, so it must be installed for the whole machine rather than per user, and activated in shared computer mode. Each person then signs in with their own licensed Microsoft 365 account. The install is usually done once in the session host image, often with the Office Deployment Tool, a command-line installer that reads a configuration file listing the products, languages and update channel.

Worked example: 40 users share a pool of four hosts. Step 1: the admin builds the image and installs Microsoft 365 Apps for the whole machine, with shared computer activation turned on. Step 2: the admin sets the update channel and stops per-user updating, so changes arrive through the image process. Step 3: a user signs in, Excel opens, and activation uses that user's own license. Step 4: when a new image is rolled out to the pool, all four hosts run the same build.

Common mistake: installing Microsoft 365 Apps per user on a multi-session host, or patching one host by hand. The consequence is that users meet activation prompts, and hosts in one pool run different versions, so a document or add-in can behave differently depending on which host a user lands on.

The rule is: install once per machine, activate per user, and keep every host in the pool on the same build through the image.

questions.prompt: A small law practice has 15 staff sharing three multi-session hosts in one host pool. The admin wants Microsoft 365 Apps with the Spanish proofing tools available on every host. Step 1: the admin writes an Office Deployment Tool configuration file that lists Microsoft 365 Apps and the Spanish language. Step 2: the admin runs the installer inside the session host image so it installs for the whole machine, not per user. Step 3: [missing]. Which step completes the setup so that each staff member can open Word on any host with their own licensed account?
choices: Each staff member installs Microsoft 365 Apps from their own profile the first time they sign in.
The admin patches one host by hand after the image is built so it matches the newest version.
The admin copies a single license key onto all three hosts so the machines hold one shared license.
The admin turns on shared computer activation in the image so each user activates with their own licensed Microsoft 365 account.
questions.why: Shared computer activation is the mode that lets each user on a shared multi-session machine sign in with their own licensed account, which is the missing step after a whole-machine install.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is shared computer activation?
choices: A licensing mode for a machine used by many people, where each user signs in with their own licensed account instead of the machine holding a license for one person.
A way to install Microsoft 365 Apps separately inside each user's profile on a shared host.
A rule that stops a host pool from running more than one session at a time.
A process that copies a user's license onto every host they connect to.
questions.why: The teaching text defines shared computer activation as the licensing mode for shared machines in which each user signs in with their own licensed account.

questions.prompt: A company runs a host pool of eight session hosts for a call centre. The admin wants every host to run the same Microsoft 365 Apps build so that a macro-enabled template behaves the same for everyone. Which approach fits this requirement?
choices: Let each user install and update Office from their own profile at first sign-in.
Install Microsoft 365 Apps for the whole machine in one image, roll that image out to all eight hosts, and stop per-user updating.
Update each host by hand on its own schedule and check the build number afterwards.
Keep the hosts on whatever build they shipped with and tell users to avoid new features.
questions.why: Building one image with a whole-machine install and rolling it to every host keeps all hosts on the same build, which is the rule the teaching text sets out.

questions.prompt: A pool of four hosts runs Microsoft 365 Apps, but an admin patched only one host by hand after the image was built. Users report that a shared workbook with an add-in works on some sessions and fails on others. What is the most likely cause?
choices: Shared computer activation was turned off, so the workbook cannot be opened at all.
The hosts were given different language packs, which only affects spelling checks.
The hosts in the pool are running different builds, so the same file can behave differently depending on which host a user lands on.
The add-in license has expired on all four hosts at the same time.
questions.why: Patching one host by hand causes version drift within the pool, and the teaching text notes that this makes documents and add-ins behave differently depending on the host.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would set up Microsoft 365 Apps on a multi-session host pool, and name one limit or tradeoff of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would install Microsoft 365 Apps once for the whole machine in the session host image, not per user, because every person on a multi-session host shares that one installation. I would turn on shared computer activation so each person signs in with their own licensed account, rather than the machine needing a license tied to one seat. I would set the update channel and stop per-user updating, so every host gets the same build from the image. The tradeoff is that updates now need an image rebuild and a rollout to the pool, so a fix takes longer to reach users than it would on a single PC, and a bad build affects every host in the pool at once unless I roll it out in stages.
rubricPoints: Installed once for the whole machine, not per user, because the installation is shared
Shared computer activation so each user signs in with their own licensed account
Consistent version across the pool, managed through the image and update channel
A named tradeoff, such as slower updates or wider impact of a bad build

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine covers Microsoft 365 Apps installation and licensing on session hosts, so reading the setup concepts is the best fit.

lessons.plain: OneDrive is a Microsoft cloud storage service that keeps a person's files in sync across their devices. In a virtual desktop setup, the question is how one personal cloud folder works when many people share the same Windows machine at the same time. Implementing OneDrive here means installing its sync program so every user session can use it, signing each user into their own account, and making sure one person's files never mix with another's. Multisession means one Windows operating system serves several users at once, each in a separate session. Think of a shared office kitchen with one fridge: everyone can use it, but each person's food stays labelled and separate.
lessons.guessPrompt: If five people sign in to the same shared Windows machine at once, and each has their own OneDrive account, what do you think could go wrong if the sync program was installed only for the first person who logged in?
lessons.teach:
Several terms first. A sync client is the program that copies files between a computer and the cloud. A session is one user's signed-in workspace on a machine. Multisession means one operating system hosts several sessions at the same time. A per-user install puts a program inside one user's profile, which is that user's private area on the machine. A per-machine install puts it in a place every user on the machine can reach.

Why this matters: the sync client has to run inside each user's session, so it must exist on the machine for everyone, but it must keep each person's account and files separate. A per-machine install gives every session access to the program, while the program itself signs in and syncs only the account belonging to the session it is running in.

Worked example. Host HP-01 is multisession with a per-machine sync client. Step 1: Asha signs in and gets session 1. Step 2: the client starts inside session 1 and reads Asha's account. Step 3: it syncs only Asha's folders under her profile. Step 4: Ben signs in to session 2 on the same host. Step 5: the same program starts in session 2, reads Ben's account, and syncs only his folders. Neither session can see the other's files.

Common mistake: installing the sync client only in one user's profile on a multisession host. The other users then have no working client, and the first user's setup can leak into shared areas.

Consequence: on a running host, a missing or per-user install means some users open sessions where folders never appear or sync errors pile up, and support tickets follow.

A multisession OneDrive setup works only when the sync program is installed for the whole machine, and each session signs in as its own user.

questions.prompt: Host LF-07 is multisession and has a sync client installed only inside the profile of paralegal Iris. Step 1: Iris signs in and gets session 1, and the client runs there and syncs her folders. Step 2: Gavin signs in to session 2 on the same host. Step 3: this step is missing. Step 4: Gavin sees no OneDrive folder and no signed-in account in his session. Which statement fills step 3?
choices: Gavin's session starts Iris's copy of the client, which quietly syncs her folders into a shared area that Gavin can open.
The host restarts when Gavin signs in, which clears session 2 and removes every OneDrive folder from the machine.
Gavin's session finds the client and signs it in with Iris's account, so he sees her files but they show a sync error.
No sync program is available to Gavin's session, because the install sits only in Iris's profile, which his session cannot use.
questions.why: A per-user install lives in one profile, so other sessions on the same multisession host have no working client, which is why Gavin sees nothing.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, which kind of install lets every session on a multisession host reach the sync program while still keeping each person's account separate?
choices: A per-machine install, placed where every user on the machine can reach it
A copy of the sync program stored on a USB drive that each user plugs in
A per-user install placed in the profile of the first user to sign in
An install that runs only while the administrator is signed in to the host
questions.why: A per-machine install is reachable by every session, and the program still signs in and syncs only the account belonging to the session it runs in.

questions.prompt: Host DS-12 is multisession. The finance team's sales users and finance users share it. An installer put the sync client only inside one finance user's profile. What is the most likely result?
choices: Only the finance user whose profile holds the client can use it, and the sales users have no working client in their sessions.
Nothing changes, because a sync client always installs for every session regardless of where it is placed.
Every user on the host, including sales, gets the client automatically at next sign-in.
The client moves into a shared area on its own, so sales and finance both sync to the same folder.
questions.why: A per-user install is visible only inside that one profile, so the other users' sessions on the multisession host have no working client.

questions.prompt: Which condition must hold for OneDrive to work correctly on a multisession host?
choices: The sync program is installed for the whole machine, and each session signs in as its own user.
Every user shares one account so that the sync program only has to sign in once for the whole host.
The sync program is installed only in the first session, and later sessions reuse its signed-in account.
The host runs one session at a time, and the sync program is installed in the profile of the administrator.
questions.why: Multisession OneDrive needs a per-machine sync program so every session can run it, and each session must sign in as its own user so accounts and files stay separate.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why OneDrive on a multisession host needs a different installation approach from a single-user laptop, and name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you describe.
lessons.modelAnswer: On a laptop, one person owns the machine, so installing the sync client for that user is enough. On a multisession host, several people share one Windows install at the same time, and each one needs the sync client running inside their own session. So the client has to be installed for the whole machine, not just one user's profile. The program then starts in each session and signs in as that session's user, keeping files separate. The tradeoff is that a per-machine install is shared by everyone, so an update, a bad setting, or a broken install affects every user on that host at once. You also need to plan for each session to sign in with a different account, and for storage limits and sync load to grow with the number of users.
rubricPoints: A single-user laptop has one owner, but a multisession host runs several user sessions at once.
The sync client must be installed for the whole machine so each session can run it.
Each session signs in as its own user, so files stay separate between people.
A per-machine install is shared, so one bad update or setting affects every user on that host.

suggested.rationale: Choosing the right OneDrive setup for a shared host is best learned by reasoning through a multi-user scenario, which this objective's exam-style situations cover.

lessons.plain: Microsoft Teams is a chat, meeting and video calling app. On a virtual desktop, Teams runs on a shared computer in a data centre, but the camera and microphone are on the user's own laptop. If the data centre handled all the video work, calls would be slow and choppy when many people shared the same machine. Teams media optimization is a way to move that heavy audio and video work onto the user's device, so the shared computer only does light work.
