Setting this up means installing Teams correctly on the shared computer and installing a small helper component on each user's device, so the two can cooperate.
lessons.guessPrompt: A user joins a Teams video call from a laptop that is connected to a virtual desktop. Should the camera video be processed on the shared session host in the data centre, or on the laptop itself, and why?
lessons.teach:
Microsoft Teams is a chat, meeting and calling app. A session host is a Windows machine in Azure Virtual Desktop that many users share. Media optimization means Teams hands its real-time audio and video work to the user's own device instead of doing it on the shared host. The Remote Desktop WebRTC Redirector Service is the small component installed on the client device that makes this possible. WebRTC is a web standard for live audio and video, and a redirector is a component that passes a stream from one place to another. Here, the redirector connects the Teams app on the session host with the laptop's camera, microphone and speakers.

Why it works: without optimization, video frames would have to be captured, encoded and decoded on the shared host, using its CPU. With optimization, the laptop handles encoding and decoding, and the host only sends control signals and the chat window's screen image.

Worked example: a user joins a meeting from a laptop. Step 1: Teams on the session host starts the call. Step 2: the host asks the laptop's redirector for the camera feed. Step 3: the laptop encodes the video and sends it toward the Teams service. Step 4: incoming audio is decoded on the laptop and played through its speakers. Result: the host's CPU stays low even when many users are in meetings.

Common mistake: installing Teams on the session host without installing the redirector on the client device, or installing Teams in per-user mode instead of machine-wide mode. Teams then falls back to processing media on the host. Calls still work, but they use more host CPU, and audio can lag when many users share one host.

Consequence: in a running pool, a missing or misconfigured optimization shows up as high host CPU during meetings and as user complaints about choppy audio and video.

questions.prompt: Northwind Clinic has a nurse, Sam, who joins a patient-family video call from a laptop. Teams runs on a session host in the clinic's pool, and the laptop has the Remote Desktop WebRTC Redirector Service installed in machine-wide mode. The call is traced as follows. Step 1: Teams on the session host starts the call. Step 2: the host asks the laptop's redirector for the microphone feed. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: incoming audio is decoded on the laptop and played through its speakers. Which completion correctly fills the missing step 3?
choices: The host encodes the microphone audio on its own CPU before sending it on.
The laptop encodes the microphone audio and sends it toward the Teams service.
The laptop sends the raw, uncompressed microphone audio straight to the other participants.
The host sends the laptop a full copy of Teams so the laptop can run the call locally.
questions.why: With media optimization, the client device handles encoding of the captured audio and sends it toward the Teams service, so the shared host's CPU is not used for that work.

questions.prompt: Which statement best defines the Remote Desktop WebRTC Redirector Service?
choices: A Windows service that schedules meetings across several session host pools.
A small client-side component that connects the Teams app on the session host with the local camera, microphone and speakers.
A Teams setting that turns off video for all users on a session host.
A shared host component that stores each user's chat history in Teams.
questions.why: The text describes the redirector as the small component installed on the client device that links the host's Teams app with the laptop's camera, microphone and speakers.

questions.prompt: A company runs six session hosts. Users report choppy audio during meetings, and host CPU climbs sharply whenever several people are in calls at once. Which cause best fits these symptoms?
choices: Teams is installed per-user rather than machine-wide, so media is processed on the host.
The chat window's screen image is being compressed too heavily on the host.
Media optimization is working, so the host is simply undersized for chat messages.
The client devices have too much free memory, so calls are routed to the host.
questions.why: Per-user installation, or a missing redirector on clients, makes Teams fall back to processing media on the shared host, which raises host CPU and causes audio lag under load.

questions.prompt: In a pool where media optimization is working correctly, a user in a video meeting is viewing a shared chat window. Which work still happens on the session host?
choices: Decoding incoming audio so it can play through the user's speakers.
Capturing the microphone feed and compressing it into a call stream.
Encoding the user's webcam video before it is sent to other participants.
Sending control signals and the chat window's screen image to the user's device.
questions.why: With optimization, the host only sends control signals and the chat window's screen image, while the client handles the camera, microphone and speaker media.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how Teams media optimization works on Azure Virtual Desktop, and name one limit or tradeoff of this approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: Teams media optimization moves the real-time audio and video work from the shared session host to the user's own device. The Teams app on the host is installed machine-wide and set to know it runs in a virtual desktop environment. On the user's device, the Remote Desktop WebRTC Redirector Service connects the host's Teams app to the local camera, microphone and speakers. The device handles encoding and decoding, so the host's CPU stays low and calls are smoother. The tradeoff is that the optimization only works when both sides are set up correctly and the client device is capable enough. Clients that lack the redirector, or devices with weak CPUs, fall back to host processing, which uses more shared resources and can make calls worse.
rubricPoints: Media optimization moves audio and video processing from the session host to the user's device.
The Remote Desktop WebRTC Redirector Service runs on the client and connects Teams to local devices.
Teams must be installed in machine-wide mode on the session host and configured for a virtual desktop environment.
A limit: if the client lacks the redirector or is underpowered, Teams falls back to host processing and performance drops.

suggested.rationale: The core skill is explaining how the host and client split the media work and what happens when one side is missing, which is best practised by explaining it back.

lessons.plain: A browser in a virtual desktop session is the web browser app, such as Microsoft Edge, that a user opens inside a remote Windows desktop rather than on their own laptop. The browser actually runs on the shared session host in a data centre, and the user only sees its screen streamed to them. Setting it up means deciding which browser is installed, which one opens when a link is clicked, where its settings and saved sign-ins live so they survive between sessions, and how it reaches the internet and internal sites. Get these right and web work feels local; get them wrong and users lose bookmarks, get stuck signing in, or wait on slow pages.
lessons.guessPrompt: A user in a remote desktop session clicks a web link and the page loads slowly, while the same link is fast on their laptop. Before we explain anything, where do you think the browser is actually running, and what would you check first?
lessons.teach:
A browser is the program that displays web pages. In Azure Virtual Desktop, users sign in to a remote Windows desktop called a session, and that desktop runs on a session host, a virtual machine in Azure that several users can share. So a browser opened in the session runs on the session host, not on the user's device. The user's device only receives the picture of the browser window and sends keyboard and mouse input back.

This matters for three things. First, the browser's own data: bookmarks, saved passwords, cookies and cache are written to the user's profile on the session host. If nothing keeps that profile between sessions, the next sign-in starts from a blank browser. Profile storage is covered elsewhere, but you need to know the browser depends on it. Second, which browser opens: a session can have several browsers installed, and one is set as the default that opens links. Third, network path: the browser fetches web pages over the session host's network, so its proxy settings, name lookups and access to internal sites are those of the session host, not the laptop.

Worked example. A nurse clicks a link to an internal portal from her session. Step one: the link opens in the default browser on the session host. Step two: that browser asks the session host's network to find the portal's address. Step three: the session host, which sits in a virtual network with access to the internal site, fetches the page and streams the result to her laptop. If the portal fails, check the session host's route, not her laptop.

Common mistake: testing browser speed on your own laptop and concluding the problem is the user's connection. The network and CPU that matter are the session host's, and a host with too few cores makes every browser tab feel slow.

Consequence: when many users share one small session host, their browsers compete for the same CPU and memory, so one heavy page can slow everyone on that host.

questions.prompt: A paralegal at a small law firm opens a court filing portal from a link inside her Azure Virtual Desktop session. The session runs on a session host, a virtual machine in Azure that the firm shares among several users. Step one: the link opens in the default browser, which is the browser set to open links, and that browser runs on the session host, not on her laptop. Step two: [missing]. Step three: the session host fetches the portal page over its own network connection and streams the result to her laptop.
choices: The browser saves the address lookup to the paralegal's laptop before contacting the session host
The browser skips the address lookup because the portal is hosted on the internet
The laptop's browser looks up the portal address so the page loads faster
The browser asks the session host's network to find the portal's address
questions.why: The browser runs on the session host, so the name lookup for the portal's address goes through the session host's network, not the laptop's.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, where does a browser opened inside an Azure Virtual Desktop session actually run?
choices: On the user's laptop, with only the picture sent to the session
On a separate browser server in the user's office network
Inside the Azure portal web page the administrator uses
On the session host, a virtual machine in Azure shared by several users
questions.why: The teaching text says the browser runs on the session host, and the user's device only receives the picture and sends input back.

questions.prompt: A design firm has one session host with two CPU cores shared by about thirty users. One user reports that every web page is slow, while a colleague on a different host loads pages quickly. Which explanation best fits the teaching text?
choices: The user's home Wi-Fi is slow, which is why the browser inside the session is slow
The user's bookmarks are missing, which makes pages take longer to load
The user changed the default browser on their laptop, which slows the session
The shared session host's CPU and memory are too small, so heavy browser use by any user slows everyone on that host
questions.why: The teaching text says a host with too few cores makes browser tabs feel slow, and that shared hosts let one heavy page slow everyone on the host.

questions.prompt: A contractor signs in to a session on Monday, adds bookmarks, and saves a password in the browser. On Tuesday, a new session shows an empty browser. Which explanation fits the teaching text?
choices: The contractor's laptop browser was reset, so the session browser was blank
The proxy settings on the contractor's laptop wiped the browser data overnight
Bookmarks are stored in the Azure billing records, which were reset on Tuesday
The browser's data lives in the user's profile on the session host, and nothing kept that profile between sessions
questions.why: The teaching text explains that bookmarks, saved passwords, cookies and cache are written to the profile on the session host, so without profile persistence the next sign-in starts blank.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says that because the browser runs in the cloud, we never need to think about where it keeps its data or which browser opens links. Explain to them, in your own words, what really happens when a user opens a web link in an Azure Virtual Desktop session, and name one limit or tradeoff of having the browser on a shared session host.
lessons.modelAnswer: Your teammate is half right. The browser does run in Azure, on the session host, and the user only sees its screen. But three things still need deciding. The browser's saved state, such as bookmarks, cookies and sign-ins, lives in the user's profile on that host, so if nothing keeps the profile between sessions, the user starts fresh each time. Which browser opens a link is set by a default that someone has to choose and keep consistent across the pool. And the page is fetched over the session host's network, so its routes and access to internal sites are the host's, not the user's. The main tradeoff is sharing: several users' browsers compete for one host's CPU and memory, so a heavy page can slow everyone on that host. Sizing and placement have to account for that, rather than assuming the cloud makes it free.
rubricPoints: The browser runs on the session host and only its screen is streamed to the user's device.
Browser data such as bookmarks, cookies and sign-ins must persist via the user's profile or it resets each session.
The default browser determines which app opens links, so it must be chosen and kept consistent deliberately.
Network access and performance come from the session host, and shared hosts create CPU and memory contention.

suggested.rationale: Choosing the right browser behaviour for a given scenario is best practised by reasoning through an exam-style situation, and no listed mission covers browsers.

lessons.plain: App attach is a way to deliver an application to a remote desktop session without installing it into the base image of the session host. The application is packaged into a disk image file, stored on a shared network location, and connected to the session host when it is needed. Dynamic delivery means the application is connected when a user signs in and disconnected when they sign out, so one host can serve different app versions or sets of apps to different people. It works like lending someone a tool from a shared shed instead of building it into the house. The core skill is choosing the right mode and knowing what breaks when the shared storage is slow.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team installs a 2 GB design tool into the master image used by 200 session hosts, so every small update to that tool means rebuilding and redeploying the whole image. What would you change so the tool can be updated without rebuilding every host?
lessons.teach:
A session host is a virtual machine that users connect to. A base image is the master copy of the operating system and installed software that new hosts are built from. App attach is a delivery method in which an application is packaged as a disk image (a single file that appears as a drive when mounted), stored on a file share the hosts can reach, and then attached to a session host so the app becomes available to users. Dynamic delivery means the attach happens on demand: the image is mounted when a user signs in and detached when they sign out. Static delivery means the image stays attached for the life of the host.

Why it works: installing an app into the base image forces you to rebuild and redeploy every host to change that one app. With app attach, the base image stays small and stable, and you update the app by pointing users at a new package. Dynamic attach also means a host carries only the apps a given user needs at that moment, and different user groups can receive different app sets from the same pool.

Worked example: a finance app, version 4, is packaged as one image on a file share. Step 1: the admin makes that package available to the finance user group. Step 2: a finance user signs in to a session host. Step 3: the host mounts the image from the share and the app appears. Step 4: the user signs out and the image is detached. Step 5: to move to version 5, the admin makes the new package available to the group. No host is rebuilt.

Common mistake: treating dynamic attach as free. The image is read over the network at sign-in, so a slow or unreachable share makes sign-in slow or the app missing. Detaching an image while a session still depends on it can also break that session.

Consequence in a running pool: if the file share fails at 09:00, every sign-in that needs the app can stall, so the share needs the same availability planning as the session hosts themselves.

questions.prompt: A dental practice packages its scheduling tool, version 7, as one disk image on a file share that its session hosts can reach. Step 1: the admin makes the version 7 image available to the front-desk group. Step 2: a front-desk user signs in, the host mounts the image from the share, and the scheduling tool appears. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: the admin packages version 8 as a new image and makes it available to the front-desk group, and no host is rebuilt. What happens in step 3?
choices: When the user signs out, the image is detached from the host.
The file share is deleted so that the version 7 image cannot be read again.
The host is rebuilt from scratch to remove the scheduling tool.
The image is copied into the base image so it stays on every host permanently.
questions.why: Dynamic attach mounts the image at sign-in and detaches it at sign-out, so detaching on sign-out is the step that completes the cycle.

questions.prompt: Which description best defines App attach?
choices: A method that packages an application as a disk image on a file share and attaches that image to a session host so the app becomes available to users.
A method that installs an application directly into the base image so every host carries it from the start.
A method that streams a user's desktop from a central server over a remote connection.
A method that backs up session host disks to a separate region for recovery.
questions.why: App attach is defined by packaging the app as a disk image stored on a share and attaching it to a host, which is what the last option describes.

questions.prompt: A pool uses dynamic App attach. At 08:55 every sign-in that needs the app becomes very slow, while hosts themselves are healthy. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: Static attach has been switched on, which blocks sign-ins until the host restarts.
The share holding the app image is slow or hard to reach, because dynamic attach reads the image over the network at sign-in.
The base image has grown too large for the hosts to start.
The user groups have been given too many apps, so each host runs out of memory.
questions.why: With dynamic attach the image is mounted over the network when a user signs in, so a slow or unreachable share directly slows or blocks sign-in.

questions.prompt: A host pool serves a claims team and a billing team. Each team needs a different app, and the admin wants a host to carry only the apps a given user needs at that moment, without rebuilding hosts. Which delivery approach fits?
choices: Use static attach so each host keeps both images mounted for its whole life.
Give every host a separate copy of each app on its local disk.
Use dynamic attach, assigning each team its own image so it is mounted only at that team's sign-in.
Install both apps in the base image and hide them with folder permissions.
questions.why: Dynamic attach mounts only the images a user's group is assigned at sign-in, meeting the need without rebuilding hosts, while static attach would keep images mounted for the host's whole life.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would choose dynamic app attach over installing the application into the base image, and name one limit or tradeoff you would plan for.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would choose dynamic app attach when an application changes often, when only some users need it, or when a large app would make the base image slow to rebuild. The base image stays stable, and we update the app by pointing the right user group at a new package, with no host rebuild. The tradeoff is that the package is read from a network file share at sign-in. If that share is slow or down, users wait longer to sign in or the app is missing. So I would plan the share's availability and capacity like any other critical dependency, test sign-in time with the attached app, and avoid detaching an image while sessions are still using it. Static attach or a baked-in install may be simpler when every user needs the app all day.
rubricPoints: Dynamic app attach mounts the application package on demand and detaches it, rather than installing it into the base image.
Choose it when apps change often, differ by user group, or make the base image heavy to rebuild.
The package is read from a shared file location at sign-in, so that storage becomes a dependency.
A slow or unavailable share causes slow sign-ins or missing apps, and detaching an in-use image can break sessions.

suggested.rationale: Choosing between base-image install, static attach and dynamic attach from a requirement is an exam-style reasoning task, so working through scenarios adds the most here.

lessons.plain: App attach is a way to deliver an application to a remote desktop session without installing it on the machine that hosts the session. You take the application's files and settings, wrap them in a single disk-style image file, and make that image available to the host. When a user signs in and is allowed to use the app, the image is attached like a removable drive and the app runs from it. Creating the package is the step where you wrap the app correctly, so it works for everyone who receives it and can be replaced with a newer image later.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose you want one application to appear in many users' remote sessions, but you do not want to install it on every session host. What would you expect to change about how the app gets onto the host, and what would you check before wrapping it up?
lessons.teach:
An application package here is a disk image file, usually a VHD or VHDX (a virtual hard disk format) or a CIM image (a compact read-only image format), that holds the app's files and the registry entries the app needs. A capture is the act of recording what an installer writes so that it lands on that image instead of on the operating system. A host pool is the group of session hosts, the virtual machines users connect to, that the package is registered with.

Why it works: the installer runs on a clean machine while the packaging process is capturing, so the app's files and registry changes are recorded into the image rather than mixed into the machine's own system. When a user signs in, the host attaches the image read-only and the app runs from it. Nothing from the app stays behind after sign-out, and the same image can be given to many sessions.

Worked example: a team packages a reporting tool. Step 1: start a clean VM with the same OS build as the session hosts. Step 2: start the packaging process, which creates a new VHDX sized for the app. Step 3: run the installer while the capture is active, so the files go to the disk. Step 4: finish the capture and detach the disk. Step 5: upload the image, register it with the host pool, and assign the app to users. A later version gets a new image rather than an in-place patch.

Common mistake: running the installer outside the capture, so the image comes out empty or missing files. Another is packaging an app that needs a driver or a Windows service, which an attached disk cannot supply.

Consequence: if the package was captured on the wrong OS build or leaves out a dependency, the app fails to start for every user it was assigned to, and every session on that host shows the same failure.

questions.prompt: A clinic's IT team packages a scheduling client, a desktop app, as a VHDX (a virtual hard disk file) for App attach (a method that attaches a read-only app image to a session at sign-in). Step 1: they start a clean VM on the same Windows build as their session hosts. Step 2: they start the packaging process, which creates a 20 GB VHDX. Step 3: they run the installer while the capture is active, so its files and registry keys are written to the disk. Step 4: [missing step]. Step 5: they upload the image, register it with the host pool, and assign the app to clinic staff. Which action fills the missing step?
choices: Finish the capture and detach the disk so the image is closed before it is uploaded
Delete the clean VM so no leftover build files remain on the host
Install the scheduling client again directly on each session host so its registry keys are present
Assign the app to staff before the capture ends, so the assignment is written into the image
questions.why: The capture must be finished and the disk detached so the installer's files and registry changes are fully recorded on the image before it is uploaded and registered.

questions.prompt: During a capture, an installer runs on a clean machine. Where do the app's files and registry entries end up?
choices: In the package image, rather than in the session host's own operating system
On the session host's system drive, where they remain after the user signs out
In the host pool's shared profile store, merged into each user's profile
In a separate driver package that the host installs when it starts up
questions.why: The capture records the installer's output onto the image itself, which keeps it separate from the host's operating system.

questions.prompt: A team packages an app on a machine running a different Windows build from their session hosts, and the app depends on a Windows service that an attached disk cannot supply. What is the most likely result?
choices: Only the first session on each host fails, because later sessions reuse a cached copy of the app
The app runs normally because the attached image copies the service into each user's profile
The app fails to start for every user it is assigned to, and every session on that host shows the same failure
The app runs but saves its files to each user's profile, so no failure is visible
questions.why: A package captured on the wrong build or missing a dependency fails for all assigned users, because the same image is given to every session on the host.

questions.prompt: A vendor releases version 2 of an app that a team already packages for App attach. Following the approach taught, what should the team do?
choices: Keep the old image and write the new installer's files onto the same disk
Copy the new files into each session host's program folder by hand
Run the new installer inside the existing image to patch it in place
Create a new image for version 2 and register it, rather than patching the old image in place
questions.why: The teaching approach gives each later version a new image rather than an in-place patch to the existing one.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks why we do not just install the reporting app on the session hosts like everything else. Explain to them, in your own words, what creating an App attach package changes and name one limit or tradeoff of this approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: Installing directly means the app is written into each host's operating system, so every host has to be kept in step and the app is always present for everyone. App attach instead captures the install into a disk image, and the host attaches that image when a user who is assigned the app signs in. The package is built on a clean machine with the same OS build as the hosts, so the files and registry entries it needs are all recorded in it. The tradeoff is that the package has limits: it cannot carry drivers or system services, so apps that depend on them still need a normal install. Also, every update means building and registering a new image, so the packaging step has to be repeated and tested each time.
rubricPoints: Describes the package as a disk image holding the app's files and registry entries, captured during install
Explains that the image is attached at sign-in and not installed into the host OS
Names a limit, such as no drivers or system services, or the need to rebuild the image for each update
Notes the clean machine must match the session host OS build

suggested.rationale: The objective is a procedural packaging workflow that no listed mission or planned engine covers, so reading the teaching text is the best fit.

lessons.plain: When many remote desktop machines run for many people, the practical way to understand a problem is to gather their records in one place. This objective is about setting that up for Azure Virtual Desktop: choosing which records each machine sends, sending the control service's records as well, and then searching the combined set to answer questions such as why sessions dropped at a particular time. Think of a mailroom. Each machine drops its notes into the same box, and you need to know which notes to ask for and how to find the one that matters.
lessons.guessPrompt: A user says their session froze, but the session host itself still looks healthy when you check it directly. Where would you look first for evidence, and why is a record stored only on that one machine a weak place to start?
lessons.teach:
A session host is a virtual machine that users connect to when they sign in to an Azure Virtual Desktop environment. Log collection means copying the useful records that a host and the control service produce, such as Windows event logs, performance counters, and service diagnostics, into one central store. That store is a Log Analytics workspace, a database that holds log records and lets you search them with a query language. Two parts make collection work. A collection agent runs on each session host and gathers what it is told to gather. A data collection rule is the set of instructions attached to that agent. It names the sources, for example specific Windows event log channels and performance counters such as CPU use and available memory. Separately, the control service that brokers connections for a host pool sends its own diagnostic categories, such as connection and error records, to the workspace through diagnostic settings. Collecting both sides lets you line up a failed connection on the control side with a host-side error from the same minute.

Why it works: one store lets you correlate records from many machines, and a query language lets you filter large volumes quickly instead of logging into each host.

Worked example: users report sessions dropping at 10:00. Step 1: confirm the connection-error diagnostic category is enabled and arriving in the workspace. Step 2: filter those records to the 09:55 to 10:05 window. Step 3: group the results by session host name. Step 4: if one host dominates, pull that host's system event records for the same window and look for a service restart.

Common mistake: assuming a quiet log means a quiet system. If the collection rule omits a channel, or the agent is missing or not associated with the host, nothing arrives, and the gap looks like calm. Check that data is actually ingesting before you trust an empty result.

Consequence: after a change, a host that silently stops sending logs can hide a failing component for days. Ingestion health is therefore something you monitor in its own right.

questions.prompt: Harbor Freight Partners runs a host pool called hp-depot-west with six session hosts. A collection rule named dcr-depot-core is meant to send performance counters and Windows event records from all six hosts to their Log Analytics workspace. After a Tuesday agent update, the team notices vm-depot-04 has produced no records since Tuesday, so its dashboard looks calm. Their checklist is: Step 1: confirm vm-depot-04 is associated with dcr-depot-core. Step 2: [MISSING STEP: the team has not yet written this step down]. Step 3: run a query for the past 24 hours of CPU counter records from vm-depot-04 and confirm rows return before trusting the dashboard. Which missing step completes the checklist?
choices: Confirm the CPU counter is listed among the sources in dcr-depot-core that applies to vm-depot-04
Check the control service's connection-error category, because host counters are sent through it
Raise the workspace retention period so older CPU records survive longer
Delete vm-depot-04 from the host pool and add it back as a new session host
questions.why: A data collection rule only gathers the sources it names, so the CPU counter must be listed in the rule for records from that host to exist, and the other choices either act on the wrong component or change storage rather than collection.

questions.prompt: A team wants connection and error records from the brokering service of their host pool to appear in their Log Analytics workspace. Which setting sends those records?
choices: A data collection rule placed on each session host
The collection agent's installation log on each host
The retention policy of the Log Analytics workspace
Diagnostic settings on the control service for the host pool
questions.why: The control service sends its own diagnostic categories through diagnostic settings, while the data collection rule and agent handle only the host side.

questions.prompt: A session host at a logistics company stops sending Windows event records to its workspace after a rule was edited. Which check should come first?
choices: Open the data collection rule and confirm the event channel for that component is listed as a source
Assume the host is healthy because no alert has fired
Increase the sampling interval of the CPU performance counter
Reboot the Log Analytics workspace to reset its ingestion
questions.why: A rule only gathers the channels it names, so an edit that drops a channel silently stops those records, and checking the rule's sources is the direct test.

questions.prompt: A query over the past hour returns zero session-host error records for a host pool. What should be verified before concluding that no errors occurred?
choices: That the workspace name matches the name of the host pool
That the query was written in the newest version of the query language
That the hosts were restarted within the past week
That records from those hosts are actually arriving in the workspace during that hour
questions.why: An empty result only means calm if ingestion is working, since a missing agent or a rule gap produces silence that looks identical to a quiet system.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why session host logs should be sent to a central workspace instead of being read on each host, and name one limit or tradeoff of central collection that you would need to plan for.
lessons.modelAnswer: Reading logs on each host works for one machine, but a pool may have many hosts, and the user's problem often spans the control service and several hosts at once. A central Log Analytics workspace lets us query all of them together and line up events by time. The tradeoff is cost and volume: every channel and performance counter we collect is ingested and billed, so a rule that collects everything can be expensive and noisy. There is also a dependency risk. If the agent or its data collection rule breaks, data stops arriving without any obvious error, so we need to watch ingestion health, not just the hosts. Retention periods also limit how far back we can look, and event logs can contain sensitive data, so access to the workspace must be controlled.
rubricPoints: Central workspace lets you correlate control-side and host-side records across many hosts by time.
Collection is driven by an agent plus a data collection rule that names the specific sources.
Cost and noise rise with the volume of data collected, so collect only what the questions need.
A broken agent or rule causes silent data gaps, so ingestion health must be monitored.

suggested.rationale: This mission practises finding and filtering the evidence that matters in logs, the same skill used to query collected session host records, although it uses Linux rather than Azure Virtual Desktop.

lessons.plain: Azure Virtual Desktop lets people sign in and work on a remote Windows desktop hosted in the cloud. Azure Monitor is the general-purpose service that collects the numbers and records such a system produces, so you can see how it is behaving. Think of it as the dashboard and flight recorder for a fleet of remote desktops: it shows whether machines are busy, whether sign-ins are slow, and whether something has failed, and it can warn you before users start complaining. Monitoring means deciding in advance which signals matter, collecting them, and acting when they cross a line you care about.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose forty people sign in to remote desktops at 9:00 and half of them say their desktop is slow, but a quick glance at the host CPU looks fine. What kind of information would you want collected beforehand so you could find out what is actually happening, and why?
lessons.teach: A metric is a number a system records at regular intervals, such as the percentage of CPU in use on a session host or the count of active user sessions. A log is a timestamped record of a single event, such as a failed sign-in or a host that stopped reporting in. Azure Monitor is the service that gathers both kinds of signal from your resources. Diagnostic settings are the per-resource switches that send a resource's metrics and logs to a destination. A Log Analytics workspace is the store where logs land, and you search it with KQL, the Kusto Query Language, which is a read-only query language for log data. An alert rule watches a metric or runs a log query on a schedule and fires when a condition holds. An action group is the list of people or systems notified when an alert fires. Why this works: metrics are small numbers that are cheap to evaluate continuously, so they suit triggers. Logs carry the detail needed to explain a trigger. Alerts are most useful when they combine a threshold with a time window, so one brief spike does not wake anyone. Worked example: you want to know when a host pool is running short of capacity. Step 1: each session host sends its CPU metric to Azure Monitor. Step 2: the alert rule averages CPU across the pool over a 15-minute window. Step 3: if that average stays above 85 percent for the whole window, the rule fires. Step 4: the action group notifies the on-call engineer. A single one-minute spike to 95 percent does not fire it. Common mistake: enabling nothing, then discovering after an outage that no logs exist because diagnostic settings were never turned on, since logs are not recorded retroactively. Consequence: a healthy-looking metric dashboard can hide a sign-in problem that only appears in logs, so on a running system both signals are needed.

questions.prompt: Brightwater Clinic runs a pool called pool-clin-02 with four session hosts. The support team wants to be warned when someone is repeatedly failing to sign in, not on every single typo. Step 1: the administrator turns on diagnostic settings for the pool so sign-in logs are sent to the Log Analytics workspace law-clinic-east, the store where logs land and where they are searched with KQL, a read-only query language. Step 2: a KQL query counts failed sign-in rows in each 30-minute window. Step 3: this step is missing and must be filled in. Step 4: the alert's action group sends a text message to the service desk on-call phone. What belongs in Step 3, where the alert rule decides whether to fire?
choices: The alert rule waits until the clinic closes for the day and then reports every failed sign-in from the past week.
The alert rule copies the sign-in logs back to each session host so the failures are visible on the host's own screen.
The alert rule fires on every individual failed sign-in row as soon as it is written to the workspace.
The alert rule evaluates the count on a schedule and fires only when the count is at least 12 within that 30-minute window.
questions.why: The alert rule runs the log query on a schedule and fires when the stated condition, a count of at least 12 inside the time window, holds, which is what stops one stray typo from paging anyone.

questions.prompt: A user record that says a particular account was locked out at 09:14 on a given day, with the account name and the source address, is best described as which kind of signal?
choices: A log, because it is a timestamped record of a single event.
A metric, because it is a number recorded at regular intervals.
An action group, because it lists who should be notified.
A diagnostic setting, because it switches a resource's output on.
questions.why: A timestamped record of one event is a log, while a metric is a number sampled at regular intervals and a diagnostic setting is only the switch that sends data onward.

questions.prompt: A company built dashboards and alert rules for its Azure Virtual Desktop pool but never turned on diagnostic settings. A sign-in outage happened last night and the team now finds no sign-in records to examine. What explains this?
choices: The Log Analytics workspace deleted the records after the outage ended to save space.
Logs are not recorded retroactively, so events from before diagnostic settings were enabled were never stored.
The action group blocked the sign-in records because nobody was listed as a recipient.
The CPU metric replaced the sign-in logs automatically when the dashboard was saved.
questions.why: Diagnostic settings are what send a resource's logs to a store, and since logs are not recorded after the fact, events that happened before the switch was turned on are simply absent.

questions.prompt: An engineer wants to be told when a single session host's memory use is above 90 percent for a sustained period, but does not want a message for a brief spike that clears in a minute. Which design best matches that goal?
choices: Turn off diagnostic settings so the memory metric stops being recorded and no alerts can fire.
Read the memory logs by hand each morning and only act if the number was above 90 percent at that time.
Set a threshold of 90 percent averaged over a time window, and send the alert to a defined action group.
Set the alert to fire on the first sample above 90 percent and send it to every engineer in the company.
questions.why: Combining a threshold with a time window means only a condition that holds across the whole window fires the alert, and the action group defines who is notified.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between a metric and a log in Azure Monitor, give one example of when you would use each to investigate slow remote desktops, and name one limit or cost tradeoff of collecting everything.
lessons.modelAnswer: A metric is a numeric value sampled over time, such as CPU percentage or active session count, and it is cheap to store and evaluate, which makes it good for alert thresholds. A log is a timestamped record of individual events, such as a failed sign-in with its error code, which is more expensive to store and query but explains why something happened. For slow desktops, I would alert on a sustained CPU or session metric to learn that something is wrong, then query the sign-in and connection logs in the workspace to see which users or hosts are failing. The main tradeoff is that collecting everything increases storage and query cost and creates noise, so you should decide which logs answer real operational questions. Also, diagnostic settings must be enabled ahead of time, because logs cannot be recovered after an incident.
rubricPoints: Metrics are numeric samples over time, suited to thresholds and alerts
Logs are timestamped event records, suited to explaining causes
Diagnostic settings must be enabled in advance to collect logs
Collecting everything raises storage, query cost and alert noise

suggested.rationale: Building metric alarms with thresholds and time windows practises the alerting half of this objective, while the Azure-specific console steps are better learned by reading.

lessons.plain: A monitoring workbook is an editable report page built on top of logs and metrics, where you choose which charts, tables and filters appear. Azure Virtual Desktop Insights is a ready-made workbook that shows how a remote desktop environment is doing: how many sessions are active, where connections fail, and how busy each host is. The starting template covers common cases, but every team asks slightly different questions. Customizing means changing that page so it answers your questions, such as which host pool is running hot or which users keep failing to connect, and then sharing that view with the people who need it. The skill is knowing what each part of the page reads from and why, so the page stays accurate when you change it.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a support team wants one screen that shows only the host pool they own, with the same charts as the standard overview, what would you change first: each chart separately, or one setting that filters what every chart reads?
lessons.teach:
A workbook is a page made of sections. Each visible piece, such as a chart or table, is backed by a query, which is a question written in KQL (Kusto Query Language), a read-only language for searching stored logs. The logs live in a Log Analytics workspace, which is a central store that collects log and metric data from your hosts and services. A parameter is a value the reader can pick, such as a dropdown, and any query can use that value as a filter. Azure Virtual Desktop Insights is a workbook template that ships with these parts already wired up.

Why it works: each query reads from the same tables, so one parameter can narrow the whole page at once instead of editing every chart.

Worked example. The support team wants a host pool filter. Step 1: open the Insights template and choose to save a copy, so the original stays untouched. Step 2: add a parameter named HostPool, populated from the host pool names found in the logs. Step 3: edit each query so it keeps only rows whose host pool field matches the parameter. Step 4: check that a chart shows data for one pool, then switch the parameter and confirm the chart changes. Step 5: share the copy with the team.

Common mistake: hard-coding one pool's name inside a query instead of using a parameter. The chart then works for that pool only, and it has to be edited again for every new pool.

Consequence: a copy drifts from the template over time. If a table or field name changes in the logs, a query can quietly return no rows, so a failing host shows up as a healthy empty chart.

A workbook is only as trustworthy as the queries behind its charts, so every customization must be checked against live data.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm runs two AVD host pools: Dispatch-West for warehouse staff and Dispatch-East for dock staff. Its admin copied the Azure Virtual Desktop Insights workbook template (a workbook is a page of charts backed by queries) and kept the original untouched. The admin added a parameter named Pool, a dropdown populated from pool names in the Log Analytics workspace (the central store that collects host and service logs). Each chart query now keeps only rows where the host pool field matches Pool. The admin selected Dispatch-West and saw session counts appear. The one remaining step before sharing the copy with the warehouse managers is: ___. Which step completes the check?
choices: Switch Pool to Dispatch-East and confirm the charts change to that pool's numbers
Delete the original template so that only the copy remains in the subscription
Set the chart refresh rate to once per second so the numbers look current
Rename every query so it contains the word Dispatch-West, making the names match
questions.why: Switching the parameter to a second pool and seeing the charts change proves that the filter actually drives the queries, which is the live-data check every customized workbook needs.

questions.prompt: In a workbook, what is a parameter?
choices: A value the reader picks, such as from a dropdown, that any query on the page can use as a filter
The read-only query language, KQL, used to search the stored logs
The Log Analytics workspace where the host and service logs are stored
A saved copy of the Azure Virtual Desktop Insights template kept for later edits
questions.why: A parameter is a reader-selectable value, such as a dropdown choice, that queries can use to narrow the data shown, which is different from the workspace, the copy, or the language itself.

questions.prompt: A team copies a workbook and builds a chart for a new host pool called Finance-Pool-2. The chart is a flat empty line even though the hosts are healthy. The query filters rows where the host pool field equals the text Finance-Pool-1, typed directly into the query. What is the most likely cause and the right fix?
choices: Turn on read-write mode for KQL so the query can match the new pool name
The query hard-codes one pool's name, so it can only match Finance-Pool-1; replace the typed name with a parameter that the reader selects
Workbooks cannot display empty charts, so the hosts must be offline and need restarting
The Log Analytics workspace is too large, so split it into two workspaces
questions.why: Hard-coding a name makes the query match only that one pool, so a different pool returns no rows; the fix is to filter on a parameter so any pool can be selected.

questions.prompt: After a platform update, a table name in the logs changes. A copied workbook query still uses the old table name and its chart goes blank. Which risk does this blank chart create?
choices: The whole workbook shows an error banner and stops rendering its other charts
The logs covered by the old table name are deleted from the workspace
The workbook automatically reverts to the original template and loses the customization
A failing host can look like a healthy empty chart, so the problem goes unnoticed
questions.why: Because the query silently returns no rows when a table or field name no longer matches, a real fault appears as an empty chart that looks normal, which is why every copy must be checked against live data.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what customizing an Azure Virtual Desktop Insights workbook means compared with building a brand-new workbook from scratch, and name one limit or tradeoff of customizing it.
lessons.modelAnswer: Customizing starts from the Insights template, which already has the queries, data sources and layout for session hosts, connections and performance. You save a copy, then change parameters, filters and individual queries so the page answers your team's questions, such as one host pool or one region. Building from scratch means writing every query and layout yourself, which takes longer and risks missing signals the template already gathers. The main tradeoff is drift. Your copy no longer updates when the template changes, so you must review it after updates. Also, if the underlying log table or field names change, your edited queries can return empty results without an error, so a broken chart can look like a healthy system. Check each customized chart against known data before relying on it.
rubricPoints: Customizing means copying the built-in Insights template and changing parameters, filters or queries rather than starting from nothing.
Parameters let one control filter many queries, which avoids hard-coding values.
A named limit or tradeoff, such as copies drifting from template updates.
A risk such as silent empty charts when log table or field names change, so charts must be validated.

suggested.rationale: Workbook customization is mostly console and portal steps plus query concepts, and no listed mission or planned engine practises it directly.

lessons.plain: Capacity means how much work a machine can do before it slows down. In Azure Virtual Desktop, each session host is a virtual machine that many people share at once. Optimizing capacity and performance means choosing how big those machines are, how many people each one should take, and checking whether they keep up. Too few people per host wastes money on machines that sit idle. Too many makes everyone's screen lag and logons take minutes. The goal is a steady, comfortable load with some room left for busy moments. Think of a bus: a nearly empty bus wastes fuel, and one packed to the doors is slow and uncomfortable for everyone on board.
lessons.guessPrompt: Ten office workers share one small virtual machine. At 9 AM everyone logs in and the desktops feel sluggish. Before reading anything, what would you check first, and what would you change?
lessons.teach:
Definitions. A session host is the virtual machine that runs users' desktop sessions. A host pool is a group of session hosts that serve the same kind of desktop. The max session limit is the number of user sessions allowed on one session host. Load balancing decides where a new sign-in lands: breadth-first spreads users across hosts, while depth-first fills one host before opening the next. Headroom is the unused share of CPU and memory kept free for spikes, and a peak is the busiest short period, often the morning logon rush.

Why it works. Each session uses a slice of the host's CPU, memory, and disk. These resources are finite, so the host's real capacity is set by its most constrained resource during peak, not by its average over the day. A host that looks comfortable on average can still stall during the 9 AM logon rush.

Worked example. A host has 4 vCPUs. At peak, 6 sessions run and CPU sits at 90 percent. Each session averages about 0.6 vCPU, so 6 sessions need 3.6 of the 4 vCPUs, which is 90 percent. Keeping 25 percent headroom means keeping the load at or under 75 percent, which is 3.0 vCPU, or 5 sessions. So the max session limit should be 5, not 6.

Common mistake. Setting the limit from a single test user, or from average CPU across a whole day. Peaks during logon are what users feel.

Consequence. When a host runs out of CPU or memory, logons slow, sessions freeze, and users can be disconnected. Measured sizing of the VM and the session limit addresses the root cause, and simply adding hosts is not always the right answer.

questions.prompt: A clinic runs a session host with 8 vCPUs. At the morning peak, each user session averages 0.5 vCPU, and the team wants to keep 25 percent headroom. Step 1: the usable ceiling is 75 percent of 8, which is 6.0 vCPU. Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: this gives a max session limit of 12. Which choice correctly fills the missing Step 2?
choices: Multiply the 8 vCPUs by 0.5 to get 4 sessions, then double that figure to allow for the logon rush.
Divide the 6.0 usable vCPU by the 0.5 vCPU each session uses at peak to get the number of sessions that fit.
Add 25 percent to the 6.0 vCPU ceiling to get 7.5 vCPU, then set the limit to 7 sessions.
Use the host's overnight average CPU instead of the peak figure, because it reflects a typical day.
questions.why: Dividing the usable ceiling by the peak per-session CPU use gives how many sessions fit before the host reaches its headroom limit, which is what the max session limit should be.

questions.prompt: A pool's sizing notes say each host keeps 20 percent headroom. What does that 20 percent represent?
choices: The number of new user sessions the host is allowed to accept in one minute.
The unused share of CPU and memory kept free so the host can absorb spikes such as the morning logon rush.
The share of active sessions that are moved to a different host during planned maintenance.
The share of the host's disk space reserved for operating system updates each month.
questions.why: Headroom is defined in the teaching text as the unused share of CPU and memory kept free for spikes, so the 20 percent is spare capacity, not disk or session movement.

questions.prompt: A dental office's session host averages 30 percent CPU across the working day but reaches 95 percent between 8:45 and 9:15 AM. Which load figure should be used to set the max session limit?
choices: The 30 percent daily average, because it covers the full working day and is the most stable number.
The 95 percent reading at the peak, because the host's real capacity is set by its most constrained resource during peak.
The lowest CPU reading recorded overnight, since the host is idle at that time and shows its base load.
The CPU use of one test user signing in alone, since it shows what a single session needs.
questions.why: The teaching text says real capacity is set by the most constrained resource during peak rather than by the daily average or a single user, so the peak reading is the figure to size against.

questions.prompt: A team's session host freezes every morning at about 9 AM. Logs show CPU and memory both near their limits during that window, while the daily average looks fine. Which first response best matches the approach in the teaching text?
choices: Turn off all headroom reserves so every host can run close to full CPU during the logon rush, since that uses the hardware fully and avoids waste.
Ignore the freezes, since the daily average shows the host has spare capacity most of the time.
Size the VM and the session limit from the measured peak load, rather than assuming another host is needed.
Raise the max session limit so that more users share the host's spare capacity during quiet hours.
questions.why: The teaching text says measured sizing of the VM and session limit addresses the root cause of peak-time stalls, and that adding hosts is not always the right answer.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks how to decide the maximum sessions per host for a new host pool. Explain your approach in your own words, and name one tradeoff of setting the limit high versus low.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by measuring rather than guessing. I would run a realistic pilot group on a host of the chosen size and record CPU, memory, and disk during the busiest period, especially the morning logon window. From that I would work out what one typical session uses at peak, then divide the usable capacity, leaving roughly a quarter as headroom for spikes, to get a session count. That number becomes the max session limit. The tradeoff is cost against experience. A high limit packs users onto fewer, cheaper hosts, but if it is too high, users see slow logons and frozen apps at peak. A low limit gives a smoother experience but leaves more hosts running and costing money while they sit partly idle. After go-live I would keep watching the metrics and adjust the limit or VM size if the real pattern differs from the pilot.
rubricPoints: Measure real peak usage such as CPU, memory and disk, especially during logon, rather than guessing or using one test user.
Convert measured per-session use into a session count, leaving headroom for spikes.
Name the tradeoff: a high limit saves cost but risks slow sessions, while a low limit is smoother but leaves more idle capacity.
Continue monitoring after go-live and adjust the limit or VM size when real usage differs.

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a sizing scenario with real numbers adds the most here, because the skill is choosing a defensible session limit under peak load.

lessons.plain: Autoscaling means the number of virtual machines serving users grows and shrinks on its own as demand changes. In Azure Virtual Desktop, a group of session hosts (the virtual machines users sign in to) is called a host pool. Running too many machines wastes money, while running too few leaves users waiting or unable to connect. An autoscaling rule watches the load and the time of day, then starts or stops machines within set limits so the pool is about the right size for the moment. Think of a shop that opens extra tills at lunchtime and closes them at night.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose a pool of 10 machines is nearly empty at 3 a.m. and crowded at 9 a.m. What would you want the system to do on its own, and what could go wrong if it only added machines after users complained that they could not sign in?
lessons.teach:
A host pool is a set of session hosts, which are virtual machines that users sign in to. Autoscaling here is done with a scaling plan, a resource you attach to a pooled host pool. The plan runs on a schedule divided into phases: ramp-up, peak, ramp-down and off-peak. Each phase sets a load balancing method (whether sessions fill one host before the next or spread across hosts), a capacity threshold (the percentage of available session slots in use that triggers starting another host), and a minimum percentage of hosts that stay running. Ramp-down can also say how users on a host being shut down are treated, for example by warning them and then signing them out.

Why it works: the plan does not guess at load. It compares current sessions with the slots that running hosts offer. When usage crosses the threshold, it powers on another host. When load falls, it drains hosts, meaning it stops placing new sessions on them and shuts them down once they are empty or their users have been logged off.

Worked example: a pool has 10 hosts, each allowing 5 sessions, so 50 slots. The capacity threshold is 80 percent. At 9:00 the ramp-up phase begins with 3 hosts running, giving 15 slots. Eight sessions are active, which is 53 percent, so nothing changes. At 9:30 there are 13 sessions, which is about 87 percent of 15. That is above 80 percent, so the plan powers on a fourth host, adding 5 slots.

Common mistake: assuming the plan can start and stop machines without permission. The scaling service needs a role assignment over the host pool's virtual machines, and without it hosts never power on.

Consequence: if the minimum host percentage is set too low, the pool may begin the morning with too few machines running. Booting hosts takes time, so sign-ins queue or fail during the rush. Autoscaling is only as good as its thresholds, its schedule and the permissions behind it.

questions.prompt: A pool at a dental clinic has 6 session hosts, and each host allows 4 sessions, so the whole pool has 24 slots. The capacity threshold is 75 percent. At 8:00 the ramp-up phase begins with 2 hosts running, which gives 8 available slots. At 8:20 there are 7 active sessions. Step 1: 7 out of 8 slots is 87.5 percent. Step 2: 87.5 percent is above the 75 percent threshold, so the plan starts another host. Step 3: the plan recounts the slots available once that host is running. How many slots does it count at that point?
choices: 4 slots, because only the new host's own capacity is counted
24 slots, because the plan always counts every host in the pool
12 slots, because the 3 running hosts each allow 4 sessions
8 slots, because the new host is not counted until its users have signed in
questions.why: The plan counts slots only from hosts that are running, so 3 running hosts times 4 sessions each gives 12 slots.

questions.prompt: In a scaling plan, what does it mean to drain a session host during ramp-down?
choices: The host is set to accept only new sessions, and it is shut down once it is empty or its users have been logged off
The host is removed from the host pool permanently and its virtual machine is deleted
The host is restarted so its disk can be cleaned up before the next peak
The host is moved to a different phase so the threshold no longer applies to it
questions.why: Draining means the plan stops placing new sessions on the host and shuts it down after its users are gone, as described in the teaching text.

questions.prompt: A host pool has 12 running session hosts. Each host allows 6 sessions, so there are 72 slots. The capacity threshold for the current phase is 70 percent. There are 52 active sessions. Will the scaling plan power on another host?
choices: Yes, but only when the next phase begins, since thresholds are checked once per phase
No, because 52 sessions is below the 72 slots, so no threshold has been crossed
No, because the threshold applies to the whole subscription rather than the host pool
Yes, because 52 out of 72 is about 72 percent, which is above the 70 percent threshold
questions.why: 52 divided by 72 is about 72 percent, which is above 70 percent, so the plan compares usage with the threshold and powers on another host.

questions.prompt: A scaling plan is attached to a pooled host pool, but the scaling service has no role assignment over the pool's virtual machines. What happens during the morning ramp-up?
choices: The plan starts the hosts anyway, because any resource attached to a host pool has the rights to power on its machines
The hosts power on at the peak phase instead, because permissions are only checked at peak
The plan works normally, but users are signed out during ramp-down instead of warned first
The hosts never power on, so the plan cannot add capacity even when usage crosses the threshold
questions.why: The scaling service needs a role assignment over the virtual machines to start them, and without it hosts never power on, as the teaching text explains.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how an autoscaling scaling plan decides when to start or stop session hosts, and name one limit or tradeoff that comes from setting its thresholds too low or too high.
lessons.modelAnswer: The scaling plan is attached to a pooled host pool and follows a schedule split into phases such as ramp-up, peak, ramp-down and off-peak. In each phase it compares the sessions in use with the total slots on the running hosts. If usage passes the phase's capacity threshold, it powers on another host. When load drops, it drains hosts so they take no new sessions, then shuts them down once they are empty or their users are logged off. The tradeoff is cost against user experience. A low threshold or a low minimum host count saves money but leaves little headroom, so a sudden surge causes queued or failed sign-ins while new hosts boot. A high threshold or a high minimum keeps capacity ready but leaves machines idle and billed. The plan also needs permission to manage the virtual machines, or the rules do nothing.
rubricPoints: Describes a scaling plan attached to a pooled host pool, with schedule phases.
Explains that capacity is measured as sessions against available slots, compared to a threshold.
Explains draining: no new sessions, then shutdown once hosts are empty or logged off.
Names a tradeoff between cost (idle hosts) and sign-in risk (too few hosts during a surge).

suggested.rationale: Tuning thresholds and seeing how a schedule reacts to load is best learned by running a simulated autoscaling policy, which the planned autoscale engine would provide.

lessons.plain: Azure Virtual Desktop lets people use Windows desktops and single apps that run on servers in the cloud. Once it is running, someone has to watch who is connected right now, decide what happens to their open work, and control which apps and desktops each person can see. This objective covers those live, day-to-day controls: looking at active sessions, sending people messages, disconnecting or signing them out, pausing a server so it takes no new users, and deciding which apps and desktops are handed out through application groups. Think of a shared office building where a manager checks who is inside, asks people to save their work before a repair, and decides who gets which room key.
lessons.guessPrompt: A server hosts 20 people's remote desktops. One person's laptop goes to sleep and their connection drops, but their work is still open on the server. Should the administrator end that person's session right away, or leave it alone? What would you think about first?
lessons.teach:
A session is one user's connection to a remote desktop or app. A session host is the virtual machine that runs those sessions. A host pool is a group of session hosts that serve the same users. An application group is the list of what a user may open: either one full desktop or a set of published apps. Users reach their application groups through a workspace, which is the catalogue they sign in to. A broker is the service that decides which session host a new user connects to.

Live sessions have three states that matter for daily control. A connected session has a user actively using it. A disconnected session is still running on the host, with its apps and unsaved work still alive, but nobody is attached to it. A signed-out session has ended, and anything unsaved is normally lost. So disconnecting keeps work safe, while signing out is a deliberate end. Before taking action, an administrator can send a message to affected users so they have a chance to save.

Drain mode is the tool for taking a session host out of rotation. When a host is in drain mode, the broker stops sending it new sessions, but existing sessions keep running. This lets you patch or restart a host without cutting people off mid-task. Application group assignments work differently: assigning an application group to a user or a directory group controls what appears in that person's workspace, and removing the assignment hides the apps from future sign-ins.

Worked example: a host has six sessions and needs a restart. Step 1: enable drain mode so no new users land there. Step 2: message the six users to save work. Step 3: watch the active count fall as people sign out or disconnect. Step 4: for any disconnected session that will not clear, sign it out after giving notice. Step 5: restart the host, then turn drain mode off.

Common mistake: restarting a host straight away, or signing out sessions without warning, which loses unsaved work. In a running system, users see sudden errors, and a host left in drain mode and forgotten sits idle while the others fill up. Safe session management means warning first, draining before maintenance, and reversing drain mode afterwards.

questions.prompt: A support team must apply a security patch to session host ops-vm-12 in their Azure Virtual Desktop host pool. Four people are connected and three sessions are disconnected. The plan is: Step 1, turn on drain mode for ops-vm-12 so the broker stops sending it new sessions. Step 2, send all seven users a message asking them to save their work within 20 minutes. Step 3 is missing. Step 4, install the patch and restart the host. What belongs in Step 3?
choices: Turn drain mode off so the patch can be tested with live users.
Restart the host straight away, because drain mode already stops new sign-ins.
Wait for the session count to fall, then sign out any disconnected session that will not clear after notice.
Sign out all seven sessions at once, since the warning has already been sent.
questions.why: Step 3 is the wait-and-clear stage: the admin watches the count drop, and only after giving notice signs out disconnected sessions that remain, before the restart in Step 4.

questions.prompt: What is a disconnected session?
choices: A session still running on its host with its apps alive, but with no user attached to it.
A session that has ended, where any unsaved work is normally lost.
An application group that a user cannot see in their workspace.
A session the broker has refused to place on any host in the pool.
questions.why: The teaching text defines a disconnected session as one still running on the host with apps and unsaved work alive, but with nobody attached.

questions.prompt: A team lead at a law firm removes the assignment of the Case Research application group from the directory group Paralegals-East, which has 14 members. Which statement describes the result correctly?
choices: The host pool moves all 14 members to a different host automatically.
The host those members use is placed into drain mode by the change.
Every open session belonging to those 14 members is signed out at once.
The apps stop appearing in those members' workspaces from their next sign-in onward.
questions.why: The text says removing an application group assignment hides the apps from future sign-ins, and it does not describe any effect on hosts or open sessions.

questions.prompt: A host in a 30-session pool at a logistics company has nine sessions on it, several with unsaved spreadsheets open. The admin restarts the host without turning on drain mode or sending a message. What is the most likely outcome?
choices: Users with unsaved work can lose it, and the broker may keep placing new users on the host while it restarts.
The restart is blocked until every user saves and signs out on their own.
The host automatically moves all nine sessions to another host without any loss.
Nothing happens, because restarts never affect users who are signed in.
questions.why: Restarting without drain mode or notice risks losing unsaved work, and without drain mode the broker can still send new sessions to a host that is about to go down.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks why you would put a session host in drain mode instead of just restarting it, and whether disconnecting a user is the same as signing them out. Explain the difference in your own words, and name one limit or tradeoff of drain mode.
lessons.modelAnswer: Drain mode stops the broker from sending new sessions to a host, but it leaves existing sessions running. That lets you restart or patch the host without cutting people off mid-task. Restarting directly would end every session on it, and people would lose unsaved work. Disconnecting and signing out are different. A disconnected session keeps running on the host with its open work, so the user can reconnect later. A signed-out session has ended, and unsaved work is usually lost. The main limit of drain mode is that it does nothing about sessions already running, so you still have to wait for them to end or sign them out with notice. Also, a host left in drain mode by mistake stays idle and reduces capacity for everyone else, so someone must turn it back on.
rubricPoints: Drain mode stops new sessions on a host but keeps existing sessions running
Disconnecting keeps the session and unsaved work alive; signing out ends it and usually loses unsaved work
Restarting a host without draining cuts off active users
Drain mode leaves existing sessions in place, so they must still end or be signed out, and a forgotten drain reduces capacity

suggested.rationale: Telling a disconnect, a sign-out and a drain apart in a live-incident situation is best practised by reasoning through a scenario, since no listed mission covers Azure Virtual Desktop sessions.

lessons.plain: Session hosts are the shared virtual computers people log into remotely to get their desktop. Like any computer they need operating system patches, security fixes and updated apps, but you cannot simply restart them whenever you like because people are working on them. An update strategy is your plan for getting those changes onto every host while users keep working. It covers when the updates happen, how many hosts change at once, how you stop new people arriving on a host that is being changed, and how you check the new version works before moving on. A good plan balances getting fixes out quickly against the risk of disrupting people or running short of capacity.
lessons.guessPrompt: You manage 10 session hosts that all serve users during the working day, and a security fix must reach all of them this week. Without any further reading, what would you do to avoid cutting people off mid-task, and roughly how many hosts would you change at a time?
lessons.teach:
A session host is a virtual machine that users connect to, and a host pool is a group of identical session hosts. Updating a host pool usually means one of two approaches. You can patch the running machines in place, or you can build a new image (a saved template of a complete machine, with the change already included) and replace the old machines with copies made from it. Replacing is generally preferred for fleets because every host ends up identical, and rollback is simply pointing the pool back at the previous image version.

Drain mode is the key control for doing this safely. It tells the pool that a host should accept no new sessions while the existing ones finish. Users already connected can keep working until they sign out, or you can send them a notification and force a sign-out after a delay. A maintenance window is a scheduled period, often overnight, when disruptive work is allowed.

Worked example: a pool of 10 hosts needs a new image. Step 1: publish the new image version. Step 2: put 2 hosts into drain mode. Step 3: wait until their sessions end, or notify those users and sign them out. Step 4: rebuild those 2 hosts from the new image. Step 5: check that they register as healthy and that a test sign-in works. Step 6: repeat with the next pair. Only 2 of 10 hosts are out at any moment, so 80 percent of capacity stays available.

Common mistake: patching live hosts while users are connected, or draining too many hosts at once so nobody can sign in during peak hours. In a running system, forced sign-outs lose unsaved work, and a capacity shortage looks to users like the whole service is down. User profile data is kept separately in profile containers, so replacing a host does not erase a person's settings, which is what makes replacement practical.

questions.prompt: A firm runs a pool of 6 session hosts for a call centre. It is moving from image version 3.0 to image version 3.1, and the team follows this sequence. Step 1: publish image version 3.1. Step 2: put host 1 into drain mode, which stops new sessions reaching it while existing sessions finish. Step 3: wait until host 1's sessions end, or notify those users and sign them out after a delay. Step 4: rebuild host 1 from image 3.1. Step 5: host 1 registers with the pool but fails its test sign-in. Step 6: [missing]. Which action belongs in the missing step?
choices: Skip the test and move on to host 2 because registration succeeded
Patch host 1 in place with the fix while users stay connected
Drain the other five hosts at once so the fix lands faster
Point the pool back at image version 3.0 and rebuild host 1 from it
questions.why: When a replaced host fails its check, the recovery is rollback, which means pointing the pool back at the previous image version and rebuilding from it, rather than patching live machines or draining more hosts at once.

questions.prompt: In a host pool, what is the main job of drain mode?
choices: It stops new sessions reaching a host while already-connected users finish their work
It copies the host's disk to a backup store before any change is made
It forces every connected user to sign out immediately and reboots the host
It deletes the host's user profiles so the new image can be applied cleanly
