questions.why: Drain mode tells the pool to accept no new sessions on that host while existing sessions are allowed to end, which keeps the change from interrupting people mid-work.

questions.prompt: A pool has 8 session hosts and must keep at least 6 available during business hours. What is the most hosts that can be in drain mode at the same time without breaking that rule?
questions.why: Eight hosts minus the six that must stay available leaves two, so no more than two hosts can be drained at once.

questions.prompt: Why is replacing session hosts from a new image usually preferred over patching live machines in a fleet?
choices: Replaced hosts keep the old users' sign-in sessions, so nobody is logged out
Every host ends up identical, and rollback is just pointing the pool back at the previous image version
Patching is not allowed by the operating system on session hosts
It removes the need for a scheduled maintenance window entirely
questions.why: Building every host from one image keeps the fleet identical, and reverting to the earlier image version is a simple pool setting, whereas in-place patching leaves hosts in different states that are harder to undo.

lessons.explainPrompt: Your team runs a 40-host pool that must receive a critical security fix within 48 hours, but the business says no user should lose unsaved work during working hours. Explain to a teammate how you would recommend an update strategy, and name the main limit or tradeoff of the approach you choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would recommend replacing hosts with a new image rather than patching them in place, so every host ends up identical and rollback is just reverting to the previous image. I would update in small batches, perhaps four or five hosts at a time. Each batch goes into drain mode so it accepts no new sessions, and I wait for existing users to sign out or give them a notification and a sign-out deadline. Then I rebuild the batch, check health, and move on. Scheduling the work in an out-of-hours maintenance window reduces disruption. The main tradeoff is time: 48 hours is tight, so batches must be sized so enough capacity remains while the rollout finishes, and if drain periods are long, the fix arrives late. I would tell the business that speed and zero disruption pull against each other, and that the batch size is where we decide between them.
rubricPoints: Explains replacing hosts from a new image versus patching in place, and why replacement suits a fleet
Describes drain mode and a maintenance window to protect active users
Names batching to keep capacity available during the rollout
States a real tradeoff between speed of the fix and user disruption or capacity

suggested.rationale: Choosing between rolling, batched and side-by-side replacement with capacity limits is a deployment-strategy decision that the planned deploy-shift engine would exercise directly.

lessons.plain: A disaster recovery plan is a written set of decisions about how a service comes back after something large breaks, such as a failed datacenter region or an accidentally deleted storage account. For Azure Virtual Desktop, the service that gives people their remote desktops, you own several pieces: the virtual machines users log into, the file share that holds their profiles, the network, and the images used to build machines. The plan states how quickly you must be working again, how much recent data you can afford to lose, and which pieces are rebuilt in a second place versus copied there ahead of time.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company says the remote desktop service must be back within 4 hours of an outage, and no more than 1 hour of user profile changes may be lost. Before reading anything, which parts of the setup would you expect to need copies somewhere else, and which could simply be rebuilt?
lessons.teach: Recovery time objective (RTO) is the longest acceptable time from an outage to users working again. Recovery point objective (RPO) is the most data, measured as time, you can afford to lose; an RPO of one hour means your copies must be no more than one hour behind the live data. These two numbers drive every other choice in the plan. Split your components into two groups. Disposable parts, such as session host virtual machines, can be rebuilt from a known-good image and a deployment template, so the plan only needs those two things stored safely in a second location. Stateful parts, such as the file share holding FSLogix profile containers, contain user data that cannot be recreated, so they need replication or copies in a second region, and the replication lag sets your real RPO. Identity is a dependency too: if users cannot sign in, nothing else helps, so the plan must confirm where sign-in works during the outage. Worked example. Requirement: RTO 4 hours, RPO 1 hour. Step 1: profile storage replicates to a second region with a lag of about 15 minutes, which meets the RPO. Step 2: the image copy is stored in the second region, and a template recreates the host pool and session hosts in about 2 hours, which meets the RTO. Step 3: a runbook names who declares the disaster, the order of steps, and how users are informed. Step 4: a practice failover measures the real time, which is compared with the 4 hour target. Common mistake: keeping the only image copy in the failed region, or writing the plan without ever testing it. In a running system, if the image or template is unavailable, rebuilding is impossible and the recovery time has no upper bound. A disaster recovery plan is only as good as the copies and tests that make it real.

questions.prompt: Recovery time objective (RTO) is the longest acceptable time from an outage until users are working again. Recovery point objective (RPO) is the most data, measured as time, that you can afford to lose. A regional dental practice group runs Azure Virtual Desktop in West Europe with a paired region, North Europe, as its disaster recovery site. Its requirement is RTO 3 hours and RPO 30 minutes. Step 1: the profile share replicates to North Europe with a lag of 20 minutes, which meets the 30 minute RPO. Step 2: copies of the session host image are stored in North Europe, and a deployment template rebuilds the host pool in about 90 minutes, which meets the 3 hour RTO. Step 3: [missing]. Which missing step completes the plan?
choices: Increase the replication lag on the profile share to 60 minutes so storage costs fall.
Confirm where user sign-in still works during the West Europe outage, because identity is a dependency that must be available for any recovery to help users.
Keep the session host image only in West Europe, because it is the primary region.
Add more session hosts to the North Europe pool so that users see a faster sign-in.
questions.why: Users cannot work if they cannot sign in, so the plan must confirm where sign-in works during the outage, and the other options either weaken the RPO, rely on the failed region, or do not address the dependency.

questions.prompt: A freight company requires an RPO of 15 minutes for the user profile storage that holds its drivers' application settings. Its replication to a second region has a lag that averages 40 minutes. Which statement is correct?
choices: The real RPO is about 40 minutes, so the plan does not meet the 15 minute requirement and the replication needs a shorter lag.
The RPO is unaffected by replication because it only measures how fast the session hosts rebuild.
The replication meets the requirement because the lag is under one hour.
The lag is acceptable because the RTO is the only number that matters for stateful data.
questions.why: RPO is the most data you can lose measured as time, and with replication the lag sets the real RPO, so a 40 minute lag fails a 15 minute target.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm keeps its only copy of the approved session host image in the same region as its production host pool. That region suffers a full outage lasting several days. What is the most accurate consequence for recovery?
choices: Recovery is only slower by the time it takes to copy the image back, which is a fixed and known delay.
Rebuilding is impossible while the image is unavailable, so the recovery time has no upper bound.
Users can continue working on existing sessions because the image is only needed at sign-in.
The host pool can be rebuilt in a few minutes from the surviving profile share.
questions.why: Session hosts are disposable parts that must be rebuilt from a stored image and template, so if that image is only in the failed region, rebuilding cannot happen and the recovery time cannot be bounded.

questions.prompt: A university runs three components for its virtual desktop service: a pool of session hosts built from a template, a file share that stores student coursework uploads, and a licence server that can be reinstalled from a vendor installer. Which component needs replication or a copy in a second region?
choices: The licence server, because a vendor installer can always be trusted to rebuild it at the exact same state.
The session host pool, because its virtual machines are the most expensive part of the service.
None of them, because the session host template already contains everything needed to restore data.
The coursework file share, because it holds user data that cannot be recreated from an image or template.
questions.why: Stateful parts contain user data that cannot be recreated and need replication or second region copies, whereas disposable parts such as session hosts and reinstallable tools can be rebuilt from stored images and templates.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would protect an Azure Virtual Desktop deployment against a regional outage, covering the session hosts and the profile storage. Name one limit or tradeoff of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by agreeing the RTO and RPO with the business, since those numbers decide everything else. Session hosts are disposable, so I would keep the golden image and the deployment template in a second region and rebuild hosts there when needed. That is cheaper than running standby machines, but the recovery time includes the rebuild, so it can be longer than the target. The profile storage holds data that cannot be rebuilt, so I would replicate it to the second region; the replication lag determines the actual RPO, and I would measure it rather than assume it. The main tradeoff is cost against speed: keeping warm standby hosts shortens recovery but costs money every day. I would also make sure identity is reachable during the outage and write a runbook that someone other than me could follow, then test it with a practice failover.
rubricPoints: Defines RTO and RPO and uses them to drive the design
Separates disposable components, rebuilt from images, from stateful data, which must be replicated
Notes that identity must remain reachable during a failover
Names a tradeoff such as cost versus recovery speed, or rebuild time versus standby capacity
Mentions testing the plan with a practice failover

suggested.rationale: A disaster-recovery planner engine would make the learner set RTO and RPO targets and check which components can be rebuilt versus must be replicated, which is the core skill of this objective.

lessons.plain: Multi-region planning is deciding where your remote desktops should run when users are spread across the world. A cloud region is a data-centre area in one geographic place. One region means distant users feel lag, and one regional outage stops everyone at once. Planning means choosing regions, assigning users to them, and making sure their profile and apps exist in each place. You weigh speed, data-location rules, cost and how much regional failure you can tolerate.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company has staff in London and Singapore, and all of its remote desktops run in a London data centre. Without any technical detail, what two problems would a Singapore user most likely notice, and what would you change first?
lessons.teach:
Multi-region planning means designing an Azure Virtual Desktop deployment so it runs in more than one Azure region, where a region is a group of data centres in one geographic area. The main reasons are latency (the delay between a keystroke and the screen update, which grows with distance), data-location rules that require some information to stay within an area, and resilience to a regional outage. A host pool is a group of session hosts, the virtual machines users actually work on. An application group is the set of published desktops or apps a user can open, and a workspace is the collection those groups are shown in. In a multi-region design you usually create a host pool with its session hosts in each region, then assign each user group to the pool closest to them.

It works because a remote session only feels responsive when the path between the user and the session host is short, so hosts near users keep the delay low. The user's data must also be close. Profiles built with FSLogix are stored as a container on a file share, and a session host that reads that profile from across the world logs in slowly. So the profile storage, the images and any file shares belong in the same region as the hosts that use them.

Worked example: a company has 300 users in London and 150 in Singapore. Step 1: create a London host pool with its own session hosts and a profile share in London. Step 2: create a Singapore host pool the same way. Step 3: build one master image and publish identical copies to both regions so the desktops match. Step 4: assign the London group to the London pool and the Singapore group to the Singapore pool. A Singapore user now connects to nearby hosts and reads a profile stored locally.

Common mistake: treating multi-region as copying the hosts and forgetting the profile store, so every sign-in reaches back to one distant share. The consequence is that logons take minutes and users report lag even though the desktops are healthy. Multi-region planning is a set of placement decisions, and each one must be checked against where the data lives.

questions.prompt: A design firm has 80 users in Mumbai and 40 users in Frankfurt. Its plan works in four steps. Step 1: create a Frankfurt host pool, meaning a group of session hosts (the virtual machines users work on), with a profile share in Frankfurt; a profile share is a network file location where each user's FSLogix profile container is kept. Step 2: create a Mumbai host pool with its session hosts in Mumbai. Step 3: publish the same master image to both pools so the desktops match. Step 4 is missing from the plan. Which action completes it so that Mumbai users read their profiles from nearby storage?
choices: Create a profile share in Mumbai and point the Mumbai host pool at it.
Create a second master image in Mumbai and publish it only to the Mumbai hosts.
Move the Frankfurt profile share to Mumbai so that Frankfurt users read from Mumbai.
Assign the Frankfurt user group to the Mumbai host pool so both groups share one pool.
questions.why: The Mumbai hosts need profile storage in the same region as themselves, so a Mumbai profile share must exist and be used by that pool, which keeps the read path short.

questions.prompt: In multi-region planning, why should the profile storage sit in the same region as the session hosts that read it?
choices: It removes the need for a workspace to show application groups to users.
It stops the hosts from having to check user identity when a session starts.
It lets one image be published to more regions at the same time.
It keeps the distance between the hosts and the profile data short, so each sign-in loads quickly.
questions.why: A session host that reads a profile from a distant share waits on that long path at every sign-in, so storing the profile locally keeps logons fast.

questions.prompt: A team in Auckland has session hosts in an Auckland host pool, but its FSLogix profile share is in Sydney. Users report that sign-in takes several minutes, while the desktops themselves respond normally once loaded. Which fix addresses the cause?
choices: Create a second workspace that shows the Auckland application groups.
Disable FSLogix so profiles are no longer read from a file share.
Add more CPU cores to each Auckland session host.
Move the profile share to Auckland so it sits in the same region as the hosts.
questions.why: The slow sign-in comes from reading profiles across the distance between Sydney and Auckland, so moving the profile share into the hosts' region removes that delay.

questions.prompt: A company must keep its European users' data inside Europe, and it wants its Asian users connected to nearby hosts. Which design fits both requirements?
choices: A European host pool for European users and an Asian host pool for Asian users, each with its own profile share in its region.
Asian users connected to the European pool because only the European region holds the master image.
One profile share in a US region shared by every host pool so the data stays in one place.
One host pool in a US region for everyone, with Asian users connecting over the longer path.
questions.why: Placing a host pool and its profile share in each user's region satisfies both the data-location rule and the need for short paths, which is the core placement decision in multi-region planning.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide whether a new group of users needs its own region of remote desktops, and name one limit or tradeoff of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by measuring where the users are and how far they sit from the current region, since a long distance usually means noticeable lag. Then I would check whether any data-location rule requires that their information stays in a particular area. If the group is large or the latency is poor, I would plan a host pool and session hosts in a closer region, along with a profile share and images in that same region so sign-in stays fast. The tradeoff is cost and operational effort: every extra region means more session hosts to size, more images to keep in step, and more monitoring to set up. For a small group, it may be cheaper to accept the delay and revisit the decision later.
rubricPoints: Places host pools and session hosts close to the users they serve to reduce latency
Keeps profile storage, images and file shares in the same region as the hosts that use them
Considers data-location or residency rules as a reason to choose a region
Names the cost and operational tradeoff of running more than one region

suggested.rationale: A scenario with users in two or more regions asks the learner to reason through placement and data-location choices, which adds the most here.

lessons.plain: A backup strategy is a written plan for keeping copies of the data you could not afford to lose, and for deciding how quickly you need to get that data back after something goes wrong. For a virtual desktop service, the important data is not the screen people see. It is the user profile settings and documents kept on shared storage, the personal desktops some users keep, and the master images that new desktop machines are built from. Think of it as a fire drill for your files. You decide what matters, how often to copy it, where the copies live, how long to keep them, and whether you have actually tested getting them back. A good plan answers these questions before anything breaks, not in the middle of the emergency.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your virtual desktops can be recreated from a template in about an hour, but users' saved profile settings live on a shared file store. Which needs a backup plan: the template, the profile store, or both? Give one sentence of reasoning.
lessons.teach: Two terms matter first. The recovery point objective (RPO) is the most data loss the business accepts, measured in time: an RPO of 24 hours means losing up to one day of changes is acceptable. The recovery time objective (RTO) is the longest the service may stay down while you restore. A backup vault is a managed container in the cloud that holds backup copies and the rules for how long they are kept. The principle is simple: back up what cannot be recreated from code. A template or image can be rebuilt from version-controlled definitions, so its real protection is keeping the definition in source control. User-created data cannot be rebuilt, so it needs scheduled copies. Worked example: a profile share changes all day, and the business sets an RPO of 24 hours. Step 1: identify the data, which is user-created and irreplaceable. Step 2: match the RPO, so a daily backup at 02:00 is enough. Step 3: set retention, keeping 30 days so a corruption noticed a week later can still be undone. Step 4: test a restore into a separate location and confirm a profile opens. Common mistake: backing up the image but never testing a restore, which means you discover the copies are unusable only during an outage. Consequence: if the share is deleted at 10:00 and the last backup ran at 02:00, users lose eight hours of profile changes, and the restore duration determines how long they wait. A backup plan is only as good as the restore you have rehearsed.

questions.prompt: An accounting firm runs Azure Virtual Desktop with a session host image built from a template stored in version control, and a shared project folder that staff edit all day. The business sets an RPO of 8 hours for the project folder. Step 1: the image template is defined in source control, so it can be rebuilt and its protection is the definition itself. The project folder holds user-created files that cannot be rebuilt, so it needs scheduled copies. Step 2: an 8-hour RPO means a backup every 8 hours is enough. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: run a test restore of the folder into a separate location and confirm a file opens. Which completes Step 3?
choices: Back up the template binaries to the vault as well as source control
Set the RTO to 8 hours so users know the wait
Set retention to one day so storage costs stay low
Set retention to 21 days so a corruption found later can still be reverted
questions.why: Step 3 is retention: keeping copies long enough that a problem noticed after a delay can still be undone, and 21 days fits that purpose for this folder.

questions.prompt: A law firm states that its RPO for client files is 4 hours. Which statement correctly describes what that means?
choices: The longest time the service may stay down during a restore
The most data loss the business accepts, measured in time
The number of hours a restore takes to finish
The number of backup copies kept in the vault
questions.why: RPO is the maximum amount of data loss the business accepts, expressed as a time window, so a 4-hour RPO accepts losing up to four hours of changes.

questions.prompt: A logistics company runs Azure Virtual Desktop. It stores its image pipeline definitions in version control and has a shared folder of scanned delivery documents that staff create each day. Which item needs scheduled copies in a backup vault?
choices: The vault retention setting itself, since it defines how long copies live
The scanned-documents share, because staff created it and it cannot be rebuilt
The built session host disk, because it is the largest item
The image pipeline definitions, which are kept in version control and need no vault copy
questions.why: User-created data that cannot be recreated from code needs scheduled backups, while definitions kept in source control can be rebuilt and so their protection is the version-controlled definition.

questions.prompt: A healthcare scheduling team backs up its profile storage every 6 hours, matches an RPO of 6 hours, and keeps 60 days of copies. It has never run a restore test. What is the main risk if the profile share is deleted?
choices: The backups run too often and waste storage
Nobody knows whether the copies restore or how long a restore takes
Retention of 60 days is too short to be useful
The RPO is set in hours instead of days
questions.why: Without a rehearsed restore the team cannot confirm the copies are usable or how long recovery takes, so it may miss its recovery time objective even though the backup schedule looks correct.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says we do not need backups for the virtual desktops because we can rebuild them from the image. Explain to them what you would back up instead, and name one limit or tradeoff of your plan.
lessons.modelAnswer: The teammate is right about the desktop machines themselves, since they can be recreated from a version-controlled image and template. What cannot be recreated is the data users create: profile settings and documents on the shared profile store, and any personal desktops with unique files. I would schedule backups of that storage, with a frequency that meets the agreed recovery point objective, and keep them in a backup vault with a retention period long enough to undo corruption noticed late. The main tradeoff is cost and recovery time. Frequent backups and long retention raise storage cost, and restoring a large share can take longer than the recovery time objective allows, so I would test a restore and measure it before trusting the plan.
rubricPoints: Distinguishes data that can be rebuilt from code or images from user-created data that needs backup
Connects backup frequency to the recovery point objective and restore speed to the recovery time objective
Mentions retention periods and why they must cover late-discovered corruption
Names a real tradeoff such as storage cost against backup frequency, or restore duration against the time objective

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine covers backup design, and deciding what to protect and why is best shown by explaining the reasoning back.

lessons.plain: Backup means keeping a second copy of something as it was at a set moment, so you can get it back after it is deleted, corrupted, or damaged by a bad change. In Azure Virtual Desktop, three things need this protection: the files that hold each user's profile settings, the virtual machines some users keep as their own desktop, and the master copies used to build new session hosts. Restore is the act of bringing one of those saved copies back into use. A good plan says what is protected, how often copies are taken, how long they are kept, and who can perform a restore.
lessons.guessPrompt: A user's profile file is deleted at 3pm, and backups run every night at 2am. Which backup would you restore from to get the profile back, and what would the user most likely lose?
lessons.teach:
Backup is a saved copy of data taken at a point in time. A restore point is one of those saved moments you can return to. Retention is how long those restore points are kept before they expire. Three things need protecting in an Azure Virtual Desktop setup, and each lives in a different place. FSLogix profile containers are the per-user profile disks, usually VHD or VHDX files, stored on a file share such as Azure Files. Personal desktops are session host virtual machines assigned to one user, so their disks hold that user's work. Images are versioned master copies, often kept in an image gallery, used to build new session hosts. Keeping older image versions lets you roll back a bad build.

Why it works: the backup service copies data on a schedule into a separate vault, and it keeps the copies for the retention period. Because the copies are kept apart from the live data, a deletion or a corruption on the live share does not reach them.

Worked example: a profile share has nightly backups kept for 30 days. On Monday a crash corrupts one user's profile container. Step 1: find the share and the container file name. Step 2: choose the most recent restore point from Sunday night, which is before the corruption. Step 3: restore that one file under a new name, check it opens, then swap it in. Step 4: changes the user made on Monday after the restore point are lost, so tell them.

Common mistake: assuming a backup of a personal desktop also protects profiles. Profiles live on the file share, so the virtual machine backup does not cover them, and the reverse is also true.

Consequence: if a pool has no restore plan, a deleted share or a bad image push can stop every user from signing in until someone rebuilds the environment by hand.

questions.prompt: Harbor Legal runs 30 personal desktops built from an image gallery, which is a store of versioned master copies used to build new session hosts. Version 2024.4 was pushed on Tuesday and broke sign-in for everyone on the new build. Step 1: list the gallery versions and confirm 2024.3 was the last version that worked. Step 2: note that 2024.4 must not be used for new session hosts. Step 3: ______ Step 4: point the pool at the restored version and rebuild the affected session hosts.
choices: Delete version 2024.4 from the gallery so nothing can select it again
Raise the gallery's retention period to 90 days so older versions stay available
Restore the FSLogix profile shares from Monday's backup to undo the sign-in failure
Build new session hosts from version 2024.3, the last version before the fault
questions.why: Rolling back a bad image means building new session hosts from the last good version still kept in the gallery, which is the missing step between confirming that version and pointing the pool at it.

questions.prompt: In backup terms, what does retention mean?
choices: The separate vault where copies are stored apart from live data
The length of time a restore point is kept before it expires
A single saved copy of data taken at one moment
The schedule on which the backup service copies data
questions.why: Retention is the period that restore points are kept before they expire, not the copy itself, the schedule, or the storage location.

questions.prompt: A firm called Brightwater has 40 personal desktops, each backed up nightly as a virtual machine. One user's FSLogix profile container, stored on an Azure Files share, becomes corrupted. Which backup should be used to recover that profile?
choices: The nightly virtual machine backup of the user's personal desktop
A snapshot of the session host's operating system disk
The image gallery version used to build that session host
A restore point from the backup service covering the Azure Files share
questions.why: Profile containers live on the file share, so only a backup of that share covers them, and the desktop's virtual machine backup does not include them.

questions.prompt: A team keeps only the latest image version in its gallery. A bad build is pushed on Friday and breaks sign-in. What is the most likely consequence?
choices: The gallery reverts the pool automatically to a working state
No older version exists to build from, so the pool must be rebuilt by hand
Each user's profile reverts to the state stored in the image
Users can roll back within minutes by picking the prior image version
questions.why: Keeping only the latest image removes the rollback option, so recovery means manually rebuilding the environment, as the consequence of having no restore plan describes.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would protect FSLogix profiles, personal desktops and session host images, and name one limit or tradeoff in your plan.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would treat each one separately because they live in different places. Profile containers sit on a file share, so I would back up that share on a schedule and keep restore points for a set retention period, so I can restore one user's file without touching anyone else. Personal desktops are virtual machines, so I would back up their disks through a recovery vault. Images I would keep as versioned copies in an image gallery, so a bad build can be rolled back to the last good version. The main tradeoff is that longer retention costs more storage, and shorter retention means an older corruption may not have a usable restore point. Also, any work a user did after the last restore point is lost, so the plan does not give a perfect recovery.
rubricPoints: Profiles are protected through the file share where they live, separate from virtual machine backups.
Personal desktops are protected as virtual machines, with a schedule and retention.
Images are kept as versioned copies so a bad build can be rolled back.
Names a real limit: restore points lose changes made after them, and longer retention costs more.

suggested.rationale: Choosing which backup control fits each of three different AVD components is best practised by reasoning through an incident-style scenario, and no listed mission covers backup.

scenarios.title: Brightwater Harbour Legal: Remote Desktop Rollout for 300 Staff
scenarios.scenario: Brightwater Harbour Legal LLP is a fictional law firm with 300 staff across two offices and a large remote workforce. Its IT lead, Priya, has been asked to plan an Azure Virtual Desktop (AVD) deployment, which is a Microsoft service that publishes Windows desktops from Azure virtual machines (VMs) to users' devices. The VMs that users connect to are called session hosts. About 60 users will be connected at the same time at peak. Users work in document software, a case management app, and video calls. Office staff use a corporate LAN with a router that has a single shared outbound link, and remote staff use home broadband with varying quality. Priya must plan three things before the pilot. First, the network: the office link must not be swamped, and remote users need a responsive connection. Second, user profile storage: each user's Windows settings and files must follow them between session hosts, and Priya plans to use FSLogix, a technology that stores the user profile as a container file on a network file share. Third, the session host image: the Windows image used to build the session hosts must be kept patched and must be rebuilt in a repeatable way. Complete the following sub-tasks. 1. Name the connection feature you would plan for remote users to reduce latency, explain what it does in plain terms, and state one QoS (quality of service, a rule that gives certain network traffic priority) setting you would apply on the office link to protect the remote desktop traffic. 2. Recommend the storage type and access method for the FSLogix profile share, and explain why it suits roughly 60 concurrent users. 3. Describe how you would build, store, and roll out an updated session host image so that patches can be applied without editing running session hosts.
subParts: Remote connection feature and QoS setting on the office link
Storage type and access method for the FSLogix profile share
Building, storing, and rolling out an updated session host image
modelAnswer: Plan RDP Shortpath for remote users. RDP Shortpath is a feature that lets the client set up a direct UDP (a fast, connectionless network protocol) path to the session host, instead of routing every frame through the gateway service that normally brokers the connection. Where a direct path can be established, latency and jitter (variation in delay) usually drop. RDP Multipath is a related option that can use more than one path at a time, but for this pilot Shortpath is the core requirement. On the office link, apply a QoS rule that marks AVD traffic with a priority code, so the router serves it ahead of bulk traffic such as large file backups and streaming, for example by matching the traffic on its UDP port range and assigning a high-priority class. Common mistake: enabling Shortpath but blocking outbound UDP on the office firewall, so the feature silently falls back to the gateway path. Consequence: remote users still connect, but latency stays high and the expected improvement never appears.

Recommend an Azure Files Premium file share, because Premium shares give steadier input and output speed (IOPS, the number of read and write operations per second) than standard tiers, and profile loads at logon are many small reads and writes that multiply quickly across 60 concurrent sessions. Use a storage account in the same region as the session hosts, and access the share through a private endpoint (a network interface that gives the storage account a private address inside your virtual network) so profile traffic never crosses the public internet. Authenticate users with the identity method that matches the directory design, and set NTFS and share permissions so each user can only reach their own profile container. Common mistake: choosing a standard-tier share to save cost, which causes slow logons and freezes at peak when many users sign in together. Consequence: users wait minutes at sign-in and the pilot gets a poor first impression.

Build the image with Azure VM Image Builder, which is a managed service that creates a custom image from a written recipe that lists the base Windows image, the customisation steps, and the apps to install. Store the output as a new version in an Azure Compute Gallery, which is a repository inside your subscription that keeps versioned images and can replicate them to other regions. Create the host pool from a specific image version, so you can point the pool at version 2 while keeping version 1 for rollback. For each monthly patch cycle, change the recipe or base image, build a new version, test it in a small pool, then move the rest of the session hosts to the new version by replacing them, not by patching them one by one. Common mistake: logging into a running session host to install updates by hand, which creates drift, meaning hosts end up slightly different from each other and from the image. Consequence: a fault appears on some users' desktops only, and the team cannot reproduce it because no two hosts match.

scenarios.title: Brightwater Dental: contractor, reception and help desk access to shared desktops
scenarios.scenario:
Brightwater Dental Group is a fictional company with 14 clinics. Staff sign in to Azure Virtual Desktop (a managed service that runs Windows desktops in Azure and streams them to users) from clinic PCs and from home. The company runs an older practice-management app that depends on on-premises Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS, the Windows directory that holds user accounts and groups for domain-joined machines), and a newer cloud-only booking app. Three changes are needed this month. Contractors from an outside billing firm must be stopped from connecting unless they prove their identity with multifactor authentication (MFA, a second proof such as an approved phone prompt or key) and use a company-managed device. Reception staff on clinic PCs should sign in without typing a password. A help desk team must restart stuck session hosts (the Azure virtual machines that run user sessions) but must not change host pool settings. Complete the following:
1. Choose the identity scenario for the session hosts, and state the one requirement the session hosts must meet so the practice-management app works.
2. Describe the Microsoft Entra Conditional Access policy you would create for the contractor group, including what it targets and what it requires.
3. Name the passwordless method you would offer reception staff, name the Azure role-based access control (RBAC, which grants a named role to a user or group at a chosen scope) role you would give the help desk, and explain why a broader role would be a mistake.
subParts: Identity scenario and session host requirement
Passwordless sign-in and help desk RBAC role
modelAnswer: The fitting scenario is hybrid join: the session hosts are joined to the on-premises AD DS domain and also registered with Microsoft Entra ID (the cloud directory that holds the sign-in identities). This fits because the practice-management app relies on Kerberos (the Windows login protocol AD DS uses) and on domain group membership. The requirement is that each session host must be domain-joined to the on-premises domain, and user accounts must be synchronised from AD DS to Microsoft Entra ID, usually with Microsoft Entra Connect (the sync tool). Worked example: a receptionist's account exists in AD DS and is synced to Entra ID; the session host is joined to the domain; when she signs in, the app reads her domain group and grants access. Common mistake: choosing Microsoft Entra Domain Services because it sounds like a cloud version of AD DS. It creates a separate managed domain, so the on-premises app would not see the same users and groups without extra setup. Consequence: on the day of go-live, the practice-management app rejects logins or fails its group checks. A Microsoft Entra joined only setup would suit apps that do not need AD DS, but not this one.

A Conditional Access policy is a rule in Microsoft Entra ID that checks who is signing in, from which device and location, and then allows, blocks, or asks for extra proof. For the contractor policy, target the contractor security group as the users and the Azure Virtual Desktop cloud app as the resource. Set the grant controls to require multifactor authentication and to require a device marked as compliant, meaning it is managed (for example through Microsoft Intune, the device management service) and meets company health rules. Start the policy in report-only mode so you can see who would be affected before enforcing it. Worked example: a contractor signs in from a personal laptop; the policy finds the device is not compliant and blocks the connection with a clear message. Common mistake: applying the policy to all users with no exclusions, which can lock out the emergency break-glass admin account (a spare account kept for when normal sign-in fails) or clinic staff. Consequence: reception cannot start desktops during clinic hours until the policy is corrected, and the lockout may also block administrators who need to fix it.

Passwordless authentication means signing in without a typed password. For clinic PCs, Windows Hello for Business fits best: it binds a PIN, fingerprint, or face scan to the specific device, so the credential stays on the machine. A FIDO2 security key (a physical USB or NFC key) is an alternative for shared or roaming use, and a smart card can be used where cards are already issued. For the help desk, assign the built-in Desktop Virtualization Session Host Operator role at the session host scope. It lets them start, stop, and restart session hosts and see sessions, but not change host pool settings. Common mistake: giving Contributor or Owner at the subscription or resource group level. Those roles can change networking, delete the host pool, or grant access to others. Consequence: an accidental delete during a restart fix can take down every desktop in the pool, and an audit would flag the overly broad right.

scenarios.title: Harbor Lane Dental: slow sign-ins and missing apps on shared desktops
scenarios.scenario:
Harbor Lane Dental Group is a fictional company with 140 front-desk and billing staff who sign in to shared Windows desktops hosted in Azure Virtual Desktop. Azure Virtual Desktop is a Microsoft service that runs users' Windows desktops and apps on virtual machines in Azure, called session hosts, which are grouped into a host pool. Because staff move between machines in a pooled host pool, each user's settings are stored in a user profile, which is the folder set (settings, desktop, documents links, and registry hive) that Windows loads at sign-in. The IT lead, Priya, has noticed three problems. First, sign-ins take over six minutes because the profiles are copied from a central file share each time, and some profiles are over 30 GB because Outlook keeps a large local mailbox copy (an OST file, which is an offline cache of the mailbox) and Teams keeps a local cache. Second, the billing team sees a legacy reconciliation tool, which only the finance group is licensed to use, in its Start menu. Third, the file share holding profiles is in the same Azure region as the session hosts, and the network link between them is stable with low delay. FSLogix is a Microsoft technology that attaches a user's profile as a single disk-image file (a container) from a file share at sign-in, instead of copying files one by one. Profile Containers is the FSLogix feature that stores the whole profile in one such container. ODFC, meaning Office Data File Containers, is an FSLogix feature that stores only the Office and Teams data files (such as the Outlook OST and Teams cache) in a separate container, so the profile container stays small. Cloud Cache is an FSLogix mode in which each session host keeps a local cache and writes changes to one or more remote file shares in the background; it is built for slow links, several storage locations, or resilience. Application masking is an FSLogix feature that uses a compiled rule set to hide or show specific installed applications for specific users or groups, without uninstalling them. Priya must answer these sub-tasks for the design review:
1. Recommend which FSLogix containers to enable for the profiles and Outlook and Teams data, and explain how the two containers divide the work.
2. Decide whether Cloud Cache is the right choice for this environment, giving a reason based on the network described.
3. Explain how application masking would hide the reconciliation tool from everyone except the finance group, and state the main risk if the rule is written against the wrong group.
modelAnswer: Enable Profile Containers so each user's full profile is attached as one container from the file share at sign-in, which replaces the slow file-by-file copy. Also enable ODFC so the Outlook OST and Teams cache are stored in a separate Office data container. The two containers split the work: the profile container holds settings and everything else, and the ODFC container holds the large Office and Teams data. Because the Office data is removed from the profile, the profile container stays small and sign-in gets faster, and the mailbox cache still follows the user across session hosts.

Cloud Cache is not the right choice here. Its main purpose is to handle slow or unreliable links and to write to several storage locations at once, with a local copy kept on the session host. The file share is in the same region as the session hosts and the link is stable and low-delay, so standard Profile Containers and ODFC with direct access to the share are simpler and do not add a second layer of background sync that could fall behind. Cloud Cache would only be worth revisiting if the company later spread storage across regions or needed a second copy for resilience.

Application masking uses a rule set that is compiled into a file and applied to the session hosts, so that the reconciliation tool is visible only to members of the finance group. The rule set lists the application and the group allowed to see it, and every other user gets that application hidden from the Start menu and launch paths. The application stays installed, so finance users are unaffected. The main risk is writing the rule against the wrong group, for example a broad group such as all staff, or an incorrectly named group, which would either expose a licensed tool to unlicensed users or hide it from finance so they cannot start it. The fix is to test the rule with one finance account and one billing account before rolling it out to every session host.

scenarios.title: Slow Monday Logons and a Missing Recovery Plan at Harbor Point Claims
scenarios.scenario:
Harbor Point Claims is a fictional insurance company with about 300 staff who work through Azure Virtual Desktop, a Microsoft service that gives users a remote Windows desktop running on virtual machines in Azure. Those virtual machines are called session hosts, and a group of them that serves the same users is called a host pool. The company runs one pooled host pool, named pool-claims, with twelve session hosts that stay on all day, even though most staff sign in between 8 and 9 am and very few sign in after 5 pm. Every Monday, people complain that sign-in takes several minutes. Their user profiles are stored with FSLogix, a tool that keeps each user's settings and files in a single container file on a shared storage location, so the profile follows the user to whichever session host they land on. The company also keeps a custom image, which is a saved template of a session host's operating system and installed apps, used to build new session hosts. Priya, the IT lead, has asked you to write up the following for her.

1. Name the monitoring setup she should use to find out whether the Monday slowness comes from session host capacity (CPU, memory, or disk being saturated) or from slow profile loading. Name the Azure service that collects the data, where that data is stored, and the pre-built dashboard she should open first. Say what she should look for before changing anything.

2. Propose an autoscaling approach for pool-claims that cuts the cost of idle session hosts outside office hours without leaving staff waiting at 8 am. Name the feature that does this, the phases of the schedule you would configure, and the settings that decide how hosts are turned off safely while users are still signed in.

3. Describe a backup and disaster recovery plan that covers the FSLogix profile share, the custom image, and a goal of running the claims desktop in a second Azure region if the primary region becomes unavailable. State the recovery point target and recovery time target you would set, and explain why those numbers fit an office that cannot lose a day of claims work.
subParts: Monitoring setup and first checks for the Monday slowness
Autoscaling approach and safe shutdown settings
Backup and disaster recovery plan with recovery targets
modelAnswer: Use Azure Monitor, which is Azure's shared service for collecting metrics (numbers sampled over time, such as CPU percentage) and logs (event records). Session hosts should send their performance counters and Windows event logs to a Log Analytics workspace, which is a database inside Azure Monitor where log data is stored and searched with queries. Open the Azure Virtual Desktop Insights workbook, which is a pre-built, editable dashboard that reads from that workspace and shows connection and sign-in timings alongside host health. Before changing anything, check the logon time breakdown for Monday between 8 and 9 am. If the delay sits mainly in profile load time, the bottleneck is the FSLogix share or the network path to it, not the number of hosts. If CPU or memory on the session hosts is near its limit during the same window, the bottleneck is capacity. Compare both on the same timeline before deciding.

Use the scaling plan feature for pooled host pools. A scaling plan is a schedule attached to a host pool that starts and stops session hosts automatically based on the number of users and sessions. Define phases for a weekday: ramp-up before 8 am, where enough hosts are started early so they are ready for the rush; peak, the working day, where a minimum share of hosts stays on; ramp-down in the late afternoon, where hosts are drained and then stopped; and off-peak overnight, where only a small minimum is kept. The settings that matter most are the minimum percentage of hosts that stay on, the capacity threshold that triggers starting another host, and the drain behavior at ramp-down. Drain mode stops new sign-ins to a host so its existing sessions can finish. You can also set a notification and a wait time before users are logged off, so their unsaved work is not lost. Apply the plan with the role that allows it to start and stop virtual machines, and confirm that the ramp-up start is early enough for the 8 am peak. The common mistake is to set the minimum too low so early arrivals wait for hosts to boot.

Protect the FSLogix profile share with Azure Backup for Azure Files, which takes scheduled snapshots of the file share and stores them in a Recovery Services vault, a managed backup store. Keep the share on zone-redundant or geo-redundant storage so a single failure does not take it down. For the custom image, keep versions in an Azure Compute Gallery, which is a library that can hold image versions and replicate them to a second region, so a new session host can be built there without relying on the failed region. For regional failure, plan a standby host pool in the second region that stays deployed but scaled to zero or to a minimum, with a replicated copy of the profile share available there. The recovery point target is the most data you can afford to lose, and it should be about one hour for profiles, given that snapshots run hourly during working hours. The recovery time target is the longest time to get staff working again, and a realistic goal is a few hours, because the standby pool has to be started and pointed at the replicated profiles. Explain these numbers in terms of what the business can tolerate, and test a restore before you rely on it.
